ch01.text: Production Rust is valuable because ownership, failure handling, concurrency, and deployment rules become explicit contracts that teams can review before release.
Opening scenario

A payments platform is moving latency-sensitive services to Rust after repeated incidents in resource ownership, failure recovery, and concurrent state updates. The business requirement is direct: make ownership, mutation authority, and fallibility explicit enough for release review before the system grows.
What Rust is asking you to state up front

items: Name the owner of the data or resource.
Say whether the next step only borrows, mutates exclusively, or takes ownership outright.
Make fallibility and concurrency visible where the boundary actually changes.

ch01.text: A reading checklist
Mental model

Rust is not “C++ with a stricter compiler,” “C# without a GC,” or “Go with harder syntax.” The operational model is different: values have owners, borrows describe temporary access, and APIs must state whether they transfer responsibility, share read access, or require exclusive mutation.

items: Ownership says who is responsible for cleanup.
Borrowing says who may access a value temporarily.
Traits describe behavior; generics usually compile via monomorphization rather than dynamic dispatch.
Thread boundaries carry trait requirements like Send and Sync.

ch01.text: Core concepts
Rust’s core promise: control without unsafety by default

Rust wants C-like control over layout, allocation, and destruction while keeping memory unsafety out of ordinary code. Safe Rust rules out use-after-free, double-free, and data races in the safe subset. When low-level work truly needs escape hatches, you use unsafe in small, auditable regions and document the invariants there.
Zero-cost abstractions in practice

“Zero-cost” does not mean “free magic.” It means abstractions do not inherently add overhead relative to a hand-written equivalent. Iterator pipelines, enums, and generics often compile to code close to an explicit loop. Traits become dynamic only when you opt into trait objects; otherwise, generic code is usually monomorphized.
The senior-developer Rust learning curve

The learning curve is mostly architectural, not syntactic. Rust pushes design choices earlier: where is ownership transferred, which references may outlive which scopes, which types are allowed across threads, and where should cloning be explicit? Later chapters go deeper on borrowing, traits, and async, but this chapter’s goal is to make the early discomfort interpretable.
Rust compared with C++, C#, and Go

The most useful comparison is not syntax. It is where each language places trust: C++ trusts discipline around aliasing, C# trusts a managed runtime, Go trusts a runtime plus simplified concurrency primitives, and Rust spends more compile time to reduce what must be trusted in production.
what changes by background
Why this feels slower before it feels faster
Compile-time guarantees vs runtime checks

items: Move-after-use and many lifetime mistakes
Overlapping mutable borrows
Thread-boundary safety via trait bounds
Missing exhaustiveness in pattern matching
Allocation, syscalls, and network failures
Bounds checks when data-dependent
Parsing invalid input and I/O availability
Contention, cache misses, and real performance costs

ch01.text: Reading compiler errors productively

items: Read the violated rule first, not just the red text.
Find the origin span: where was the move, borrow, or trait bound introduced?
Change ownership shape before changing syntax.
Only clone or heap-share after deciding that duplication or sharing is actually correct.

ch01.text: Typical repair:
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
A borrow-checker error is not an obstacle to work around. It is exposing an ownership protocol you have not stated clearly enough yet. Treat that as design feedback, especially in production code.
Examples
Example 1: iterator pipeline with no extra abstraction tax
This reads like high-level code, but the abstraction can still compile down close to an ordinary loop.
Quick check: press Run first to confirm the baseline output, then change the threshold or input data and see how the pipeline stays readable while remaining executable.
Iterator adapters, closure types, and the final return type describe structure. In ordinary generic code, that structure does not imply a heap allocation or a vtable lookup.
The CPU still walks the slice, evaluates the predicate, branches, and counts matches. Zero-cost abstractions remove abstraction tax, not the cost of real work.
Example 2: ownership handoff into a worker thread
Moving the job into the closure makes the lifetime and thread boundary explicit.
Quick check: reproduce the expected output, then change the job name or move more data into the closure to explore how ownership makes the thread boundary explicit.
The move closure consumes captured non-Copy data so the worker owns what it needs. That makes the handoff explicit instead of leaving lifetime questions to convention.
Queues, threads, and async tasks are ownership boundaries. Borrow locally when you can, but hand off owned work items when execution may outlive the current scope.
Exercises

The companion exercise page contains exercises for warm-up comprehension, code reading, implementation, debugging, and production design. One exercise explicitly asks you to interpret three compiler diagnostics and propose repairs.
Next chapter

Chapter 02 turns this intuition into an operational model: values, bindings, moves, drops, stack versus heap-backed ownership, and why lifetimes are about borrowed references rather than object survival.
Summary

items: Rust feels different because it makes resource protocols part of the type-checked API instead of part of team folklore.
The goal is not abstract safety rhetoric. It is earlier feedback on ownership, mutation, and thread-boundary mistakes.
Zero-cost abstractions remove abstraction tax, not the real cost of parsing, allocation, synchronization, or IO.
Once you can read compiler errors as design notes, later chapters get much easier to use well.

ch02.text: Reliable Rust services depend on a precise model of values, ownership transfer, drops, stack and heap storage, expressions, and references. This chapter defines that model for code review and debugging.
Builds on Chapter 01

Chapter 01 explained why Rust feels different at a high level. This chapter turns that intuition into an operational model: who owns a value, what actually moves, what gets dropped, and why lifetimes are proofs about references rather than a runtime memory system.
Opening scenario

A message-ingestion service parses inbound bytes, enriches records, and dispatches owned jobs to workers. The business requirement is a precise value lifecycle: where data is created, which component owns it, where heap storage is used, and when cleanup occurs.
Operational checklist
Mental model
Core concepts
translating prior instincts
Two corrections that remove a lot of confusion

The useful model is simpler: ownership transferred. For small fixed-size `Copy` values the data is copied. For non-`Copy` types, think of the old binding as no longer owning the value. That is the rule that matters when reading APIs and diagnostics.
Owned values live until their owner is dropped. Lifetimes constrain references that point at those values. If the owner is dropped, no annotation can keep a reference to it valid.
Expressions, statements, and blocks in one pass
A statement performs work in the enclosing scope. It does not become the value of that scope.
An expression produces a value. In Rust, if, match, and blocks are often value-producing tools, not only control-flow syntax.
The last line without a semicolon becomes the block’s value. Add a trailing semicolon and the block evaluates to () instead.
Lifetime repair rule of thumb

When a lifetime error appears, repair ownership before you reach for annotations. Usually the real choice is one of two shapes: borrow from caller-owned input that already lives long enough, or return an owned value so the function transfers data instead of a reference. Randomly adding 'a to a signature rarely fixes the model because lifetimes describe valid borrowing relationships; they do not extend how long an owner lives.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

Deterministic destruction is powerful, but it is not magic. Destructors should release resources and maintain invariants, not hide slow network calls, lock acquisition chains, or critical business logic that is hard to reason about during unwinding and shutdown.
Examples
Example 1: move a value and observe deterministic drop
The binding in `main` stops owning the value after the function call, and cleanup runs when the new owner leaves scope.

ch02.expected:
before move
shipping audit.log
drop audit.log
after ship

ch02.text: Quick check: run the baseline once, then rename the file or move more fields through the handoff to make the ownership timeline concrete.
Example 2: use block expressions to build owned heap data with narrow mutation
The outer bindings stay immutable while a short inner block uses mutation to assemble the final value.
Quick check: confirm the expected output, then experiment with the block contents and see how narrow mutation still produces an owned final value.
Exercises

The exercise page asks you to predict move and drop behavior, classify stack and heap ownership precisely, refactor imperative code into expression-oriented Rust, and explain a lifetime error in operational terms.
Summary

items: Rust gets calmer when you treat bindings as names and ownership as the cleanup contract.
Stack and heap explain storage placement; ownership explains who is responsible for the value that uses it.
Immutability by default and expression-oriented blocks push mutation into narrower, more reviewable scopes.
RAII in Rust is explicit and deterministic, which is exactly why `Drop` should stay small and unsurprising.
Lifetimes talk only about borrowed references. They never extend the life of owned data.

ch03.text: Large Rust repositories need predictable crate boundaries, module visibility, feature flags, dependency policy, and CI commands. This chapter sets the project structure that keeps builds repeatable and maintainable.
Repository note

The current repository is a web book template, not a live Cargo workspace. To stay aligned with the existing template, this chapter uses standalone Rust example files under examples/ch03_project_structure_and_tooling/ and explains the Cargo layouts you would create in a real Rust repository.
Opening scenario

A product repository must deliver an API service, a worker, a support CLI, and a shared domain model from one Rust workspace. The business requirement is clear package ownership, crate boundaries that match release and dependency policy, module visibility that protects invariants, and repeatable Cargo commands in CI.
Mental model
Core concepts
Cargo, crates, packages, and workspaces

The easiest mistake is to treat these words as synonyms. They are not. A package is what Cargo manages from one Cargo.toml. A crate is what the compiler builds. A workspace groups packages so the repository can share one Cargo.lock, one target directory, and one top-level command set.

In practice, start with fewer crates than your instincts may suggest. A new crate is justified when it gives you a real boundary: dependency isolation, compile-time separation, reuse with a stable surface, or a clean public/private split. If the change is only organizational, a module is often the cheaper unit.

The relationship is strictly nested, and the diagram is worth fixing in memory before anything else: a workspace contains packages, each package is defined by exactly one Cargo.toml and produces one or more crates, and each crate contains a tree of modules. Note where the units do and do not line up: one package can yield several crates, but a module never escapes its crate.

ch03.chart:
flowchart TD
  W[Workspace one Cargo.lock and target dir] --> P1[Package domain]
  W --> P2[Package api]
  P1 --> L1[lib crate]
  P2 --> B1[bin crate]
  P2 --> L2[lib crate]
  L1 --> M1[mod model]
  L1 --> M2[mod error]
  B1 --> M3[mod routes]
ch03.caption: Workspace contains packages, a package can build several crates, and modules live inside one crate. Cargo manages the package; the compiler manages the crate.

items: The dependency graph truly differs and you want to keep heavyweight crates out of the core.
The package exports a stable API consumed by multiple binaries or external users.
The team wants a separate release cadence or a separately testable integration layer.
You need a compile boundary, not just a folder boundary.

ch03.text: Modules and visibility

Modules are how you hide detail inside a crate. The default visibility is private, which is a strong default to keep. Reach first for pub(crate), then pub(super), and only then full pub when you truly mean external callers.

The crate root is where you shape the surface. Internal modules may stay deep and specific while the public API becomes smaller and calmer through deliberate pub use re-exports. That keeps callers stable while giving you room to refactor internals.

What to look at: visibility is a ladder, not a switch. Each rung widens who can reach an item, and each rung up is harder to walk back later because more callers can depend on it. Climb only as far as a real caller forces you to, and shape the public path with a deliberate pub use at the crate root.

ch03.chart:
flowchart TD
  A[private default] --> B[pub super]
  B --> C[pub crate]
  C --> D[pub re-exported at crate root]
  D --> E[external callers]
  A -.->|widening is an API promise| E
ch03.caption: Each step widens the audience for an item. Default private is the cheapest to change; a name re-exported at the crate root is the hardest, because outside code can now depend on it.

items: Fields stay private until callers truly need direct structural access.
Constructors and accessors are often cheaper than exposing layout forever.
Re-export names at the crate root when you want a stable path but flexible internals.

ch03.text: Features and conditional compilation

Cargo features work best as additive capability switches: optional integrations, platform-specific plumbing, or extra instrumentation. The real tools are compile-time conditions such as #[cfg(feature = "metrics")], #[cfg(test)], and optional dependencies.

The trap is to encode runtime mode systems as feature matrices. Features are resolved once for the whole build graph. If the question is “what mode is this service in today?”, a runtime config file or environment variable is usually the better abstraction.

What to look at in the diagram: the feature is decided once, on the left, before the compiler runs, and everything downstream is fixed for that whole build. A runtime decision sits on the opposite side — it branches per request inside a single binary. Choosing the wrong side is the classic feature-flag mistake.

ch03.chart:
flowchart TD
  F[Cargo feature on or off] --> R[Cargo resolves graph once]
  R --> G1[cfg metrics on: code compiled in]
  R --> G2[cfg metrics off: code absent from binary]
ch03.caption: Compile-time side: a feature is a fork resolved once, before the binary exists. The code is either compiled in or absent from the shipped binary.

ch03.text: The runtime side is the opposite: one already-built binary that branches per request.

ch03.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Runtime[Single built binary]
    CFG[config or env var] --> Mode1[mode A this request]
    CFG --> Mode2[mode B next request]
  end
ch03.caption: Runtime side: a mode is a branch inside the one binary you shipped, chosen per request. Capability belongs on the compile-time side; operational state belongs here.

ch03.text: Keep feature design boring. Additive features compose. Mutually exclusive features multiply test matrices, documentation burden, and integration surprises.
Dependency management

Be strict about direct dependencies. Each direct crate becomes part of your maintenance surface, your security review surface, and sometimes your public API surface. If several packages share the same policy, centralize it with workspace-level dependency declarations such as workspace.dependencies instead of duplicating versions.

Commit Cargo.lock for binaries and services so production resolution stays reproducible. Library crates also keep a lockfile in the repository for CI sanity, but downstream consumers still resolve their own graph.

items: Prefer fewer transitive surfaces over convenient one-off crates.
Audit default features before accepting them blindly.
Ask whether a dependency belongs in the core crate or at an outer adapter layer.
Review version and feature changes the way you review schema and protocol changes.

ch03.text: Testing, benchmarking, linting, and formatting
The repository also includes examples/ch03_project_structure_and_tooling/testing_layers.rs as a small, standalone example of colocated tests.
A recommended Rust workflow

items: Sketch the crate boundary first: core domain, adapters, binaries, and external integration points.
Start with modules inside one crate, then split crates only where the dependency or API boundary is real.
Run fast structural checks early and often: check, test, format, then Clippy.
Keep feature flags additive and dependency additions reviewed, not casual.
Only benchmark after the boundary and ownership model are stable enough to interpret the numbers.

ch03.text: How prior instincts translate

Almost every confusion in this chapter comes from carrying a structural assumption from another language and quietly assuming Rust agrees. It usually does not. The cards below name the one shift to make for each background before any of the concrete layout advice will land.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
Repository structure is architecture. In Rust, visibility, crate boundaries, and feature design are not cleanup chores after the code works. They are part of how the code keeps working.
Examples
Example 1: shape a narrow module surface
Keep layout private where possible and expose behavior or focused accessors instead of raw structure.

What to look at: service_name is public, but bind_addr is a private field reached only through a method. Callers get the value without getting the right to depend on how it is stored, which is exactly the seam the diagram traces.

ch03.chart:
flowchart TD
  C[main caller] -->|new| K[AppConfig::new constructor]
  K --> S[(private bind_addr field)]
  C -->|read| A[bind_addr accessor]
  A --> S
  C -.->|cannot touch directly| S
ch03.caption: The caller reaches the private field only through the constructor and accessor. The dashed edge is the path the compiler refuses, which is what frees you to change the field's storage later.

ch03.text: Quick check: run the baseline, then change the constructor arguments and keep the private field private. The point is not accessor boilerplate; it is preserving the right to change internal layout later.
Example 2: model an optional capability cleanly
The editor uses a simple constant so you can run the idea in one file. The repository example feature_gated_metrics.rs shows the real `#[cfg(feature = "metrics")]` shape.

What to look at: the example uses a plain const so it runs in one file, but read it as the right-hand runtime branch in the diagram below. The exercise is to decide whether this choice should instead move left, to a compile-time feature, so the unused backend never enters the binary at all.

ch03.chart:
flowchart TD
  Q[Is this a capability or a mode?] --> Cap[Capability: optional integration]
  Q --> Mode[Mode: which way today]
  Cap --> Feat[cfg feature metrics at compile time]
  Mode --> Const[const or env check at runtime]
  Const --> Out[metrics backend = disabled]
ch03.caption: The decision tree behind the example: a true optional capability belongs in a Cargo feature, while a 'which mode right now' question belongs at runtime. The const here stands in for the runtime branch.

ch03.text: Quick check: toggle METRICS_ENABLED between false and true. Then ask whether the decision really belongs at runtime or should move to a compile-time feature.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to design a multi-crate product layout, repair a feature matrix, choose dependency policy, and write the baseline test/lint/benchmark commands you would expect in a production Rust workspace.
Summary

items: Package, crate, module, and workspace are different units with different jobs. Keep the distinctions crisp.
Split crates only where the architectural boundary is real; use modules for cheaper internal structure.
Visibility is design. Narrow it by default and shape public API intentionally at the crate root.
Features work best as additive compile-time capability switches, not as a runtime mode system in disguise.
A strong Rust workflow is ordinary and repeatable: check, test, format, lint, and benchmark deliberately.

ch04.text: Ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes define who may read, mutate, retain, or transfer data at every API boundary. This chapter applies those rules to production interfaces and resource management.
Builds on Chapters 02 and 03

Chapter 02 established values, moves, drops, and lifetimes as reference constraints. Chapter 03 showed that repository boundaries are also ownership boundaries. This chapter connects those models into the day-to-day rules you will feel in function signatures, method design, worker handoff, and API shape.
Opening scenario

An ingress service parses HTTP data, derives routing keys, emits audit labels, and queues work for downstream processors. The business requirement is explicit data ownership at each layer: request bytes stay borrowed only while local, and derived outputs become owned when they cross queues, caches, or worker boundaries.
A reliable order for asking the questions

items: Who owns this value right now?
Can the next operation borrow it, or must it take ownership?
If a reference is returned, which input owner keeps that data alive?
If the answer is awkward, should this API return owned data instead?

ch04.text: Mental model

The three ideas stack in one direction. Ownership is the foundation; a borrow is a temporary permission granted by an owner; a lifetime is just the compiler’s name for the span during which that borrow stays valid. Read the diagram top to bottom and notice that nothing below the owner can outlive it.

ch04.chart:
flowchart TD
  O[Owner: holds the value, runs cleanup] --> S[Shared borrow &T: read-only view]
  O --> M[Mutable borrow &mut T: exclusive access]
  S --> L[Lifetime: borrow valid only while owner lives]
  M --> L
  L --> D[Owner dropped: all borrows must already be gone]
ch04.caption: Ownership sits underneath; borrows are permissions the owner grants; the lifetime is the window in which a borrow is usable. The owner cannot be dropped while any borrow is still live.

ch04.text: Core concepts
Ownership as Rust’s central abstraction

Ownership is the reason moves, drops, borrows, thread handoff, and many API decisions line up into one model. The owner is the place where cleanup responsibility lives. Once that is clear, borrowing becomes a temporary permission story instead of a second memory-management model.

This is why Rust often feels strict at subsystem edges. Queues, async tasks, caches, and stored structs are all ownership decisions. They force you to state whether the next stage only observes data or must outlive the current owner.
Borrowing rules

The whole borrow checker reduces to one exclusivity rule, and it is easier to hold as a small state machine than as a paragraph. At any moment a value is in exactly one of three states: nobody is borrowing it, several readers are, or one writer is. The forbidden combination is the one the diagram never lets you reach.

ch04.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Free
  Free --> Shared: take &T
  Shared --> Shared: take another &T
  Shared --> Free: last reader ends
  Free --> Exclusive: take &mut T
  Exclusive --> Free: writer ends
  note right of Exclusive: only one &mut T, and no &T at the same time
ch04.caption: Any number of shared readers, or exactly one exclusive writer, never both. Every borrow error is the compiler keeping you out of the missing fourth state: a writer plus a reader at once.

ch04.text: Use &T when the callee only needs to inspect data. Many readers are allowed at once because no one is mutating through those aliases.
Use &mut T when the callee needs to change the value. Rust requires exclusivity here because mutation plus aliasing is one of the places memory and concurrency bugs are born.
Lifetimes in function signatures

A lifetime parameter answers one question for a function that returns a reference: which input does the output borrow from? When there is only one candidate input, the answer is obvious and Rust writes it for you; when there are several, you have to point at the right one. The diagram traces that decision.

ch04.chart:
flowchart TD
  R[Function returns a reference?] -->|no| Own[No lifetime needed]
  R -->|yes| C[How many input borrows could it come from?]
  C -->|one| El[Elision ties output to that input]
  C -->|several| Ex[Write an explicit lifetime to pick which input]
  El --> Ok[Output borrow tied to a real owner]
  Ex --> Ok
ch04.caption: The lifetime is not extending anything; it only records which input owner the returned reference is tied to. One input means elision can do it; several means you choose.

ch04.text: A lifetime annotation matters when the compiler must understand how output references relate to input references. A classic example is choosing one of two input references and returning it. The function is not extending lifetime; it is documenting which borrowing relationship must hold.

When a function borrows from one input and returns a slice of that same input, the relationship is often simple enough that Rust can infer it. This is where lifetime elision helps keep common signatures small without changing the underlying model.
Lifetime elision
Elision is convenience, not a second ruleset. Rust still reasons about lifetimes; it simply fills in common cases for you. The useful operational reading is below.

The practical takeaway is simple: if there is one input borrow, elision often works. If there are several candidate input borrows and one output borrow, the relationship usually needs to be written explicitly.
Common lifetime traps for C++ and Go developers
Designing APIs around ownership

A strong default for service code is this: accept borrowed input for local inspection, parsing, and validation; return owned output when the result should be stored, queued, retried, or otherwise decoupled from the caller’s input buffer.
Coming from another language

The mechanics of borrowing are not the hard part. The hard part is that ownership and aliasing rules you used to enforce by habit, by convention, or by trusting a runtime are now checked by the compiler. Each of these cards names the single mental-model shift that trips people up most when they bring instincts from a specific language.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
The wrong repair for a lifetime problem is often “add more lifetimes.” The right repair is usually one of three moves: shorten the borrow, change the owner, or return owned data.
Examples
Example 1: shared borrow first, mutable borrow second
Read through a shared reference, then take an exclusive mutable borrow only for the short mutation step.

What to look at: the shared borrow for request_size is created, used, and finished before append_trace ever asks for its mutable borrow. The two borrows do not overlap in time, which is exactly why the code compiles.

ch04.chart:
flowchart TD
  Own[request: owned String] -->|&request| Read[request_size reads len]
  Read --> End[shared borrow ends]
  End -->|&mut request| Write[append_trace pushes trace id]
  Write --> Own2[request mutated in place]
ch04.caption: Shared borrow first, then it ends, then the exclusive mutable borrow. Sequencing the two so they never coexist is the design move, not cloning.

ch04.text: The immutable borrow used for request_size ends before the mutable borrow begins. That sequencing is the real design tool.
Inspect first, mutate second, and keep the exclusive borrow narrow. This pattern resolves a surprising number of logging, parsing, and request-enrichment borrow errors.
Example 2: explicit lifetime where needed, owned output where cleaner
One helper uses lifetime elision, one requires an explicit relationship, and one deliberately returns an owned string.

What to look at: compare where each function’s result gets its validity. Two of them return a slice that borrows from an input, so their output lives only as long as that input; the third builds a brand-new String it owns outright. The diagram groups the three by that distinction.

ch04.chart:
flowchart TD
  FS[first_segment path: &str] -->|one input, elided| Slice1[returns &str into path]
  PL[pick_longer left, right: &'a str] -->|two inputs, explicit 'a| Slice2[returns &str into one of them]
  Slice1 --> Borrowed[Output borrows: valid only while input lives]
  Slice2 --> Borrowed
ch04.caption: The two functions that return slices: first_segment uses elision because it has one input; pick_longer needs an explicit 'a to pick which of two inputs the result borrows from. Either way the output is valid only while that input lives.

ch04.text: The third function takes the opposite path: instead of borrowing from an input, it builds and returns a value it owns.

ch04.chart:
flowchart TD
  ML[make_audit_label service, key: &str] -->|builds new value| Owned[returns owned String]
  Owned --> Free[Output is independent: outlives the inputs]
ch04.caption: make_audit_label returns an owned String that survives on its own. Returning owned data is the deliberate escape from a borrow relationship.

ch04.expected:
segment = api
longer = request-id
label = gateway::api

ch04.text: first_segment borrows from one input, so elision keeps the signature compact.
pick_longer chooses between two inputs, so the returned reference relationship must be written.
make_audit_label returns String because the label should outlive the borrowed inputs cleanly.
Exercises

The exercise page asks you to repair borrow-checker failures without cloning by reflex, decide when explicit lifetime annotations are required, and design APIs that take borrowed input while returning owned output.
Summary

items: Ownership is the main abstraction. Borrowing and lifetimes refine it; they do not replace it.
Shared references permit many readers. Mutable references require exclusive access for the duration of mutation.
Lifetimes describe valid reference relationships. They do not extend object lifetime or keep a dropped owner’s data alive.
Elision handles common cases, but multiple input borrows often require an explicit output relationship.
Good production APIs often accept borrowed input and return owned data at subsystem boundaries.

ch05.text: Struct design fixes ownership policy in public data models. This chapter covers owned fields, borrowed views, shared pointers, and stable representations for systems that must expose safe state without hidden aliasing.
Builds on Chapters 02 and 04

Chapter 02 established values, moves, drops, and heap-backed ownership. Chapter 04 explained borrowing and lifetime relationships. This chapter moves those rules into struct design, where production Rust either becomes clear or becomes accidentally lifetime-heavy.
Opening scenario

A command-processing service converts request text into normalized records, stores selected data, and sends background work to processors. The business requirement is to classify every struct as a transient view or owned state, so lifetimes stay local and durable data remains easy to store, test, and move.
A durable design order

items: Decide whether the struct is a view or an owner.
If it borrows, say which outer owner keeps it alive.
If it owns, decide whether the owned fields are inline, boxed, or shared.
If you are tempted by self-reference, change the representation instead.

ch05.text: Mental model
Core concepts
Owned fields vs borrowed fields

The choice is not about which is faster to type. It is about which direction the dependency points. An owned field copies the data inside the struct, so the struct stands alone. A borrowed field stores a reference back to data someone else holds, so the struct can only live as long as that owner does. Trace both arrows before you read the signatures.

ch05.chart:
flowchart TD
  O1[Input buffer] -->|copied in| O2[StoredAlert owns String]
  O2 -->|stands alone| O3[Vec, cache, queue, thread]
ch05.caption: Owned field: the data is copied inside the struct, which then carries it forward into long-lived storage on its own.

ch05.text: The borrowed case points the dependency the other way:

ch05.chart:
flowchart TD
  B1[Input buffer must stay alive] -->|reference| B2[HeaderView holds and a str]
  B2 -.->|dies when owner drops| B3[no independent storage]
ch05.caption: Borrowed field: the struct only points back at an owner that must outlive it, so it has no independent storage.

ch05.text: A borrowed-field struct is usually a temporary lens over someone else’s data. An owned-field struct is usually a value the rest of the system may keep, move, test, queue, and reason about independently.
Structs containing references and lifetime parameters on structs

The thing to watch is contagion. The moment one field is a reference, the struct gains a lifetime parameter, and that parameter has to be named everywhere the struct appears: in the functions that build it, in the fields of any struct that holds it, in the return types that hand it back. The diagram shows the same lifetime ’a threading through each of those positions.

ch05.chart:
flowchart TD
  Field[name: and a str field] --> Struct[MessageView of a]
  Struct --> Builder[fn parse of a takes and a str]
  Struct --> Holder[Session of a embeds the view]
  Struct --> Return[fn view returns MessageView of a]
ch05.caption: One reference field forces a lifetime parameter, and that single 'a has to be named in the builder, in any holder, and in the return type.

ch05.text: That parameter does not stop at the type definition. It reaches all the way out to call sites:

ch05.chart:
flowchart TD
  Builder[fn parse of a takes and a str] --> Caller[every caller must supply an owner that lives long enough]
ch05.caption: The builder propagates the same 'a outward, so ultimately every caller must supply an owner that lives long enough.

ch05.text: If this struct ended up inside a Vec, a cache, a worker message, or a test fixture, would you still want it tied to some external owner’s lifetime? If the answer is no, give the struct owned fields.
Interior ownership using Box, Rc, and Arc

These three smart pointers all put a field behind heap indirection, but they answer different questions. The deciding factor is how many owners the value has and whether any of them live on another thread. Walk the two questions in the diagram and each pointer falls out of the answer.

ch05.caption: Two questions decide the pointer: how many owners, and whether ownership crosses a thread. Box for one owner, Rc for shared on one thread, Arc for shared across threads.

ch05.text: The pointer type is part of the domain model. Box<T> means one owner plus indirection. Rc<T> means shared ownership in one thread. Arc<T> means shared ownership across threads, provided T is itself safe there.
Structs that own buffers and expose views

This is one of the most Rust-native patterns in systems and service code. Let the struct own the buffer. Then derive borrowed slices from &self as needed. The struct manages lifetime. Callers get safe read-only views.
The repository example examples/ch05_ownership_inside_structs/owned_buffer_views.rs mirrors the first example below.
Self-referential struct problems

The tempting shape is something like struct Parsed<'a> {" raw: String, first: &'a str "} . You cannot construct it in safe code: filling first requires borrowing self.raw, which conflicts with moving raw into the same value, and the lifetime 'a is supplied by the caller — no lifetime can name the struct's own field. The deeper soundness reason self-references generally need Pin is that for address-sensitive inline data, moving the struct moves the storage that the internal pointer aims at. For String or Vec the bytes live on the heap and survive moves, so it is the construction rule, not the move, that rules this layout out.
The repository example examples/ch05_ownership_inside_structs/stable_indices_instead_of_self_reference.rs shows the most practical repair: own the buffer, store ranges, and derive views when needed.
Translating from C++, C#, and Go
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The cheapest-looking field type is not always the cheapest design. Saving one allocation by borrowing can cost far more if the whole object graph becomes lifetime-coupled and hard to store, test, or hand off.
Examples
Example 1: own the buffer, borrow the view
The struct owns the raw line. Methods derive lightweight views from that owned buffer.

What to look at: the struct holds exactly one owned field, the raw line. Every accessor returns a &str that is sliced out of that field on demand, so the borrows live and die with each call instead of being stored. Follow the single owner down to the short-lived views in the diagram, then read it in the code.

ch05.chart:
flowchart TD
  Raw[LogLine owns raw: String] -->|borrow on call| L[level returns and str]
  Raw -->|borrow on call| M[message returns and str]
  L -.->|tied to and self, dropped after use| Caller[caller prints the slice]
  M -.->|tied to and self, dropped after use| Caller
ch05.caption: One owned buffer, many transient borrows. The returned slices are bound to &self, so the struct stays movable and storable.

ch05.expected:
level = INFO
message = user signed in

ch05.text: Quick check: run the baseline, then change the raw line passed to LogLine::new. The output changes, but the ownership stays simple: one owner, many short borrows.
The returned &str values are tied to &self, not stored inside the struct. That keeps the representation movable and ordinary.
This pattern shows up in log parsing, protocol headers, request lines, and binary message frames: own once, slice many times, store offsets only when repeated lookup deserves it.
Example 2: choose Box, Rc, and Arc by ownership semantics
One field needs single-owner indirection, one needs single-thread shared ownership, and one must cross a thread boundary.

What to look at: read the three field types, not the strings they hold. Each field encodes a different ownership story, and the code downstream is forced to respect it. The boxed config is consumed by one owner, the Rc template is cloned and used only on the main thread, and the Arc schema is the one value that is allowed to move into the spawned worker. The diagram lines up each field with the boundary it may cross.

ch05.chart:
flowchart TD
  Cfg[Box config] -->|single owner| Main[Main thread]
  Tmpl[Rc template] -->|clone, refcount up| Main
  Tmpl -.->|cannot send, not Sync| Worker[Spawned worker thread]
ch05.caption: Box keeps one owner on the main thread, and Rc can be cloned there but is barred from crossing into the worker.

ch05.text: The Arc-wrapped schema is the one field allowed to cross the thread boundary:

ch05.chart:
flowchart TD
  Schema[Arc schema] -->|clone, atomic refcount| Main[Main thread]
  Schema -->|safe to move across| Worker[Spawned worker thread]
ch05.caption: Only the Arc-wrapped schema uses atomic counting, so it is the field that can safely move into the worker.

ch05.expected:
box delimiter = =>
rc clones = 2
thread schema = v2

ch05.text: Quick check: keep the three field types distinct, then change the string literals and rerun. The point is not the output itself. The point is that the field type communicates the ownership model.
The parser config still has one owner. The box gives indirection without changing ownership count.
The UI template is shared on one thread only. That is why the example clones it locally and never sends it to the worker.
The shared schema crosses a thread boundary, so the reference count must be atomic and the inner type must remain thread-safe.
Exercises

The exercise page asks you to choose owned versus borrowed fields for real domain objects, refactor a self-referential design into stable indices, select between `Box`, `Rc`, and `Arc`, and build a struct that owns data while exposing safe read-only views.
Summary

items: Struct field types are ownership decisions, not mere storage details.
Borrowed fields are useful for short-lived views, but they spread lifetime coupling through the type.
Box<T>, Rc<T>, and Arc<T> solve different ownership problems. Pick by semantics, not habit.
Owning a buffer and deriving views from `&self` is a strong Rust-native pattern for parsers and protocols.
Most self-referential designs should be rewritten as offsets, ranges, stable IDs, or separate owner/view types.

ch06.text: A vector owns one resizable buffer, and growth can move every element it holds. This chapter is about choosing the right handle into that buffer: when a borrowed reference is safe, when an index or ID is the durable choice, and when the model genuinely needs stable addresses from boxed or arena-style storage.
Builds on Chapters 04 and 05

Chapter 04 explained borrowing and lifetime relationships. Chapter 05 moved those rules into struct field design. This chapter applies the same discipline to collections, where growth, reordering, and temporary views make ownership mistakes especially easy to import from C++, C#, or Go.
Opening scenario

A worker registry tracks live connections, appends new workers during scaling, scans readiness, and removes unhealthy entries. The business requirement is a stable handle policy: use short borrows only while the vector shape is fixed, and use indices, IDs, boxed storage, or arena handles when growth and reordering are normal.
A practical review order

items: Will the vector’s length, capacity, or ordering change while this handle is alive?
If yes, should the handle be an index or ID instead of a reference?
If address stability truly matters, should each element be separately allocated?
If the algorithm needs both inspection and reshaping, can it run in two phases?

ch06.text: Mental model
Core concepts
What a vector actually is

A vector is one owner of one resizable buffer. The value stored in a local binding is only the control block: pointer, length, and capacity. The elements live in heap-backed contiguous storage managed by that owner.
Moving the Vec<T> moves ownership of the buffer. Growing beyond capacity may move the elements themselves into a new buffer. That second fact is the one that makes element references delicate.
The thing to picture is the split between the small fixed-size handle on the stack and the heap buffer it points at. The handle stays put; the buffer underneath it can be replaced.

ch06.chart:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Stack
    H["Vec handle: ptr, len, cap"]
  end
  subgraph Heap
    B["buffer: e0 e1 e2 ... free cap"]
  end
  H -->|ptr| B
ch06.caption: The Vec value on the stack is just a pointer, length, and capacity. The elements live in a separate heap buffer the vector owns.

ch06.text: References into vectors and invalidation

A borrowed element such as &jobs[i] is tied to the current buffer and the current aliasing rules. It says, in effect, "while this borrow lives, nobody may perform conflicting access that would make it invalid or ambiguous."

Rust therefore rejects many patterns that would be merely dangerous in other languages: take a borrow, then append, reserve, insert, or otherwise reshape the same vector while still using the borrowed element later.

The hazard is easiest to see as a sequence. A borrow names a slot in the current buffer; a growth past capacity allocates a new buffer and moves the elements; the old borrow would now point into freed memory. Rust rejects the code at the second step rather than letting the third one happen at runtime.

ch06.chart:
flowchart TD
  A["take r = &vec[0]"] --> B["call vec.push(x)"]
  B --> C{"len > cap?"}
  C -->|no| D["same buffer, r still valid"]
  C -->|yes| E["allocate new buffer, move elements"]
  E --> F["r points at freed memory"]
  F --> G["compile error: cannot borrow vec as mutable while borrowed"]
ch06.caption: Growth past capacity relocates the buffer, which would dangle the earlier borrow. Rust forbids the conflicting mutable access at compile time.

items: push, extend, and insert may move the buffer when length grows past capacity.
reserve is an explicit request for more capacity and may also relocate storage.
remove, swap_remove, sorting, and compaction may shift element positions even when the buffer does not relocate.

ch06.text: Index-based designs
Indices are the default durable handle for a plain vector. You store the position, mutate the vector as needed, and then reborrow from the vector when you are ready to use the element again.

This works well when you control reordering policy. If the code uses swap_remove, sorting, or compaction, the index is a location, not an identity. Production code often wraps indices in typed IDs or adds generation checks when stale handles matter.
Choosing a handle

Before reaching for any representation, the decision worth making explicit is what kind of handle the code needs. The first question is whether the vector’s shape is fixed for the lifetime of the handle. If it is, borrows and slices are ideal. If it is not, the choice is between a location handle (an index or ID) and a representation that gives genuinely stable addresses.

ch06.chart:
flowchart TD
  Q1{"Shape fixed while handle is alive?"}
  Q1 -->|yes| R["use &T, &mut T, or a slice"]
  Q1 -->|no| Cont["shape can change: continues below"]
ch06.caption: First question: if the vector cannot grow, shrink, or reorder while the handle lives, a short borrow or slice is ideal.

ch06.text: When the shape can change, the choice is between a location handle and genuinely stable addresses:

ch06.caption: If shape changes, prefer an index for plain growth; reach for boxed or arena storage only when an address itself must stay put.

ch06.text: Stable-address allocation patterns

Sometimes the correct requirement really is stable addressability. A parser cache, intrusive structure, or FFI boundary may need each element to stay put even if the collection grows. That is when you change the representation, not when you try to stretch a plain borrowed element reference farther than it should go.

A precise note on Pin: pinning can matter for address-sensitive pointees such as certain async or self-referential low-level machinery, but it does not make references into a plain Vec<T> stable on its own. For ordinary collection design, indices, boxes, or arena-style handles are the usual tools.
Vec<Box<T>>, arenas, and slab allocation
Vec<Box<T>> is a tactical choice: indexing stays simple, and each element lives in its own heap allocation. Growing the vector moves boxes, not pointees.

Arena and slab-style stores solve a different problem. They usually give you stable logical handles, efficient reuse, and explicit deletion policy. The ecosystem offers several variants, but the shared idea is more important than any one crate: store by owner-managed pool, access by ID.
Borrowing slices from vectors
How this lands by background

Every language with a growable array has the same underlying reallocation behavior. What differs is whether you normally hold a reference into a slot, and whether anything stops you from using it after the array moves. The mental shift below is the trap most likely to surprise an engineer coming from each language.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The cheapest-looking handle is often the most expensive long-term design. A borrowed element reference is wonderful when the vector shape is fixed. It is a trap when growth and reshaping are part of the normal lifecycle.
Examples
Example 1: index handles instead of borrowed elements
The vector may grow, so the durable handle is the index. The code reborrows from the vector only when it actually needs the element.

What to look at: push_task returns the index it just wrote, not a reference. Later pushes are free to reallocate the buffer, and the code only reborrows through tasks[billing] after all growth is done. The index is the handle that survives the mutation.

ch06.chart:
flowchart TD
  P["push_task returns index 0"] --> S["store billing = 0"]
  S --> G["push search, push indexer (may grow buffer)"]
  G --> M["mark_not_ready(tasks, billing)"]
  M --> R["reborrow tasks[0] to read name and ready"]
ch06.caption: The index stays valid across growth. Each access reborrows the current buffer instead of holding a reference through the pushes.

ch06.text: Quick check: keep the handle as an index, then change task names or add more pushes. The design stays correct because the vector is allowed to grow without carrying old element borrows through the mutation.
If the collection may reallocate, keep a location handle such as an index and borrow later.
Worker tables, scheduler queues, and parser token streams often become easier once durable handles stop being raw references into resizable storage.
Example 2: stable pointees plus two-phase mutation
Each job lives in its own box, and shape-changing logic is split from inspection logic.

What to look at: first_ptr records the heap address of the first job before two more pushes. Because each job is its own Box, growing the vector relocates the boxes but not the jobs, so the address still matches afterward. The retry update then runs in two phases: collect indices first, mutate second, so no borrow is held across a shape change.

ch06.chart:
flowchart TD
  A["record first_ptr = address of jobs[0]"] --> B["push two more boxed jobs (buffer may grow)"]
  B --> C["ptr::eq(first_ptr, &jobs[0]) is still true"]
  C --> D["phase 1: collect retry_indices by reading needs_retry"]
  D --> E["phase 2: for each index, bump attempts and clear flag"]
ch06.caption: Boxes move when the vector grows; the boxed jobs keep their addresses. Inspection (phase 1) is fully separated from mutation (phase 2).

ch06.expected:
same address = true
attempts = 2
retry pending = 0

ch06.text: Quick check: keep the boxed representation, then add more jobs or change the retry flag. The point is not boxing by habit. The point is that stable pointees and two-phase updates are explicit, reviewable choices.
The vector may move boxes around, but the boxed job itself stays at one heap address.
The first pass records retry targets. The second pass performs mutation. Inspection and reshaping stay separate.
Extra allocation buys stronger address stability. Use it when the model needs it, not by reflex.
Exercises

The exercise page asks you to repair vector reallocation hazards, convert reference-heavy designs into index-based ones, choose between plain vectors and stable-address patterns, and implement safe mutation while iterating.
Summary

items: A vector owns a resizable contiguous buffer, and growth may move every element.
References and slices are short-lived views into the current buffer, not durable handles across shape changes.
Indices are the default stable handle for plain vectors, provided the code manages reordering policy explicitly.
Stable-address needs usually call for a different representation such as Vec<Box<T>>, arenas, or slab-style storage.
When mutation changes vector shape, inspection-first and mutation-second is often the cleanest production pattern.

ch07.text: Whether a value moves, copies, or clones decides latency, memory use, and what an API promises about ownership. This chapter separates those events so that a reader, and a code reviewer, can always tell which one is happening and why the cost was chosen on purpose.
Builds on Chapters 04, 05, and 06

Chapter 04 explained ownership and borrowing. Chapter 05 moved those rules into struct design. Chapter 06 showed why resizable collections make handle choice matter. This chapter adds the duplication model on top: when values move, when they copy, when they clone, and how to keep that decision visible in production APIs.
Opening scenario

A request service fans work out to several workers and keeps retry state for failed jobs. The requirement is a reviewable duplication policy: borrow read-only data on hot paths, move owned jobs at boundaries, copy tiny values implicitly when that is safe, and clone only where independent ownership is genuinely required. The goal is not to ban clones; it is to make every clone explainable in review.
A fast decision order

When you hit a value that needs to be used more than once, walk these questions in order. The first one that answers yes is usually the right tool, and the diagram after it shows the same decision as a single path.

items: Can the next step borrow instead of owning?
If ownership must transfer, is a move the correct model?
If duplication is needed, is the type a plain Copy value or an explicit Clone value?
If many readers share one value, is Rc or Arc the real model?

ch07.caption: First half: borrow if the next step can, otherwise move when a single owner is handing the value on. If you actually need a duplicate, follow the second half.

ch07.text: When a duplicate is genuinely needed, the second half decides which kind:

ch07.caption: Second half: a Copy type duplicates implicitly; otherwise clone explicitly for an independent owner, or add a shared owner with Rc or Arc when many readers share one value.

ch07.text: Mental model
How this lands by background

Most engineers do not meet move, Copy, and Clone with a blank slate. They arrive with a duplication model from another language, and the useful question is which part of that model transfers and which part quietly misleads. The shift is almost never about API names. It is about where duplication becomes visible: Rust drags the deep copy out of the constructor and the assignment and onto a line you can read.
Core concepts
Three different events, not one blurry idea

The whole chapter rests on keeping three things apart. A move hands a single value from one owner to the next. A copy is an implicit bitwise duplicate that a type opts into for small values. A clone is an explicit, possibly expensive duplication that you write by hand. The diagram shows what happens to the source binding in each case, which is the detail that trips people up.

ch07.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Move
    A1[src owns value] -->|let b = src| B1[b owns value]
    A1 -.->|src unusable| X1[compile error if used]
  end
ch07.caption: Move: assignment hands the single value to the new binding and the source can no longer be used.

ch07.text: Copy and Clone behave differently: in both cases the source stays usable. The split is who pays and whether the duplication is implicit or written down.

ch07.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Copy
    A2[src small value] -->|let b = src| B2[b is a duplicate]
    A2 -->|src still usable| C2[src stays valid]
  end
  subgraph Clone
    A3[src owns data] -->|let b = src.clone| B3[b owns a deep copy]
    A3 -->|src still usable| C3[src stays valid]
  end
ch07.caption: Copy and Clone both leave the source valid. Copy is an implicit bitwise duplicate of a small value; Clone is an explicit, possibly expensive duplication you write by hand.

ch07.text: What Copy and Clone share, and where they differ

These two traits are related, not independent. Clone is the general duplication trait. Copy is a marker that sits on top of Clone and adds a promise: the duplicate is a trivial bitwise copy, so the language may make it implicit and leave the original usable. That relationship is why every Copy type must also be Clone, and why a type that owns heap data can be Clone but never Copy.

ch07.chart:
flowchart TD
  Clone[Clone trait: explicit duplication] --> Copy[Copy marker: implicit bitwise duplicate]
  Copy --> Small[u64, bool, char, Span]
  Small --> Why[small and bitwise-trivial, so duplication is implicit]
ch07.caption: Copy is a special case of Clone: a marker for small, bitwise-trivial values where implicit duplication is safe and unsurprising.

ch07.text: The other families stay Clone-only on purpose. Heap-owning and reference-counted types can duplicate, but never implicitly:

ch07.chart:
flowchart TD
  Clone[Clone trait: explicit duplication] --> Heap[String, Vec, HashMap]
  Clone --> Shared[Rc and Arc handles]
  Heap -.->|cannot be Copy| NoCopy[owns heap, needs explicit clone]
  Shared -.->|cheap clone, not Copy| Counted[increments a reference count]
ch07.caption: Heap-owning types must clone explicitly; reference-counted handles clone cheaply but only bump a count, so neither is ever Copy.

ch07.text: Topics this chapter treats as source of truth
Reference-counted cloning is sharing, not copying

The most common confusion in this whole topic is treating an Arc clone as if it deep-copied the inner value. It does not. Both handles point at the same allocation; the clone only bumps a counter so the allocation lives until the last handle is dropped. That is what makes it cheap, and also what makes it different from an independent clone: a mutation through one handle is visible to the other unless you go through make_mut.

ch07.chart:
flowchart TD
  H1[Arc handle a] --> Alloc[(one allocation: count 2)]
  H2[Arc handle b] --> Alloc
  Alloc --> Data[the actual String or struct]
  Note[Arc::clone bumps the count; it copies the handle, not Data]
ch07.caption: An Arc clone adds a second handle to one shared allocation and increments the reference count. The underlying data is never duplicated.

ch07.text: When is implementing Copy safe?

A useful default is conservative: if the type owns heap memory, file descriptors, sockets, locks, or any state where two implicit duplicates would be misleading, it should not be Copy. The compiler enforces the mechanical half of this (no Drop, all fields Copy); the semantic half (would two of these be surprising?) is yours to judge.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
“Just clone it” is not always wrong. It becomes wrong when the review can no longer explain why independent ownership is needed, or when the hidden allocation cost shows up in the hot path later.
Examples
Example 1: move, Copy, Clone, and receiver choices in one pass
One tiny ID copies, one config clones explicitly, one method reads by &self, one mutates by &mut self, and one consumes by self.

What to look at: follow the live config. It is mutated through &mut self, then explicitly cloned so the consuming replace_name(self, ...) can take the clone by value while the original keeps living. The diagram traces that single value; the code is the same path written out.

ch07.chart:
flowchart TD
  Id[RequestId 42] -->|Copy: let copy = id| IdCopy[copy, original still valid]
  Live[live config] -->|&mut self: bump_retries| Live2[live, retries bumped]
  Live2 -->|clone| Dup[independent copy]
  Dup -->|self: replace_name| Built[replaced config]
  Live2 -->|&self: name| Read[still readable after]
ch07.caption: RequestId copies and the original survives; live is borrowed mutably, cloned once, and the clone is consumed by a by-value method while live stays usable.

ch07.expected:
request id copy = 42
live retries = 2
builder consumed = ingest-v2
current name = ingest-v1

ch07.text: Quick check: run the baseline, then try removing the .clone() before replace_name. The compiler refuses, because replace_name(self) would move live away and the last line still reads it. That is the move-versus-clone decision made concrete.
RequestId is a tiny value. Implicit duplication is predictable and the original stays valid.
live.clone() creates a second independent config before the consuming builder-style call.
&self views, &mut self mutates, and self finalizes or transforms ownership.
Example 2: clone-on-write normalization and cheap shared ownership
Borrow the common case with Cow, allocate only on transformation, and use Arc::clone when shared ownership is the real model.

What to look at: normalize_label branches on whether the input already fits the normalized form. An already-clean label returns Cow::Borrowed with no allocation; a dirty one returns Cow::Owned and pays once. The Arc lines are a second, separate idea: cloning a handle adds a shared owner rather than copying the string. The diagram splits those two paths so you can read each in the code.

ch07.chart:
flowchart TD
  In[input label] --> Check{already normalized?}
  Check -->|yes| Borrowed["Cow::Borrowed: no allocation"]
  Check -->|no| Owned["Cow::Owned: allocate once"]
ch07.caption: Cow borrows the clean path and only allocates when it must transform the label.

ch07.text: The Arc lines are a separate idea: cloning a handle adds a shared owner rather than copying the string.

ch07.chart:
flowchart TD
  Schema[Arc schema] -->|Arc::clone| Worker[second handle]
  Worker --> Count[strong count = 2, data not copied]
ch07.caption: Arc::clone adds a shared owner and leaves the schema string untouched: the count goes to 2, the data is not duplicated.

ch07.expected:
borrowed = ready
owned = mixed-case
strong count = 2

ch07.text: Quick check: change the labels and rerun. Inputs that already fit the normalized form stay borrowed; transformed inputs become owned. The Arc side shows the other distinction: cheap shared ownership is still not the same as deep cloning.
Cow lets the API return a borrowed value when no rewrite is needed.
The owned branch pays for normalization once, at the boundary that actually needs it.
Arc::clone increments the count. It does not copy the underlying schema string.
The repository also includes standalone Rust files under examples/ch07_copying_data_vs_cloning_data/ so the chapter can be reviewed outside the web editor as ordinary Rust source.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to classify operations as move, copy, or clone, implement Clone manually for a realistic type, decide when Copy is safe, remove unnecessary clones from an API, and choose receiver forms deliberately.
Summary

items: Moves, Copy, and Clone are different ownership events with different review meanings: a move invalidates the source, while Copy and Clone leave it usable.
Copy is a marker on top of Clone for small bitwise-trivial values; Clone is the general, explicit duplication trait.
Manual Clone should clone owned fields and copy plain scalar fields directly, and is a signal that duplication does something nontrivial.
Rc and Arc cloning add shared owners; they increment a reference count and do not deep-copy the inner value.
Borrow by default, allocate at real boundaries, and choose self, &self, and &mut self to match the ownership the method actually needs.

ch08.text: Unsafe Rust is justified only when a small boundary must enforce invariants the compiler cannot verify. This chapter defines the audit obligations for raw pointers, initialization, aliasing, FFI, and safe wrappers.
Builds on Chapters 04 through 07

Ownership, borrowing, struct layout, vector invalidation, and move versus clone decisions all lead here. Unsafe Rust is not a separate language. It is the place where those earlier rules stop being compiler guarantees and start becoming explicit human obligations.
Opening scenario

A packet-processing service validates fixed headers, calls a native library, and reuses buffers on a measured hot path. The business requirement is a narrow unsafe boundary with written invariants for pointer validity, initialization, aliasing, thread safety, and safe wrapper behavior.
A useful rule before writing unsafe code

items: Write the safe version first if the shape is still unclear.
State the exact reason unsafe is needed: FFI, layout, partial initialization, or a measured hot path.
Write down the invariant before the block, not after the bug report.

ch08.text: Mental model

The picture to hold in your head is a containment boundary. Almost everything you write is ordinary safe Rust, where the compiler proves memory safety. A few operations cannot be proven that way, so they live inside an explicit region with a written invariant. Cross that line correctly and the program is sound; cross it on a false assumption and you are in undefined behavior, where the optimizer is free to do anything.

ch08.chart:
flowchart TD
  S["Safe Rust, compiler-proven"] --> U{unsafe block}
  U -->|invariant holds| OK["Sound program"]
  U -->|invariant violated| UB["Undefined behavior"]
  UB --> X["Crash, corruption, or silent miscompile"]
ch08.caption: Unsafe is a boundary, not a mode. The compiler proves the safe region; you prove the unsafe region. A broken invariant does not fail loudly, it leaks into undefined behavior.

ch08.text: Core concepts
What Rust considers undefined behavior

Treat the list below as the operational map, not as a claim of complete exhaustiveness. The key idea is that UB is exactly where the optimizer is allowed to assume the impossible states cannot occur, so reasoning based on what the hardware happens to do no longer holds.
Safe Rust vs unsafe Rust

Safe Rust rules out use-after-free, double-free, and data races in ordinary code. References, ownership transfer, `Send`, `Sync`, and borrowing rules do most of the structural work long before a test suite runs.

Unsafe Rust keeps the same language around you, but it permits operations the compiler cannot fully verify. The rest of the code still obeys ordinary Rust rules. The unsafe block is the proof boundary, not a local switch to “anything goes.”
The role of unsafe blocks

`unsafe` grants specific capabilities. It does not disable ownership, type checking, or syntax rules, and it does not make UB acceptable. It simply says: the compiler cannot prove this, so a human must.

The practical consequence is simple: a tiny unsafe block with a precise `// SAFETY:` comment is usually a better design than a large region whose real invariants are only understood after several meetings.
Raw pointers and aliasing rules

The thing to watch is the asymmetry between a raw pointer and a reference. A raw pointer is just an address with no promises attached, so making one and doing arithmetic on it is always safe. A reference is an address plus a contract the optimizer relies on: `&T` promises the data stays valid and unmutated for the borrow, and `&mut T` promises exclusive access. The dangerous step is not the dereference itself, it is turning a raw pointer back into a reference, because at that moment you are re-asserting the contract. If the address is dangling or aliased, you have lied to the optimizer and the resulting reference is invalid even though the machine instruction ran without complaint.

ch08.chart:
flowchart TD
  R["reference, carries promises"] -->|as cast, safe| P["raw pointer, no promises"]
  P -->|arithmetic, safe| P2["adjusted raw pointer"]
  P2 -->|deref or re-borrow, UNSAFE| R2["reference again"]
  R2 -->|valid, aligned, non-aliasing| OK["Sound"]
  R2 -->|dangling or aliased| UB["Undefined behavior"]
ch08.caption: Dropping a reference down to a raw pointer is free; the address loses its promises. Climbing back up to a reference is the unsafe step, because it re-asserts validity and exclusivity that may no longer be true.

ch08.text: `*const T` and `*mut T` may be null, dangling, misaligned, or aliased. That is why creating them is safe but dereferencing them is not. Raw pointers are representation tools, not evidence that a memory access is valid.

References are stronger than raw pointers because they promise something to the optimizer. Turning a raw pointer back into `&T` or `&mut T` means you are reintroducing those promises. If exclusive mutation is not actually exclusive, the resulting reference is invalid even if the machine instruction succeeds.
Data races and UB

In Rust, a data race is not merely a bug; it is undefined behavior. Safe Rust prevents it by construction through ownership transfer, borrowing rules, and `Send`/`Sync` requirements at thread boundaries. Unsafe code can still create conflicting unsynchronized accesses. That is why shared mutability, raw pointers, and concurrency belong in the same audit conversation, not in separate review queues.
Uninitialized memory and MaybeUninit<T>

The shape to keep in mind is a one-way ratchet. Storage starts in a not-yet-valid state, you write every required byte or field exactly once, and only at the end do you assert that it now holds a real value. The error to avoid is calling assume_init while the storage is still partially written, which produces a value that the rest of the program will treat as valid even though it is not.

ch08.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Uninit: MaybeUninit uninit
  Uninit --> Partial: write some fields
  Partial --> Partial: write more fields
  Partial --> Full: every field written
  Full --> Value: assume_init
  Value --> [*]
  Partial --> UB: assume_init too early
  Uninit --> UB: read as real value
ch08.caption: assume_init is the single legal exit, and only from the fully written state. Reading the storage as a real value before that, or asserting it early, is undefined behavior.

ch08.text: Uninitialized memory is not a valid value of any type. Reading it as a real `T` is UB. The same is true for constructing invalid bit patterns for types that have invariants, such as references, many enums, and `bool`.

MaybeUninit<T> is the sanctioned way to represent storage that does not yet contain a valid `T`. Write every required field or element first. Only then call assume_init. The type exists so the invalid state is modeled explicitly rather than hidden behind fake values.
FFI-related UB

The useful framing for a C boundary is a translation layer with a single direction of travel. Raw C values come in as pointers, status codes, and lifetime-free buffers; you translate each into a Rust type that carries the guarantee, and from there inward everything is ordinary safe Rust. The UB lives in the thin translation step, so that is the only place that needs the unsafe audit. Letting raw C pointers travel deeper into your code is how an FFI contract mismatch turns into a memory-safety bug far from the boundary.

ch08.chart:
flowchart TD C["C library:
raw ptr, status
code, buffer"] --> W{unsafe FFI wrapper} W -->|null check| O["Option for
nullability"] W -->|status to result| Res["Result for
errors"] W -->|validated lifetime| Ref["owned type or
scoped reference"] O --> Cont["translations flow inward
continues below"] Res --> Cont Ref --> Cont
ch08.caption: First half: the unsafe wrapper translates each C convention into a Rust type. Nullability becomes Option, status codes become Result, raw buffers become owned values or scoped references.

ch08.text: Inward of the wrapper, those three translated values converge into ordinary safe Rust:

ch08.chart:
flowchart TD O["Option for
nullability"] --> Safe["Safe Rust core"] Res["Result for
errors"] --> Safe Ref["owned type or
scoped reference"] --> Safe Safe --> Done["all later code is
ordinary safe Rust"]
ch08.caption: Second half: the translated values feed the safe Rust core. Once past the wrapper, no raw C pointer travels deeper, so the rest of the code stays ordinary safe Rust.

items: Match the ABI exactly.
Document who owns the pointer and who frees it.
Convert nullability into `Option` or explicit error handling at the boundary.
Validate string assumptions: encoding, lifetime, and termination.
Do not invent references from raw FFI pointers unless the lifetime story is real.
Be explicit about layout expectations and `repr(C)` where required.
Do not let unwinding expectations stay fuzzy across the boundary.
Keep the unsafe part in one wrapper layer so the rest of the code can stay ordinary Rust.

ch08.text: Auditing unsafe code
Writing safe abstractions over unsafe internals

If the callee can check bounds, maintain ownership, and prevent aliasing mistakes, keep the public API safe and isolate the raw operation internally. This is the common pattern for slices, small buffer wrappers, parsers, and data-structure internals.

If correctness depends on facts the callee cannot validate, such as a pointer being valid for a chosen lifetime or a caller-controlled aliasing guarantee, make that obligation explicit with `unsafe fn` and document the preconditions precisely.
How this lands by background

Almost nobody meets unsafe Rust without a prior model of how memory safety works in another language. The useful thing to know is which part of that model transfers and which part will quietly mislead you. The shift is rarely about syntax. It is about where the proof of safety lives and who is responsible for it once the compiler steps back.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

Unsafe Rust is a cost, not a shortcut. Use it where the representation win is real, document the invariant where reviewers can see it, and keep the surface area small enough that future maintainers can still re-derive the proof.
Examples
Example 1: a safe slice API over raw-pointer writes
The caller gets a safe function. Bounds and exclusivity are enforced before the raw-pointer write loop begins.

What to look at: every check that makes the unsafe write legal happens before the loop. The bounds test and the exclusive &mut [u8] borrow turn the caller-facing function into a safe one, so the raw-pointer write at the center inherits an already-proven invariant rather than asserting a new one.

ch08.chart:
flowchart TD
  In["fill_window: slice, start, value"] --> Chk{"start plus len within bounds?"}
  Chk -->|no| Err["return early, no write"]
  Chk -->|yes| Ptr["as_mut_ptr then offset"]
  Ptr -->|unsafe ptr write| W["write bytes in range"]
  W --> Done["safe return"]
ch08.caption: The bounds check guards the only unsafe step. Because the slice arrives as an exclusive &mut [u8], exclusivity is already established, so the write cannot alias another live reference.

ch08.text: The public function is safe because it can check bounds and it borrows the slice as &mut [u8], which already gives exclusive access.
The only unsafe step is pointer arithmetic plus write. Everything around it exists to make that one step justified.
Overwriting with the raw-pointer write method (.write()) is fine here because the element type is u8. For a drop-carrying type such as String, skipping the old destructor would matter.
Example 2: build initialized bytes with `MaybeUninit`
The storage starts explicitly uninitialized, each byte is written once, and `assume_init` appears only after the invariant is fully true.

What to look at: the order of operations. The array is declared as uninitialized storage, each slot is written exactly once, and only the final assume_init turns the storage into a real value. Trace the diagram and confirm that no read happens on any branch before the last write.

ch08.chart:
flowchart TD
  U["MaybeUninit array, uninit"] --> W0["write index 0"]
  W0 --> W1["write index 1"]
  W1 --> W2["write index 2"]
  W2 --> W3["write index 3"]
  W3 -->|all slots written| AI["unsafe assume_init"]
  AI --> V["real fixed-size array"]
ch08.caption: Initialization is a straight line with one exit. Every slot is written before assume_init runs, so the value the rest of the program sees is always fully valid.

ch08.text: All four elements must be written before the array becomes a real [u8; 4].
It models the not-yet-valid state explicitly, which is far better than treating arbitrary bytes as if they already represent a valid value.
The critical review question is simple: can any path read the value before every element is initialized? If yes, the abstraction is wrong.
Exercises
The exercise page asks you to audit a raw-pointer abstraction, identify UB risks, repair `MaybeUninit` misuse, and design a Rust wrapper that keeps unsafe obligations at the correct boundary.
Summary

items: Unsafe Rust allows operations the compiler cannot prove safe; it does not weaken the actual safety requirements.
Undefined behavior includes invalid pointer dereferences, reference aliasing violations, data races, invalid values, and many bad FFI contracts.
Raw pointers are representation tools. References are promises. Turning one into the other is where invariants matter most.
MaybeUninit<T> is the right model for genuinely uninitialized storage. assume_init belongs at the end of a proven initialization path.
The best production pattern is usually a safe API with a tiny, documented, auditable unsafe core.

ch09.text: Smart pointers encode ownership count, mutation authority, thread sharing, and address stability. This chapter uses Box, Rc, Arc, Weak, interior mutability, and Pin as production design choices.
Builds on Chapters 05, 07, and 08

Chapter 05 introduced ownership inside structs. Chapter 07 separated move, copy, and clone. Chapter 08 explained why some low-level invariants matter enough to be audited explicitly. This chapter brings those threads together around the standard smart pointers and pinning model.
Opening scenario

A service combines recursive parser state, shared planning data, cross-thread schemas, mutable retry coordination, and pinned async work. The business requirement is to encode each ownership and movement rule in the pointer type: single owner, shared owner, synchronized mutation, non-owning back edge, or immovable state.
A good review order

items: How many owners are semantically real: one or many?
Is mutation local, runtime-checked, or synchronized across threads?
Is a back-edge observing or owning?
Does the value merely live on the heap, or must it actually stop moving?

ch09.text: Mental model
Core concepts
Box<T>: heap ownership

Box<T> means one owner plus heap indirection. It does not imply sharing, reference counting, or interior mutability. It is the right answer when the pointee should still have one owner but the outer type needs recursive shape, a smaller stack footprint, or a stable-sized field.

What to look at: the box is a thin owning handle that lives wherever the field lives, while the pointee it owns sits on the heap. That indirection is what lets a recursive type have a finite size, because the field is one pointer wide no matter how deep the chain goes.

ch09.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Stack
    H[Box handle]
  end
  subgraph Heap
    N[Node data]
    N -->|next: Option Box| N2[Node data]
  end
  H -->|owns, one owner| N
ch09.caption: A Box is a single owning pointer on the stack; the value it owns lives on the heap, which is what makes a recursive node a fixed-size field.

ch09.text: Think of it as owned heap storage, not as “shared pointer lite.”
Rc<T>: single-threaded shared ownership
Rc<T> is shared ownership inside one thread. Cloning an Rc adds another owner by incrementing a non-atomic count. Because the count is not atomic, Rc<T> is not for thread boundaries.

What to look at: several handles point at one allocation, and the allocation carries a count. Each clone bumps the count; each drop lowers it; the value is freed only when the count reaches zero. The data itself is shared and read-only through these handles.

ch09.chart:
flowchart TD
  A[Rc handle a] --> V[(value, strong=3)]
  B[Rc handle b] --> V
  C[Rc handle c] --> V
  V -.->|count hits 0| F[freed]
ch09.caption: Cloning an Rc adds an owner and raises the strong count; the allocation lives until the last owner drops and the count reaches zero.
