ch09.text: If you later need shared mutation as well, that is a second decision. Many single-thread designs use Rc<RefCell<T>>, but you should read that type honestly: multiple owners plus runtime borrow checking.
Arc<T>: thread-safe shared ownership
Arc<T> is the cross-thread sibling of Rc<T>. The reference count is atomic, so cloning is safe across threads. The atomic work is usually modest, but it is not free.

The key correction is this: Arc<T> solves ownership count, not arbitrary mutation safety. If multiple threads need mutation, add a second mechanism such as a lock or redesign toward message passing. Also remember that thread use still depends on the inner T satisfying the relevant Send and Sync bounds.
Interior mutability: moving the borrow check somewhere else

What to look at: all three of the types below let you mutate through a shared handle, which ordinary borrowing forbids. The difference is purely where and how the aliasing rule is enforced. A Cell<T> sidesteps borrowing by only swapping whole values, a RefCell<T> keeps the same rule but checks it at runtime and panics on violation, and a Mutex<T> enforces it across threads by blocking on a lock.
RefCell<T>: runtime borrow checking

RefCell<T> lets shared owners borrow mutably at runtime. The same borrowing law still exists, but violations become runtime panics instead of compile-time errors. That is useful in single-thread graphs, UI trees, and other genuinely dynamic borrow patterns. It is also a tradeoff you should feel.
Cell<T> and interior mutability

Cell<T> is the smaller, calmer interior-mutability tool when you only need to copy out, replace, or swap values. It works well for counters, flags, and small cached scalars in one thread. Unlike RefCell<T>, it does not hand out interior references.
Mutex<T>: ownership under synchronization

Mutex<T> provides interior mutability by handing out exclusive access only after lock acquisition. It is the shared-state sibling of ordinary exclusive borrowing. Lock scope, contention, poisoning policy, and deadlock risk are now operational concerns.
Weak<T> and cyclic references

Reference counting alone cannot collect cycles. If parent owns child and child also owns parent through a strong Rc or Arc, neither side reaches a strong count of zero. The usual repair is simple: owning edges stay strong, observational back-edges become weak.
A Weak<T> does not keep the allocation alive. Calling upgrade() returns Option<Rc<T>> or Option<Arc<T>>, which forces you to handle the “owner already gone” case explicitly.
Pin<T> and immovable values

Pinning matters when moving a value would break an address-sensitive invariant. The classic example is future polling: Future::poll takes Pin<&mut Self>. The compiler can generate state machines whose internal references assume the future stays put while polled.

Pinning does not stop all mutation. It stops moves that would invalidate the address-sensitive part of the invariant. For most ordinary types, this distinction does not matter because they are effectively movable and implement Unpin.
Pin<Box<T>> and Pin<&mut T>

Pin<Box<T>> means you own the value and pin the pointee in its heap allocation. This is common when storing futures you want to poll later. Pin<&mut T> is the temporary pinned view used when actually operating on the pinned value.
The sharp edge is projection. For !Unpin types, you cannot casually recover a plain &mut T because that would re-enable movement. Later async and unsafe chapters revisit this with deeper machinery.
Choosing the right pointer type

What to look at: the choice is a short series of independent questions, not a single menu pick. Answer them in order, and the type usually falls out. How many owners are real? If many, do they live on one thread or cross thread boundaries? Does anything need to mutate the shared value, and if so, is the borrow pattern static enough for the compiler or dynamic enough to need a runtime check or a lock? Only at the end do you ask whether the value must also stop moving.

ch09.caption: First the ownership questions: how many owners, and if many, do they cross thread boundaries. A single owner picks Box, and only Box faces the separate question of whether the value must stop moving.

ch09.text: Once owner count and thread boundary are settled, the remaining question is whether the shared value also needs mutation, and under which enforcement model:

ch09.chart:
flowchart TD
  Cont[shared mutation needed] --> Rc[shared on one thread, Rc T]
  Cont --> Arc[shared across threads, Arc T]
  Rc --> Mut1{Borrow pattern}
  Mut1 -->|small copy or swap| Cell[wrap in Cell]
  Mut1 -->|dynamic borrows| RefCell[wrap in RefCell]
  Arc --> Mut2{Need shared mutation}
  Mut2 -->|yes| Mutex[wrap in Mutex]
ch09.caption: The second half resolves shared mutation: a single-thread Rc reaches for Cell or RefCell depending on the borrow pattern, while a cross-thread Arc reaches for a Mutex.

ch09.text: A useful correction for senior engineers is this: pointer choice is often two or three independent questions layered together. Arc<Mutex<T>> means shared ownership and synchronized mutation. Rc<RefCell<T>> means shared ownership and runtime borrow checking on one thread. Read the composition literally.
How this lands by background

Most senior engineers do not meet smart pointers as a blank slate; they arrive with a pointer model from another language. The useful thing to know is which part of that model carries over and which part will quietly mislead you. The shift is almost never about which type maps to which library class. It is about the fact that ownership count, mutation authority, and address stability now live in the type and are checked, rather than being left to convention or a runtime.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
Smart pointers are not escape hatches from ownership design. They are ownership design written into the type. If the type looks complicated, the runtime story is probably complicated too.
Examples
Example 1: shared tree edges with weak back-references
The children are strongly owned. The parent edge is weak, so the graph stays acyclic.

What to look at: the two edges between root and leaf are deliberately different kinds. The root owns the leaf through a strong Rc in its children list, while the leaf only observes the root through a Weak parent pointer. Trace the two arrows in the diagram, then notice that the leaf reads its parent through upgrade(), which can fail if the owner is already gone. That asymmetry is what keeps the graph acyclic and lets the count actually reach zero.

ch09.chart:
flowchart LR
  Root[root Rc] -->|strong: owns child| Leaf[leaf Rc]
  Leaf -.->|weak: observes via upgrade| Root
  Note[strong edge keeps alive, weak edge does not]
ch09.caption: Owning edges stay strong and point down the tree; the back-edge to the parent is weak, so no cycle pins the allocation alive.

ch09.expected:
root children = 1
leaf parent = root
root strong = 1

ch09.text: Quick check: change the node names or add another child. The useful signal is not the printout itself. It is that the ownership graph reads clearly from the types: strong edges own, weak edges observe.
A child can discover its parent only by upgrading a weak pointer. The parent is not kept alive by the child.
Trees, observer lists, dependency graphs, and cache indexes often need one-way ownership plus non-owning lookup edges.
Example 2: polling a pinned future with Box::pin
The example is deliberately small so you can see both forms: owned pinned storage and a pinned mutable view during polling.

What to look at: Box::pin creates the owned, pinned storage once, and then the loop polls it repeatedly through as_mut(), which hands poll the Pin<&mut Self> it requires. Each poll either reports it is still pending and yields, or returns a ready value and ends the loop. Follow that one-future, two-exits cycle in the diagram, then read the same shape in the match arms.

ch09.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Pinned: Box pin creates owner
  Pinned --> Poll: as_mut gives Pin and mut Self
  Poll --> Pending: not done yet
  Pending --> Poll: poll again
  Poll --> Ready: value produced
  Ready --> [*]: break loop
ch09.caption: One pinned future is polled in a loop; each poll yields Pending and repeats, or yields Ready and exits. The pin stays fixed across every poll.

ch09.text: Quick check: increase the starting count and rerun. The visible behavior changes, but the structural point stays the same: Box::pin gives you a pinned owner, and as_mut() produces the pinned mutable view required by polling.
The pointee inside the box, not the box handle itself, is the thing treated as immovable for the poll protocol.
The poll API must be safe for compiler-generated state machines whose internal layout may rely on a stable address while the future is alive.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch09_smart_pointers_and_pinning/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The exercise page asks you to choose pointer types for realistic scenarios, replace an owning cycle with Weak, distinguish Cell, RefCell, and Mutex, and explain why async futures are commonly manipulated through pinned pointers.
Summary

items: Choose smart pointers by ownership truth: one owner, many owners, one thread, many threads, movable, or pinned.
Box<T>, Rc<T>, and Arc<T> answer ownership-count and thread questions, not arbitrary mutation questions.
Cell<T>, RefCell<T>, and Mutex<T> are different interior-mutability contracts with different enforcement costs.
Weak<T> is the standard repair for non-owning back-edges in reference-counted graphs.
Pin matters only when movement itself would break correctness. Heap allocation alone is not the same thing.

ch10.text: Contiguous storage choices affect allocation, cache locality, and API flexibility. This chapter defines arrays for fixed shape, slices for borrowed access, and vectors for owned growth.
Builds on Chapters 04, 06, and 07

Borrowing rules from Chapter 04, vector ownership hazards from Chapter 06, and allocation-aware API design from Chapter 07 all meet here. Arrays, slices, and vectors are not beginner-only material. They are where many production Rust performance and API decisions become concrete.
Opening scenario

An ingestion service parses fixed headers, scans metric windows, and builds dynamic retry batches. The business requirement is to choose the narrowest storage shape for each path: fixed arrays for protocol invariants, slices for borrowed contiguous access, and vectors for owned runtime growth.
A practical decision order
Read the diagram top to bottom: each question narrows the choice to one storage shape before you write a single line. The same four questions drive every example in this chapter.

ch10.caption: Length in the type means an array; a borrowed view means a slice; runtime ownership means a vector, with inline-first reserved for profiled hot paths.

ch10.text: Mental model
Core concepts
Which tool when?
Fixed-size arrays

An array such as [u8; 32] is one value whose size is known at compile time. That makes arrays useful for bounded protocol fields, cryptographic material, coordinates, and other cases where the exact count is semantically real.
The length is in the type. `[u8; 4]` and `[u8; 8]` are different types, not the same type with a stored runtime length.
Slices as views

A slice is a borrowed view into contiguous elements. It is not an owner, and it does not decide allocation strategy. That is why slice parameters are usually the right API shape for parsing, scanning, hashing, serialization, and most read-only transforms.
The same function can accept an array, a vector borrow, or a sub-slice. That keeps callers flexible and keeps the algorithm honest about what it actually needs.
How a Vec<T> is laid out in memory

The thing to notice is that the vector value itself is tiny and lives wherever you put it (stack, struct, another vector). It is three words: a pointer, a length, and a capacity. The elements live somewhere else, in one contiguous heap allocation that the vector owns.

ch10.chart:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Owner[Vec value - 3 words]
    P[ptr]
    L[len = 3]
    C[cap = 4]
  end
  P --> E0
  subgraph Heap[Heap buffer - capacity 4]
    E0[elem 0]
    E1[elem 1]
    E2[elem 2]
    E3[spare slot]
  end
  Slice[and T view] -. ptr + len .-> E0
ch10.caption: The owner is three words; the elements sit in one heap allocation. len marks how many are live, cap marks how many fit, and a slice is just a borrowed pointer-and-length into the same buffer.

ch10.text: Because the owner is so small, moving the vector value moves only those three words. Ownership of the buffer transfers, but the elements are not copied or re-touched at the move. This is why returning a vector from a function is cheap even when it holds millions of elements.

items: length = how many elements are currently initialized and logically present.
capacity = how many elements can fit before another allocation may be needed.
buffer = contiguous owned storage, usually on the heap.

ch10.text: Capacity, allocation, and growth

Preallocation is one of the simplest meaningful vector optimizations. If you know an upper bound, use Vec::with_capacity or reserve space before the hot push loop. That reduces allocation churn and often makes profiles cleaner.

Do not depend on an exact growth factor. Rust does not promise one in the language contract. Treat growth behavior as an implementation detail and validate the workload with measurements, capacity logs, or allocation tracing.
Capacity planning is an optimization, not a license to hard-code folklore. Use it when a bound is real. Skip it when the bound is fake or when the complexity costs more than the saved allocations.
Iterators over arrays, slices, and vectors
Mutation patterns

The recurring rule is familiar by now: if the algorithm only mutates existing elements, slices and iter_mut() are excellent. If the algorithm also changes vector shape, end any active borrows first or split the work into phases.
Small-vector optimizations

Some workloads create many tiny vectors whose most common size is just a few elements: tags, short path segments, tiny batch keys, or parser-side scratch buffers. In those cases, an inline-first representation can avoid heap allocation for the common path and spill to the heap only when the collection grows past an inline threshold.

This is an ecosystem pattern, not the default answer. Inline-first containers usually make the parent struct larger, increase move cost, and can inflate stack pressure. Use them only after profiling shows that ordinary vectors are a real problem.
Cache locality and contiguous storage
What changes coming from another language

The three shapes have close analogues in most languages, so the syntax is rarely the hard part. The mental shift is that ownership and resize rules are now part of the type system, which changes how you read an API signature and which mistakes the compiler catches for you.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The cheapest-looking signature is not always the cheapest design. A slice-first API often removes needless ownership constraints. A vector-only API often leaks an allocation assumption that the algorithm never needed in the first place.
Examples
Example 1: one slice-first function works for arrays and vectors
The algorithm wants a contiguous read-only view, so the function accepts a slice and callers keep their own storage choices.

What to look at: three different owners all reach the same function through one &[u64] parameter. The array, the vector borrow, and a sub-slice converge to the same borrowed view, so no caller is forced to allocate or give up ownership.

ch10.chart:
flowchart TD
  A["fixed: array u64;4"] -->|and fixed| S["and u64 slice"]
  V["dynamic: Vec u64"] -->|and dynamic| S
  Sub["any sub-slice"] -->|and v 1..3| S
  S --> F["tail_sum reads contiguous view"]
  F --> R["u64 result"]
ch10.caption: One slice parameter accepts an array, a vector borrow, or a sub-slice; the function never learns or cares which owner it came from.

ch10.text: Quick check: run the baseline, then change the array contents or the take counts. The useful lesson is not the arithmetic. It is that the API shape stays calm because the function borrows a slice rather than forcing a vector.
A slice says “contiguous borrowed data.” That is exactly the contract this function needs.
Arrays, vectors, and sub-slices all call the same function without extra allocation or a narrower public signature.
Example 2: preallocate when a trustworthy upper bound exists
The batch size is bounded by the input slice length, so capacity planning is simple and justified.

What to look at: the capacity is reserved once from a real bound (the result can never be longer than the input), and then the loop only filters and pushes. The diagram is the pipeline; the listing fills in the arithmetic.

ch10.chart:
flowchart TD
  In["ids: and u32 slice"] --> Cap["Vec::with_capacity(ids.len())"]
  Cap --> Loop{for each id}
  Loop -->|id is even| Push["push id * 10"]
  Loop -->|id is odd| Skip["skip"]
  Push --> Loop
  Skip --> Loop
  Loop -->|done| Out["return owned Vec u32"]
ch10.caption: Reserve once from a bound that cannot be exceeded, then filter-and-push without further reallocation; the helper hands back an owned vector the caller keeps.

ch10.expected:
len = 3
can fit two more = true
last = 220

ch10.text: Quick check: keep the upper bound tied to the input length, then change the IDs or appended values and rerun. The point is that preallocation follows a real bound, not a guessed folklore capacity.
The function returns an owned vector because the batch must survive after the helper returns.
Capacity is chosen from a real bound: the result cannot exceed the number of input elements.
You pay a small planning step up front to reduce later allocation churn in the push loop.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch10_arrays_slices_and_vectors/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to benchmark preallocation against push-only growth, rewrite a helper over slices instead of vectors, and choose among arrays, slices, vectors, and inline-first storage for realistic workloads.
Summary

items: Use arrays when size is part of the invariant, slices when the algorithm needs a view, and vectors when the code needs owned growth.
A Vec<T> is an owner of contiguous storage with separate logical length and allocation capacity.
Slice-first APIs are usually the most flexible and honest public contract for contiguous read or write algorithms.
Preallocation helps when the bound is real. Exact growth strategy is not something production code should assume.
Contiguous storage buys locality for scans and batch work, but middle insertions, stable-address needs, and inline-first tricks all carry tradeoffs.

ch11.text: Hash maps and sets sit on critical lookup paths. This chapter covers key ownership, borrowed lookup, entry-based updates, deterministic output, and hashing policy for production data access.
Builds on Chapters 06, 07, and 10

Chapter 06 explained durable handles versus temporary borrows in collections. Chapter 07 separated moves, copies, and clones. Chapter 10 covered contiguous storage and allocation-aware API shape. This chapter applies those same design instincts to hashed and ordered associative collections.
Opening scenario

An ingress service maintains route counters, active feature flags, in-memory indexes, and deterministic operator-facing configuration dumps. The business requirement is explicit key ownership and lookup policy: own normalized keys in collections, borrow for read paths, update with one table access, and choose ordered structures when output order is contractual.
A reliable review order

items: Does this call path own keys and values, or only borrow them temporarily?
Is the collection unordered membership, unordered key-value lookup, or ordered key traversal?
Is the hot update path doing one lookup or several?
Does the boundary need denial-of-service resilience more than raw hash speed?

ch11.text: Mental model
Core concepts
HashMap fundamentals

Use HashMap when you want expected fast key lookup and update, and key order is not part of the external contract. Use HashSet when the value is really membership and deduplication rather than key-value association.

Sets are not a secondary topic. In production code they often replace improvised boolean maps, duplicate filtering passes, or repeated linear searches over vectors. If the question is “have I seen this key already?”, a set is usually the right structure.
Ownership of keys and values

The whole API divides cleanly along one line: which calls move data across the table boundary and which only borrow across it. Insert is the one inbound move; remove and into_iter are the outbound moves; everything on the read path borrows and leaves the table owning what it owned before. Hold that picture and the rest of the chapter is mostly choosing the right edge for each call site.

ch11.chart:
flowchart TD
  Caller[Caller owns key and value] -->|insert moves in| Map[(HashMap owns entries)]
  Map -->|get and contains borrow| Read[Read path keeps borrow]
  Map -->|iter borrows| Loop[Borrowed iteration]
  Map --> Cont[outbound moves below]
ch11.caption: Inbound: insert moves owned data in; read paths borrow and leave ownership where it was.

ch11.text: The same table also has two paths that move data back out:

ch11.chart:
flowchart TD
  Cont[(HashMap owns entries)] -->|remove moves out| Out[Caller owns value again]
  Cont -->|into_iter consumes| Drain[Table consumed, items moved out]
ch11.caption: Outbound: remove moves one value back out; into_iter consumes the table and moves every item out.

items: insert moves owned keys and values into the collection.
get and contains usually borrow.
remove moves the removed value back out.
iter borrows; into_iter consumes the collection and moves items out.

ch11.text: That ownership story matters operationally. If your parser already produced an owned route key, the map can take it directly. If your request path only has a borrowed `&str`, you can often look up by borrow without allocating, but storing a new entry still requires some owned key to live in the table.
Borrowed lookups

The reason a table of owned String keys accepts a borrowed &str query is a small trait relationship rather than magic: the lookup methods are generic over a borrowed form of the key, and String can be borrowed as str with matching equality and hashing. The diagram shows that bridge; the code below is what it looks like at the call site.

ch11.chart:
flowchart TD
  Q["&str query"] -->|same Eq and Hash| Bridge["Borrow bridge: String borrows as str"]
  Bridge --> Slot["Owned String key in table"]
  Slot -->|match| Hit["Some borrowed value"]
  Slot -->|no match| Miss[None]
ch11.caption: The query type and the stored key share equality and hashing through a borrow relationship, so no owned key is built to look one up.

ch11.text: One of Rust's best collection features is borrowed lookup. A HashMap can be queried by &str. A HashSet can test membership with &str.

This is usually what you want on the read path. Store owned strings once. Query them by borrowed slices. That avoids allocating just to answer a membership or lookup question. For standard string keys, the equality and hashing behavior line up the way you expect.
Entry API

The Entry API is the right tool when one key path does read-modify-write work: counters, last-seen timestamps, aggregation, or “initialize if absent, then mutate.” It removes duplicate table lookups and makes the intent obvious.

There is one nuance worth keeping explicit: with ordinary stable std Entry APIs, the entry key itself is owned. If your key path is a borrowed `&str`, `entry(route.to_owned())` still allocates the owned key. That can still be the right design, but do not pretend the allocation disappeared. What disappeared is the second hash-table lookup.
The practical rule is simple: Entry is perfect when the caller already owns the key. Borrowed lookup is perfect when you only need to read. Treat those as two different fast paths.
Custom hashers

A standard library hash map has a third type parameter for the build hasher. In ordinary code you rarely need to name it. The default choice uses randomized state and is a strong default for public or untrusted inputs because collision behavior is part of your operational risk surface.

Faster non-randomized or domain-specific hashers can be a good fit for trusted internal workloads with measured hot paths, especially when keys are small and frequent. But that is an engineering decision, not a reflex. Benchmark first. Document the trust boundary. Keep security posture in view.
BTreeMap vs HashMap

The choice between the four collections is two yes-or-no questions, not a performance debate. First: do you need a value per key, or only membership? That picks map versus set. Second: does anything downstream depend on iteration order? That picks the hashed variant versus the ordered B-tree variant. Answer those two and the type falls out.

ch11.chart:
flowchart TD
  Start[What do you store] -->|value per key| Map[Need a map]
  Start -->|only membership| Set[Need a set]
  Map -->|order matters| BMap[BTreeMap]
  Map -->|order does not matter| HMap[HashMap]
  Set -->|order matters| BSet[BTreeSet]
  Set -->|order does not matter| HSet[HashSet]
ch11.caption: Two questions decide the collection: value-per-key versus membership, then ordered iteration versus not.

items: Expected fast lookup, insert, and membership checks.
No stable iteration order guarantee.
Good default for caches, counters, indexes, and dedup sets.
Ordered keys and deterministic iteration.
Natural fit for sorted output and range-oriented logic.
Often simpler than “use HashMap, then sort later” when ordering is always required.

ch11.text: Stable ordering considerations
If operators, tests, logs, snapshots, or downstream systems care about output order, plain hash iteration is the wrong boundary contract. Choose an ordered structure or sort at the render edge.

A common production pattern is this: keep the hot mutable index in a HashMap, then project into a BTreeMap or a sorted vector only when you emit deterministic output. If ordering is needed everywhere, start ordered.
Hashing performance and denial-of-service tradeoffs

items: Hash cost is real work. Key size, equality cost, and cardinality all matter in hot paths.
Collision behavior is also real work. Public endpoints should treat adversarial keys as part of the design.
Ordered trees may win operationally when they remove a later sort pass or simplify deterministic behavior.
Capacity planning still matters here too. Use with_capacity when the bound is real, not guessed.
Benchmark workload shapes, not only microbenchmarks on one synthetic key distribution.

ch11.text: How this lands by background

Every one of these languages gives you a dictionary and a set, so the data structure is not the new part. What changes in Rust is who owns the key after you insert it, and the fact that reading does not have to build a key at all. The cards below name the one mental-model shift each background tends to trip over, not the API spelling, which you can read off the standard library in a minute.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The collection choice is not only about asymptotic lookup speed. In real systems it also shapes ownership, determinism, test stability, memory pressure, and how resilient the service is to hostile key patterns.
Examples
Example 1: owned key handoff plus Entry API
When the caller already owns the key, Entry is the clean update path: one table lookup, direct mutation, and no extra duplicate logic.

What to look at: entry(route) is a single trip into the table. If the slot is missing it is created with or_insert(0); either way you get a mutable reference and add one in place. There is no separate contains_key branch and no second lookup. Follow the two paths in the diagram, then read the same fork in record_hit.

ch11.chart:
flowchart TD
  Call[record_hit with owned route] --> Entry[entry on one lookup]
  Entry -->|key present| Found[Existing counter]
  Entry -->|key absent| New[or_insert 0 creates slot]
  Found --> Bump[Add one in place]
  New --> Bump
  Bump --> Store[Stored count updated]
ch11.caption: Both the present and absent cases converge on one mutable reference, so the update is a single table access.

ch11.text: The route key is moved into the map. The returned entry reference mutates the stored counter in place.
No duplicated `contains_key` branch, no second hash-table lookup, and no ambiguity about who owns the key.
Example 2: borrowed lookup for reads, ordered projection for output
Store owned strings once. Query them by borrow. Project into an ordered structure only when stable render order matters.

What to look at: this is a pipeline with three distinct stages. The reads in the middle, get("api") and contains("worker"), borrow the owned-string keys without allocating. Only at the render edge does into_iter().collect() move the entries into a BTreeMap so output is deterministic. The diagram is that pipeline; the three printed lines are its three outputs.

ch11.chart:
flowchart TD
  Build[Insert owned String keys] --> HMap[(HashMap and HashSet)]
  HMap -->|borrowed &str reads| Reads[api count and has worker]
  HMap -->|into_iter collect| BMap[(BTreeMap, ordered)]
  BMap --> Render[Deterministic ordered line]
ch11.caption: Build with owned keys, read by borrow, and only convert to an ordered structure at the moment output order has to be stable.

ch11.expected:
api count = 2
has worker = true
ordered = api=2,billing=1,worker=3

ch11.text: get("api") and contains("worker") do not need fresh owned strings.
The set answers membership directly. There is no need for a parallel boolean map when membership is the only question.
Converting to a BTreeMap gives deterministic output without pretending hash iteration order was stable all along.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch11_hash_maps_and_sets/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The exercise page asks you to remove duplicate lookups with the Entry API, implement borrowed lookups for `String` keys, compare `HashMap` and `BTreeMap` for deterministic output, and reason about hasher choices at production boundaries.
Next chapter

Hashed and ordered associative collections cover keyed access. Chapter 12 turns to matrices and multidimensional data, where the question shifts from who owns a key to how a logical grid maps onto one contiguous block of memory. The same ownership and borrowing instincts carry over; the new concern is layout, indexing, and the cost of the access pattern.
Summary

items: Maps and sets are ownership boundaries. Insert moves owned data in; lookups usually borrow.
Borrowed lookup is one of the strongest Rust-native patterns for string-keyed indexes and membership sets.
The Entry API removes duplicate table lookups on update paths, but ordinary stable entry still needs an owned key.
`HashMap` and `HashSet` are about expected fast lookup; `BTreeMap` and `BTreeSet` are about ordered traversal and deterministic behavior.
Hasher choice is a production tradeoff involving speed, key shape, and denial-of-service posture, not just a benchmark number.

ch12.text: Matrix and multidimensional workloads need explicit layout, shape, ownership, and traversal rules. This chapter covers dense and sparse representations used for numeric pipelines and accelerator handoff.
Builds on Chapters 08, 10, and 11

Chapter 08 explained unsafe Rust and FFI proof obligations. Chapter 10 covered contiguous storage and slice-first APIs. Chapter 11 covered workload-aware data-structure choice. This chapter applies those same instincts to multidimensional numeric and domain data, where layout becomes part of the performance, correctness, and interop contract.
Opening scenario

Picture a data-processing service that handles three shapes of numeric data at once: dense image grids it convolves with a kernel, a recommendation score matrix it slices into per-user windows, and a large mostly-zero feature matrix it hands to an accelerator. None of these is well served by the same representation, and the expensive failures here are not arithmetic bugs. They are a column-oriented BLAS call fed a row-major buffer, a view that copied a megabyte it should have borrowed, or a sparse matrix stored in the format that was cheap to build and ruinous to multiply. The job of this chapter is to make layout, ownership, and traversal explicit decisions you take on purpose rather than defaults you discover under a profiler.
A reliable design order

items: Decide whether the data is dense, jagged, or sparse.
Choose the physical layout before you optimize the arithmetic.
Choose owned storage for long-lived buffers and borrowed views for windows and tiles.
Make foreign-library layout assumptions explicit at the boundary, not in a comment after the bug.

ch12.text: Mental model
Core concepts
Row-major and column-major representations

What to look at: both layouts store the same six logical cells in the same six bytes of memory; the only difference is the order. Row-major lays the first row down first, so walking a row is unit-stride and walking a column jumps by the row width. Column-major flips that. The diagram below shows the same 2x3 matrix under both rules, so you can see why one loop order is contiguous and the other is not.

ch12.caption: One logical matrix, two linearizations. Row-major keeps each row contiguous; column-major keeps each column contiguous.

ch12.text: The important operational consequence is not the formula itself. It is which loop order is unit-stride, which access pattern is cache-friendly, and which foreign library can consume the buffer without conversion.
Nested vectors and their costs

The difference between a flat Vec and a Vec of Vecs is not syntax, it is the heap shape. A flat buffer is one allocation the CPU can stream through. A nested buffer is an outer array of pointers, each one leading to a separately allocated row that can sit anywhere in memory, so every row access pays for an extra hop and the locality is gone before any arithmetic begins.

items: Each row is a separate allocation and a separate owner.
Rows need not be adjacent in memory.
Jagged shapes are easy, but dense numeric kernels pay with pointer chasing.
FFI handoff becomes awkward because there is no single buffer to pass.

ch12.text: That does not make nested vectors wrong. They are a good fit when row lengths truly differ or when the domain is naturally ragged. They are just not the calm default for dense matrices.
Matrix views and slices

What to look at: a view does not allocate. It points back into the owner’s buffer and carries the metadata needed to skip past the rows it does not care about. The lifetime parameter is the part that earns its keep: the borrow checker refuses to let the view be used after the buffer is dropped, so a dangling submatrix is a compile error rather than a runtime fault.

ch12.chart:
flowchart TD Owner["Owner: one Vec buffer"] -->|"&'a [T] borrow"| View["MatrixView
rows, cols
stride, offset"] View -->|"offset + row*stride + col"| Cell["element inside
the buffer"] Owner -. "checked: view cannot
outlive owner" .-> View
ch12.caption: A view is a borrow plus an index rule. It reads the owner's bytes through stride and offset; the lifetime keeps it from outliving the buffer.

ch12.text: A view usually borrows a slice and carries metadata: rows, cols, stride, and maybe an offset. That lets you describe submatrices, tiles, and windows without copying data into a second owner.
The view does not own the buffer. It interprets borrowed storage under an explicit layout contract.
SIMD-friendly layouts
Whether you use compiler auto-vectorization, explicit intrinsics, or an ecosystem SIMD abstraction, the layout question arrives first. Syntax cannot fix a bad stride pattern.
Sparse matrices

When most cells are zero, you stop storing the grid and start storing only the nonzeros plus the structure needed to find them. COO is the easy ingestion format, a bag of (row, col, value) triples; CSR and CSC are the compressed formats that traverse fast in one direction. The usual lifecycle is to build in COO at the edges, then compress into CSR or CSC for the traversal your kernels actually perform.
A useful rule is to separate build format from execution format. The easiest format to ingest is not always the cheapest format to multiply or traverse.
Interoperating with BLAS, LAPACK, CUDA, and HPC libraries

What to look at: the cost at a numeric boundary is rarely the math. It is the handoff. Your Rust buffer may be the wrong layout, the wrong leading dimension, or in host memory when the kernel wants device memory, and every mismatch turns into a repack or a transfer before any arithmetic runs. The diagram lays out the stages so you can see where the hidden copies hide and measure them on purpose.

ch12.chart:
flowchart TD
  Rust["Rust-owned Vec<T>"] -->|"check layout, stride, type"| Pack["repack if layout differs"]
  Pack -->|"host to device copy"| Dev["device buffer"]
  Dev -->|"launch with layout contract"| Kernel["foreign kernel: BLAS / CUDA"]
  Kernel -->|"results back, copy or transpose"| Rust
ch12.caption: Each arrow is a potential copy. The arithmetic is one box; the repacks and transfers around it often dominate the runtime.

ch12.text: Be careful with claims of zero-copy interop. A foreign kernel may still require a different layout, leading dimension, alignment rule, memory domain, or device residency than your Rust-side buffer currently has.
Interop boundary checklist
This checklist is deliberately boring. Boring is good here. Most expensive matrix interop bugs come from unstated layout or ownership assumptions, not from exotic arithmetic.
How this lands by background

Almost nobody meets Rust matrices as a blank slate. You arrive with a mental model from another ecosystem, and the useful question is which part of that model carries over and which part will quietly mislead you. With matrices the shift is rarely about API names; it is about who owns the buffer, where the layout contract lives, and how much of the indexing and lifetime work the language does for you versus asks you to spell out.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
Dense numeric code often looks like “just math,” but the hard bugs and hard performance losses are usually layout bugs. Treat layout as a first-class API decision.
Examples
Example 1: row-major Matrix<T> over Vec<T>
One contiguous owner, explicit offset calculation, and row views derived from the flat buffer.

What to look at: there is one buffer and one place where a (row, col) becomes a linear index, the offset method computing row * cols + col. Every accessor (get, set, row) routes through it, and row hands back a borrowed slice rather than a copy. Trace one cell through the diagram, then read the same path in the code.

ch12.chart:
flowchart TD
  Call["get(0, 2)"] -->|"row, col"| Off["offset = row * cols + col"]
  Off -->|"= 0 * 3 + 2 = 2"| Idx["data[2]"]
  Idx --> Val["&30"]
  Row["row(1)"] -->|"start = 1 * cols"| Slice["&data[3..6] (borrowed)"]
ch12.caption: One offset rule feeds every accessor. get returns a borrowed element; row returns a borrowed slice of the same buffer.

ch12.text: Quick check: change the inserted values or the matrix dimensions and keep the offset logic row-major. The exercise is not the printing. It is making the storage contract obvious in code.
One allocation keeps the matrix contiguous. Row slicing is just range arithmetic over one buffer.
Dense grids, image kernels, tensor-like feature blocks, and FFI handoff all benefit from one explicit owner plus a documented layout policy.
Example 2: borrowed matrix view plus const-generic fixed kernel
A view borrows without copying, while a fixed-size compile-time kernel keeps shape in the type.

What to look at: two different ways shape is carried. The MatrixView borrows a 12-element backing buffer and uses runtime stride and offset to address a 2x2 window without copying, so get(1, 1) resolves to index 5 + 1*4 + 1 = 10, the value 11. The trace function instead takes the size as a const-generic N so the shape is fixed at compile time. Follow both paths in the diagram before reading the code.

ch12.chart:
flowchart TD
  Buf["backing: 12 elements"] -->|"&'a [T] borrow"| V["MatrixView (stride 4, offset 5)"]
  V -->|"get(1,1) = 5 + 1*4 + 1"| Idx["data[10] = 11 (no copy)"]
  Fixed["[[3,1],[2,4]] (owned)"] -->|"trace<const N>"| Tr["sum diagonal 3 + 4 = 7"]
ch12.caption: Left path: a borrowed view addresses a window by runtime stride and offset. Right path: a const-generic kernel carries N in the type.

ch12.text: Quick check: change the backing data or the fixed matrix values, then rerun. The useful distinction is that the view borrows storage while the fixed kernel carries shape information at compile time.
The submatrix window is metadata plus a borrowed slice, not a copied dense owner.
The trace helper knows the square size at compile time and works for any fixed `N`.
View metadata such as stride and offset is exactly the kind of information foreign numeric APIs often need.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch12_matrices_and_multidimensional_data/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to build a row-major matrix wrapper, replace nested vectors with flat storage, design a view without copying, and choose among dense, sparse, and foreign-library layouts under production constraints.
Summary

items: A matrix in Rust is usually explicit storage plus explicit indexing policy, not a built-in abstraction.
Row-major and column-major layouts change address calculation, traversal cost, and interop correctness.
Dense matrices usually want flat Vec<T> storage; nested vectors are better for ragged data than for dense numeric kernels.
Const generics help when shape is part of the invariant. Borrowed views help when you need windows without copying.
SIMD, sparse formats, and foreign-library interop all begin with layout discipline rather than clever syntax.

ch13.text: Arena allocation supports workloads that create many related values under one lifecycle. This chapter uses region ownership and stable handles to reduce allocation overhead and simplify teardown.
Builds on Chapters 04, 06, 09, and 10

Borrowing rules from Chapter 04, handle design from Chapter 06, smart-pointer tradeoffs from Chapter 09, and contiguous-storage reasoning from Chapter 10 all converge here. Arenas are easiest to understand once you see them as lifetime grouping plus locality, not as a mysterious allocator trick.
Opening scenario

A query service parses requests, builds ASTs, resolves names, creates plans, and discards the working graph when each request finishes. The business requirement is region ownership: allocate phase-local data together, traverse it through arena references or stable handles, and release the whole region predictably.
Why arena allocation matters
Mental model

The shape to hold in your head is two columns. On the left, the general heap tracks each object on its own: every allocation and every free is an independent event the allocator has to bookkeep. On the right, an arena tracks one region: every object is born into it, and the whole region is released in a single step. The arena does not make any one allocation magically faster so much as it collapses many free operations into one.

ch13.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Heap[General heap]
    A1[alloc node] --> F1[free node]
    A2[alloc node] --> F2[free node]
    A3[alloc node] --> F3[free node]
  end
ch13.caption: General heap: every object is freed on its own, so each allocation has a matching independent free the allocator must track.

ch13.text: Side by side, the arena collapses all of those individual frees into one region teardown:

ch13.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Arena[Arena region]
    B1[alloc node] --> R[reset / drop once]
    B2[alloc node] --> R
    B3[alloc node] --> R
  end
ch13.caption: Arena region: many objects share one lifetime, so a single reset or drop reclaims all of them at once.

ch13.text: How this maps to other languages

Most engineers arrive at arenas with a habit from another language, and the habit is usually close enough to be misleading. The cards below name the one mental-model shift that matters for each background, rather than the API differences, because the API is the easy part once the model is right.
Core concepts
Bump allocators

A bump allocator is the simplest arena shape. It maintains a cursor into a region. Allocation moves the cursor forward. There is usually no per-object free. The cheap operation is whole-region reset or drop.
That model is strong when most temporary objects share one scope. It is weak when individual objects must be freed independently.
Object graphs without reference cycles

A common Rust repair for graph-shaped data is simple: let one arena own all nodes, then let edges store NodeId handles instead of Rc<Node> pointers. The graph becomes one owner plus cheap handles, not a web of ref-counted owners.

This is often calmer than Rc<RefCell<T>> for ASTs, IR, routing graphs, and domain DAGs. You remove cycles by construction because edges are not owners. You also regain explicit control over mutation and traversal from the arena root.

The diagram below is the same graph drawn two ways. Look at where ownership lives. On the left every edge is an owner, so a back-edge from D to A forms a reference cycle that never drops to zero and leaks. On the right the arena is the only owner and every edge is just an index, so the identical back-edge is harmless data and one drop frees the whole region.

ch13.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph RC[Rc edges own]
    A[Node A] -->|owns| B[Node B]
    B -->|owns| D[Node D]
    D -->|owns, back-edge| A
  end
ch13.caption: Owning Rc edges: the back-edge from D to A closes a reference cycle that never drops to zero, so the whole loop leaks.

ch13.text: Side by side, the same shape redrawn so the arena is the only owner and every edge is just an index:

ch13.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph IDX[Arena + index edges]
    Ar[(Arena owns all)] --> N0[id 0]
    Ar --> N1[id 1]
    Ar --> N3[id 3]
    N0 -->|edge id 1| N1
    N1 -->|edge id 3| N3
    N3 -->|edge id 0, back-edge| N0
  end
ch13.caption: Index edges into a single-owner arena: the identical back-edge is now a harmless integer, and one drop frees the whole region.

ch13.text: Arena-backed ASTs

ASTs are a near-perfect arena workload. You parse once, build many small nodes, connect them densely, run analysis passes, and then discard the whole tree. A region allocator or ID arena usually matches the operational truth better than individually boxed nodes.

items: Node creation is append-only during parsing.
Traversal is read-heavy after construction.
Edges are usually logical identity, not shared ownership.
The whole tree often dies as one batch.

ch13.text: Lifetimes with arenas

The difference is what crosses the boundary back to the caller. A reference arena hands back a borrow that is chained to the arena’s lifetime, so the borrow checker will not let that reference outlive the arena. An index arena hands back a small plain value that owns nothing, so it can travel anywhere; the cost is that you must go back to the arena to turn the handle into data.

ch13.chart:
flowchart TD
  C[Caller] -->|"alloc(value)"| Ar[Arena]
  Ar -->|"&'a T borrow, tied to arena"| RefPath[Use within arena lifetime]
  Ar -->|"NodeId, plain value"| IdPath[Travel anywhere]
  IdPath -->|"arena.get(id)"| Ar
ch13.caption: Two return shapes from the same alloc call: a borrow welded to the arena's lifetime, or a handle that owns nothing and must be resolved back through the arena.

ch13.text: A useful rule: if you want data to cross async tasks, queues, caches, or other long-lived subsystem boundaries, prefer owned values or stable handles. Arena-borrowed references are strongest when the whole phase stays local and synchronous.
Generational arenas and slab allocation

The whole point of a generation counter is what happens to a slot after it is freed and reused. A plain usize index would still point at the slot and silently read whatever now lives there. A generational handle carries the generation it was issued for: when a slot is removed its generation is bumped, so a handle minted earlier no longer matches and the lookup fails cleanly instead of aliasing the new occupant. That clean failure is exactly the bug class a raw index cannot protect against.
Tradeoffs: deallocation, fragmentation, locality
Practical crates and implementation patterns
The choice is less about crate popularity than about model fit. Ask three questions first: do I want arena-tied references or handles, do I need deletion, and does stale-handle protection matter?
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The best arena optimization is often not “allocation became faster.” It is “the lifetime model became honest.” If the workload does not actually share one region lifetime, the arena will eventually expose that mismatch.
Examples
Example 1: a tiny bump allocator for request-scoped scratch
Allocation only moves the cursor forward. Reset drops the whole region's logical contents in one step.

What to look at: there is exactly one piece of mutable state, the used cursor. Every allocation only moves it forward, and the single cheap teardown sets it back to zero. There is no per-allocation free path anywhere in the type. The diagram traces what the cursor does for the exact byte strings in main.

ch13.chart:
flowchart TD
  S["used = 0"] -->|"alloc b'arena123' (8)"| A["used = 8"]
  A -->|"alloc b'logs' (4)"| B["used = 12"]
  B -->|"read slice (0..8)"| R["arena123"]
  B -->|"reset()"| Z["used = 0"]
ch13.caption: The cursor only ever moves forward on alloc; reset snaps it back to zero in one step, logically discarding everything at once.

ch13.text: Quick check: change the byte strings or arena size and rerun. The important part is the lifetime model: append-only allocation now, coarse reset later.
The example returns ranges, not long-lived borrowed slices, so later allocations stay simple and safe.
This is the shape to use for request-scoped scratch buffers, parser workspaces, and temporary packing regions.
Example 2: arena-backed AST with stable IDs instead of Rc edges
One owner stores all nodes. Expressions point to each other by ExprId, and evaluation reborrows from the arena root.

What to look at: the enum variants hold ExprId values, not Box<Expr> or Rc<Expr>. A node never owns another node; the arena owns them all in one vector, and an edge is just an index into that vector. The diagram is the tree this program builds, with each node labelled by the slot it lands in.

ch13.chart:
flowchart TD
  Root["id 4: Mul"] --> Sum["id 3: Add"]
  Root --> Four["id 2: Number(4)"]
  Sum --> Two["id 0: Number(2)"]
  Sum --> Three["id 1: Number(3)"]
ch13.caption: The expression (2 + 3) * 4 as five arena slots. eval walks the tree by resolving each ExprId back through the arena, so 2 + 3 = 5 then 5 * 4 = 20, across 5 nodes.

ch13.text: Quick check: change the numbers or operator structure and rerun. The real lesson is that the graph has one owner and no reference cycle problem to solve.
The arena owns every node in one contiguous table.
ExprId is logical identity, not shared ownership.
You give up direct references in exchange for simpler mutation, simpler graphs, and clearer ownership.
Exercises
The companion exercise page asks you to build a tiny arena-backed AST, compare an Rc graph with an arena-and-handle graph, and reason explicitly about deallocation, locality, and deletion tradeoffs.
Summary

items: Arena allocation is batch lifetime management, not only fast allocation.
Bump allocators are strongest when many objects share one phase and can be reset together.
Arena-backed graphs often replace pointer ownership with handles, which removes many cycle and mutation problems.
Arena-tied references are powerful for local read-heavy phases; handle-based arenas are often calmer for mutation and subsystem boundaries.
Generational arenas and slabs exist for workloads that need deletion, reuse, and stale-handle protection.

ch14.text: Trait interfaces define capability contracts across library and service boundaries. This chapter treats bounds, associated types, generic dispatch, trait objects, and object safety as reviewable API choices rather than syntax, so you can decide deliberately what a type must prove and what each call site pays for at runtime.
Builds on Chapter 01

Chapter 01 noted that traits describe behavior and that generics usually compile via monomorphization rather than dynamic dispatch. This chapter makes that operational: how to write the contract, how bounds check it, and when to pay for a vtable instead.
Opening scenario

A service needs a pluggable processing stage: today it normalizes text, tomorrow it will validate, redact, or enrich, and operators want to enable stages by configuration. At the same time, a retry layer needs to ask a policy whether another attempt is allowed, and that policy must be checkable at compile time so a misuse fails the build, not production. Both are interface problems, and both are solved with traits, but they pull in opposite directions on dispatch.
A practical decision order

items: Name the capability as a small trait: the exact methods a type must provide.
Decide what each implementer outputs once: associated type, or a generic parameter if it varies.
Pick dispatch per call site: generic bound for speed, dyn for a heterogeneous collection.
If dyn is needed, keep the trait object-safe and move generic helpers out of the core.

ch14.text: Mental model

The shape worth memorizing is a triangle. At one corner sits the trait, a named set of methods. At another sit the concrete types, each with its own impl block. At the third sit the call sites, which name the trait as a bound or as a dyn object. A type and a trait are linked only by an impl, and a call site reaches a type only through the trait. Nothing is connected by inheritance; everything is connected by an explicit implementation.

ch14.chart:
flowchart TD
  Trait[Trait: required methods] -->|impl for A| A[Type A]
  Trait -->|impl for B| B[Type B]
  Call[Call site] -->|bound or dyn| Trait
  A -.honors contract.-> Trait
  B -.honors contract.-> Trait
ch14.caption: A trait links to types only through impl blocks; call sites reach types only through the trait. There is no shared base.

ch14.text: Core concepts
Traits, impls, and default methods

Because an impl is separate from the type definition, the same struct can implement Display, Iterator, and a domain trait of your own, none of which know about the others. That is the practical meaning of composition over inheritance here: capability is added in independent layers rather than fixed in a chain of parents.
Static dispatch and dynamic dispatch

The single most consequential trait decision is how a call reaches the implementation. A generic bound is resolved at compile time into a direct call; a trait object is resolved at runtime through a vtable. The diagram below contrasts the two paths so the cost of each is visible before you commit a call site to one.

ch14.chart:
flowchart TD
  G[Generic call: T bound] -->|monomorphized| GA[Direct call into A]
  G -->|monomorphized| GB[Direct call into B]
ch14.caption: Static dispatch: a generic call is specialized per concrete type into a direct, inlinable call.

ch14.text: The dynamic path instead funnels every concrete type through one shared indirection:

ch14.chart:
flowchart TD
  D[dyn Trait call] --> V[vtable lookup]
  V --> DA[Indirect call into A]
  V --> DB[Indirect call into B]
ch14.caption: Dynamic dispatch: a dyn call funnels every type through one vtable indirection before reaching the implementation.

ch14.text: Associated types versus generic parameters

Both let a trait talk about types it does not yet know, but they answer different questions. An associated type asks the implementer to commit to one output. A generic parameter lets the same type implement the trait several ways. Choosing the wrong one shows up later as turbofish noise on every caller or as an implementation you cannot write.
Object safety

You can only build a Box when the trait is object-safe, because the compiler has to lay out a vtable with one fixed slot per method. The rules are not arbitrary; each one exists so that a single indirect call works without knowing the concrete type. The flow below is the check the compiler runs when you reach for a trait object.

ch14.caption: Object safety is a checklist: a self receiver, no generic methods, and no by-value Self return. Fail any one and dyn is rejected.

ch14.text: Supertraits, blanket impls, and markers

Traits compose. A supertrait says one capability presupposes another, a blanket impl grants a behavior to every type that already meets a bound, and a marker trait carries no methods but still participates in the type system. The snippet shows a supertrait: any Audit type must also be Identify, so the default method can call across the requirement.
Traits as API design

At a boundary, the trait is the contract you publish and the concrete type is an implementation detail you keep. The discipline is the same one you would apply to any interface, with one Rust-specific lever: the bound on a parameter is the precise list of capabilities the caller must supply, so it is worth writing exactly, no wider and no narrower than the body needs.
How this lands by background

Most engineers already have an interface mechanism in muscle memory. The useful question is which part of that mechanism transfers to traits and which part quietly misleads. The shift is rarely about syntax; it is about where implementation is attached, when dispatch is resolved, and whether the compiler verifies the contract before the program runs.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

A trait is a contract you will live behind for a long time. Adding a generic method or a by-value Self return is easy today and quietly forecloses dynamic dispatch tomorrow. Decide early whether the trait must work behind dyn, because retrofitting object safety is a breaking change.
Examples
Trait bounds and associated types
A retry policy trait with an associated output type, a default method, and a generic function bounded so the output is exactly the bool the caller can use.

What to look at: the trait declares type Decision, so each implementer commits to one output type. The function evaluate is generic over the policy but bounds the associated type with Decision = bool, which is static dispatch: the compiler specializes it for FixedLimit. The should_log call uses the trait default, untouched by the impl. Trace the call through the diagram, then read it in code.

ch14.chart:
flowchart TD
  Main[main] -->|and policy, 2| Eval[evaluate generic over P]
  Eval -->|bound P RetryPolicy Decision bool| Decide[FixedLimit decide]
  Decide -->|2 less than 3| True[true]
  Eval --> Label[label override: fixed-limit]
  Main --> Log[should_log default: true]
ch14.caption: evaluate is specialized for FixedLimit; the associated Decision is pinned to bool, label is overridden, and should_log falls through to the default.

ch14.text: Each implementer commits to one Decision output.
The where-clause pins the output so the caller can trust it is a bool.
should_log is inherited without an override.
Quick check: run it to confirm the baseline, then change max or the attempts passed to evaluate and watch the decision flip while the contract stays the same.
dyn Trait plugin pipeline
A heterogeneous list of plugins stored as trait objects, each running the same input through one shared function that dispatches dynamically.

What to look at: two unrelated structs, Uppercase and Prefix, implement the same object-safe Plugin trait. They live together in a Vec>, which is only possible because the concrete types are erased. The function run_all iterates that list and calls through the vtable, so one loop drives every plugin. The diagram is that fan-out.

ch14.chart:
flowchart TD
  Input[input: rust] --> RunAll[run_all over dyn Plugin]
  RunAll --> V[vtable dispatch]
  V --> Up[Uppercase.run]
  V --> Pre[Prefix.run]
  Up --> O1[uppercase => RUST]
  Pre --> O2[prefix => svc-rust]
ch14.caption: One run_all loop calls each boxed plugin through its vtable; different concrete types share a single code path because the type is erased.

ch14.text: Both methods take &self and avoid generics, so the trait can be boxed.
Vec> holds different types behind one element type.
Each run call goes through the vtable at runtime.
Quick check: run it, then add a third plugin or change the prefix value and confirm the pipeline keeps working without touching run_all, which is the whole point of the trait-object boundary.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to pick the right bound for a function, choose between an associated type and a generic parameter, decide whether a trait is object-safe, and build a small plugin API that works both as a generic and behind dyn.
Next chapter

Traits are the interface mechanism. Chapter 15 uses them to express the patterns engineers reach for out of object-oriented habit: polymorphism, encapsulation, and shared behavior modeled with composition, enums, and trait objects instead of inheritance. The dispatch and object-safety choices from this chapter are exactly the tools that work makes use of.
Summary

ch15.text: Rust object modeling uses composition, traits, enums, and explicit state transitions to represent domain behavior. This chapter maps those choices to maintainable service and library APIs.
Builds on Chapters 05, 13, and 14

Chapter 05 explained how structs carry ownership and layout. Chapter 13 showed that storage and identity are separate design choices. Chapter 14 covered traits, dispatch, and object safety. This chapter puts those pieces together into Rust’s practical answer to OOP modeling.
A worked scenario: the document-workflow platform

Throughout the chapter we will keep one concrete system in view. A document-workflow platform moves documents through a fixed approval lifecycle, lets services share retry and notification logic, hides invoice representation behind a clean API, and accepts third-party transport plugins for delivering output. Each of those four needs maps to a different Rust tool, and the whole point of the chapter is to see why. In a class-first language all four would likely become subclasses of some Workflow base type; in Rust they deliberately do not.

The deciding question for each need is the same: is the set of cases closed and known at compile time, or open and extended later? That single question routes the design to an enum, a struct, a module boundary, or a trait object, and reading the diagrams below in that order is most of the chapter in one picture.

ch15.chart:
flowchart TD
  Start[Modeling need] --> Q1{Set of cases closed?}
  Q1 -->|Yes, a fixed lifecycle| Enum[Enum plus match]
  Q1 -->|No, plugins added later| Dyn[Trait object dyn Trait]
ch15.caption: First question: is the set of variants closed (an enum) or open (a trait object)?

ch15.text: The same modeling need also routes the other two questions, sharing and hiding, to their own tools:

ch15.caption: Sharing routes to a composed field or a trait; hiding routes to a module with private fields. Rust does not fold all four into one inheritance tree.

ch15.text: A practical decision order

items: Start with concrete structs and enums before you invent a trait hierarchy.
Decide whether the variant set is open or closed.
Use traits for shared behavior, not for pretending Rust has base-class fields.
Use runtime trait objects only when runtime heterogeneity is semantically real.

ch15.text: Mental model
Core concepts
Rust without classical inheritance

Rust has no class inheritance with shared fields. A type does not extend another type to inherit state. That is a sharp correction for C++ and C# engineers: traits describe behavior, but data reuse comes from ordinary fields, helper types, and composition.

This sounds like a loss until you notice what disappears with it: fragile base classes, partially initialized parent state, hidden inherited invariants, and broad object graphs whose aliasing story is unclear. Rust makes each of those choices explicit instead.
Composition over inheritance

The shape to notice is that inheritance grows data downward through a chain of parents, while composition grows it sideways as named fields you can name, swap, and test one at a time. The two pictures hold the same information, but only the composed one keeps each dependency visible and independently replaceable.

ch15.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Inheritance
    direction TB
    Base[Service base: retry, metrics] --> Mid[Billing base]
    Mid --> Leaf[ConcreteBilling]
  end
ch15.caption: Inheritance buries shared state in a parent chain: each level inherits the one above.

ch15.text: Side by side, composition holds the same parts but lays them out as fields the struct owns directly:

ch15.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Composition
    direction TB
    Svc[BillingService] --> R[retry: RetryPolicy]
    Svc --> N[notifier: N]
    Svc --> M[metrics: Metrics]
  end
ch15.caption: Composition lists the same parts as named fields, each one visible, swappable, and testable on its own.

ch15.text: The default Rust reuse pattern is simple: a struct owns the components it needs. Shared logic lives in those components or in traits implemented by them. The design reads directly from the fields instead of from a base-class tree, so there is no hidden parent state to reason about when you read the type.

This is especially useful in services and pipelines. A BillingService can compose a retry policy, a notifier, a cache, and a metrics recorder without pretending those pieces are one inheritance family. Each dependency remains visible, testable, and replaceable, and a test can supply a fake notifier by setting one field rather than subclassing the whole service.
Encapsulation through modules and visibility

In Rust, encapsulation usually lives in modules, private fields, narrow constructors, and focused methods. You do not need inheritance to hide representation. You need a good module boundary and the discipline to expose only what callers actually need.

The translation is this: the public surface is the contract. The internal layout is still allowed to change. Rust’s module system often gives tighter encapsulation than a deep protected-member hierarchy because the exported API is narrower and more deliberate.
Polymorphism with traits
Traits are Rust’s main behavior abstraction. They let generic code ask for capabilities without naming one concrete type too early. This is Rust’s primary answer to interface-like OOP design.

The important distinction from inheritance is that the trait does not bring data fields with it. The implementor chooses its own storage and ownership shape. That is why the same trait can fit a stack value, a boxed object, or an arena-backed node equally well.
Trait objects as runtime polymorphism

When the system truly needs runtime heterogeneity, Rust uses trait objects such as Box<dyn Processor>. This is the closest thing Rust has to virtual-dispatch OOP, but it is opt-in and object-safety rules still apply.

Use this for plugins, strategy registries, sinks, handlers selected from configuration, or any boundary where one collection must hold several concrete implementations at once. Do not use it just because an old base class existed. Chapter 14 covered the dispatch and object-safety details underneath this choice.
Enums as closed polymorphism

The contrast worth holding in your head is how the three options dispatch. A generic trait bound is resolved at compile time into one specialized copy per type; a trait object defers the choice to a vtable at run time; an enum keeps every case in one type and lets the compiler force every match to cover all of them. The diagrams below line them up so the tradeoff is visible before you read any code.

ch15.chart:
flowchart TD
  Call[Call site] --> G["Generic fn P: Trait"]
  G -->|monomorphized| GT[One copy per concrete type]
  Call --> D["dyn Trait via Box"]
  D -->|vtable lookup| DT[Any type, chosen at run time]
ch15.caption: Static path: a generic bound is monomorphized at compile time; a trait object defers the choice to a vtable at run time.

ch15.text: The third option keeps every case in one type rather than dispatching across types:

ch15.chart:
flowchart TD
  Call[Call site] --> E[Enum value]
  E -->|exhaustive match| ET[Fixed set, compiler checks all cases]
ch15.caption: Closed path: an enum holds a fixed set of cases and the compiler forces every match to cover all of them.

ch15.text: Enums are Rust’s strongest answer when the variant set is closed. Instead of a base class plus derived types, you declare the full set of variants and let pattern matching drive behavior. The data for each case lives inline, so there is no boxing and no pointer chase to reach it.

This is often better than a traditional OOP hierarchy for commands, events, workflow state, AST nodes, transport types, and many domain models. The compiler checks exhaustiveness, which means adding a new variant turns into a compile-time repair across every match rather than a quiet runtime default that ships to production unhandled.
State pattern in Rust

A lifecycle is the clearest case of a closed set: there is a finite list of states and a finite list of legal transitions between them. The classical state pattern models each state as its own object behind an interface; in Rust the same shape is usually an enum whose match arms are the transitions. The three cards below split the choice by where you want an illegal transition to fail: at run time, at compile time, or only when the set is genuinely open. The document example later in the chapter draws the actual lifecycle graph.

The practical default is usually enum state or typestate, not boxed state objects. A state object model can still be correct, but Rust makes the alternatives so strong that many classical implementations become needlessly dynamic.
Visitor pattern and alternatives

Rust often improves on classical visitor-heavy designs because enums and exhaustiveness make closed trees easier to traverse. But when operations or node families stay open across crates, visitor-like trait seams can still be the right model.
Translating instincts from other languages

The hardest part of OOP in Rust is rarely a missing feature; it is an instinct that no longer pays off. Each card below names the one mental-model shift that trips up engineers from that language, not a table of which crate replaces which library.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
The most common translation mistake is trying to preserve the old class shape instead of preserving the actual domain rules. Rust rewards re-modeling. It often punishes mechanical porting.
When Rust improves on traditional OOP
When Rust makes OOP harder
Examples
Example 1: composition, visibility, and trait-based behavior
The service composes a notifier instead of inheriting a base class, and the invoice keeps its fields private behind methods.

What to look at: trace where the behavior comes from. The service holds the notifier as a field (notifier: N), reaches the invoice only through public methods because its fields are private to the billing module, and delegates notification to whatever Notifier it was built with. Nothing is inherited; every capability is a field or a trait bound.

ch15.chart:
flowchart TD
  Main[main] -->|owns| Svc[BillingService N]
  Svc -->|field| Not[notifier: EmailNotifier]
  Main -->|borrow Invoice| Svc
  Svc -->|notifier.send| Not
  Not -->|reads via id| Inv[Invoice private fields]
  Svc -->|process via methods| Inv
ch15.caption: Reuse flows through a field and a trait bound, not a parent class. The invoice is reached only through its public methods.

ch15.expected:
invoice = 41 cents = 1250
notification = queued email for 41
sent = 1

ch15.text: Quick check: change the invoice ID, cents, or notifier prefix and rerun. The point is not the string formatting. It is that reuse comes from fields plus trait bounds, not from a parent service class.
BillingService owns a notifier component directly.
The invoice fields stay private, so callers cannot violate representation casually.
Trait-based behavior stays open without dragging storage inheritance along with it.
Example 2: enum-based state pattern
The state set is closed, so an enum plus explicit transitions is calmer than a family of dynamic state classes.

What to look at: each transition takes self by value and returns a new Document, so the old state is consumed and cannot be used again. The chain in main walks the lifecycle one move at a time, and any transition that does not apply to the current state falls through to the catch-all arm that returns the state unchanged.

ch15.chart:
flowchart TD
  D["Draft { title }"] -->|request_review| R["Review { title, reviewer }"]
  R -->|publish| P["Published { title, slug }"]
  D -.->|publish: no-op| D
  R -.->|request_review: no-op| R
ch15.caption: The builder chain consumes self at each step: Draft becomes Review becomes Published. Dashed edges are transitions that do not apply and return the value untouched.

ch15.text: Quick check: change the title and rerun. The variant set stays closed and the transition logic stays in one visible place, which is usually easier to review than a dynamic state-object lattice.
The compiler knows every valid document state ahead of time.
Illegal transitions can be made explicit instead of disappearing behind shared mutable flags.
If you want compile-time-only transitions, the typestate exercise page pushes this idea one step further.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch15_oop_models_in_rust/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises
The companion exercise page asks you to replace inheritance with composition, choose between traits and enums for a given variant set, and refactor a state machine into a more Rust-native model.
Summary

items: Rust does not offer classical inheritance with shared fields. It splits OOP concerns into smaller, clearer tools.
Composition is the default reuse mechanism. Traits express behavior. Modules and visibility express encapsulation.
Traits and trait objects solve open polymorphism. Enums solve closed polymorphism. Confusing the two is a common design mistake.
State machines are usually better modeled with enums or typestate than with boxed state objects ported mechanically from older patterns.
Rust often improves traditional OOP by making ownership, state validity, and variant closure explicit, but it also makes some inheritance-shaped designs harder on purpose.

ch16.text: Domain-driven Rust encodes business rules in types, constructors, aggregate boundaries, and repository interfaces. This chapter keeps invalid states and persistence concerns out of core domain code.
Builds on Chapters 05, 14, and 15

Chapter 05 established ownership inside structs. Chapter 14 covered traits as interface boundaries. Chapter 15 explained why Rust prefers composition, enums, and explicit state models over classical inheritance. DDD in Rust sits on top of all three.
Opening scenario

An order platform coordinates pricing, inventory reservation, payment authorization, and fulfillment. The business requirement is to encode business language and invariants directly in Rust types: domain identifiers, value objects, aggregate methods, repository seams, and transport-independent error contracts.
A practical decision order

items: Identify the domain concepts that deserve names in types.
Decide which invariants belong in value-object constructors and which belong at aggregate methods.
Keep application services responsible for orchestration, not for becoming the only place rules exist.
Make repository and integration boundaries speak in domain language or explicit translations.

ch16.text: Mental model
What changes by background

Domain-driven design is older than Rust, so most senior engineers arrive with habits from a language whose type system made different promises. The vocabulary carries over; the mechanism does not. The shift below is the one worth internalizing before reading any code in this chapter.

The common thread across all four: in Rust the domain model is not enforced by a framework at runtime, by a base class, or by convention. It is enforced by types that refuse to hold an invalid value. The diagram below shows where those types sit relative to the infrastructure they protect.

ch16.chart:
flowchart TD
  HTTP[HTTP / CLI edge] --> App[Application service]
  App --> Domain[Domain model]
  App --> RepoT[Repository trait]
  RepoT -. implemented by .-> RepoImpl[SQL repository]
  RepoImpl --> DB[(Database)]
  Domain -. no dependency .-> RepoImpl
ch16.caption: Dependencies point inward toward the domain. The application service depends on a repository trait; the SQL implementation depends on the trait, not the other way round, so the domain never imports infrastructure.

ch16.text: Core concepts
Entities, value objects, aggregates, repositories

These four pieces nest into one shape worth memorizing. Value objects are owned by the aggregate root, which is the entity that guards the invariants; the repository is the only door through which the whole aggregate is loaded and saved. The root owns everything inside the boundary, so there is no way to mutate a line item without going through a method that can re-check the rule.

ch16.chart:
flowchart TD
  Repo[OrderRepository trait] -->|load / save| Root[Order aggregate root]
  Root -->|enforces| Inv[Invariants: non-empty, valid status]
  Root -.->|owns, see below| Cont[Aggregate boundary continues below]
ch16.caption: Outside view: the repository moves the whole aggregate in and out of storage, and invariants are checked on the root rather than scattered across callers.

ch16.text: Looking inside that boundary, the root owns the order lines and the value objects they carry:

ch16.chart:
flowchart TD
  Cont[Aggregate boundary] --> Root[Order aggregate root]
  Root -->|owns| Lines[Vec of OrderLine]
  Lines --> VO1[Sku value object]
  Lines --> VO2[Quantity value object]
  Lines --> VO3[MoneyCents value object]
ch16.caption: Inside view: the root owns its value objects through the order lines, so there is no way to mutate a line without going through a method that can re-check the rule.

ch16.text: Encoding invariants in types

The important rule is simple: if the invalid state is local and stable, encode it in the type. If the rule depends on aggregate-wide state, encode it in the aggregate method. Rust gives you both tools.
Newtypes for domain safety
