Newtypes are one of the most practical DDD tools in Rust. They are cheap, explicit, and easy to compose with traits. They prevent primitive obsession without pretending a runtime framework will keep your identifiers straight for you.
That small amount of ceremony buys strong review benefits: fewer swapped parameters, clearer logs, narrower traits, and sharper boundaries between internal and external identifiers.
Rich domain models without inheritance

A strong correction for C++ and C# readers is this: a rich model in Rust means behavior near state and invariants, not a base class with protected fields. Rust wants `impl` blocks, value objects, traits, and modules to each do their own job.
Error modeling in domain layers
Application services and domain services
Repository interfaces with traits
Async repositories and lifetime issues

A reliable production rule is this: if the repository method performs IO and may suspend, return owned data or an owned projection. Do not fight the lifetime model just to preserve a borrowed shape that no longer matches the boundary.
Event sourcing in Rust
DDD boundaries in monoliths and distributed systems
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

DDD is not an excuse for heavy ceremony. In Rust, the best version is often the lightest one that gives the domain real names, protects invariants locally, and keeps infrastructure outside the core language of the model.
Examples
Example 1: aggregate invariants with newtypes and rich methods
The aggregate root owns the mutable consistency boundary. Value objects reject invalid local state, and the aggregate decides when the order may be submitted.

What to look at: the order is a tiny state machine with two states. While it is Draft you may add lines; submit refuses an empty order and otherwise moves it to Submitted, after which add_line is rejected. The value-object constructors reject the local errors first, so by the time a line reaches the aggregate every quantity is non-zero and every SKU is non-empty. Trace the transitions in the diagram, then read the same guards in the code.

ch16.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Draft: construct
  Draft --> Draft: add_line ok
  Draft --> Submitted: submit when non-empty
  Draft --> Draft: submit fails EmptyOrder
  Submitted --> Submitted: add_line fails CannotModify
  Submitted --> [*]
ch16.caption: Two states, with the guards drawn as edges: add_line only works in Draft, and submit only advances when at least one line exists.

ch16.text: `Order` has identity and behavior. It is not only a record bag.
`Quantity`, `MoneyCents`, and `Sku` protect local rules at construction time.
`submit` refuses an empty order. The rule stays on the model, not in a handler comment.
Example 2: event-sourced aggregate rehydration
The aggregate is rebuilt from domain events. Rehydration is a fold, and versioning follows the applied stream length.

What to look at: there is no stored balance to read. Current state is computed by folding the event stream into a fresh accumulator, one event at a time. Each call to apply validates against the state built so far — a deposit before the account is open is rejected, a withdrawal larger than the running balance is rejected — and the version counter is simply how many events were applied. The diagram is that fold; the three output numbers are the accumulator after the last event.

ch16.chart:
flowchart TD
  Start[balance 0, version 0, closed] --> E1[Opened 1000]
  E1 --> S1[balance 1000, version 1, open]
  S1 --> E2[Deposited 400]
  E2 --> S2[balance 1400, version 2]
  S2 --> E3[Withdrawn 150]
  E3 --> S3[balance 1250, version 3]
ch16.caption: Rehydration is a left fold: each event is applied to the running state, version increments per applied event, and the final accumulator is the current account.

ch16.text: The stream records domain facts, not persistence internals.
`rehydrate` applies each event in order and rebuilds current state explicitly.
You gain temporal history, but you also accept projection and migration work.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch16_domain_driven_design_in_rust/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary Rust files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to implement newtypes for domain identifiers, encode aggregate invariants in constructors, compare anaemic and rich models, and design repository traits with sync and async variants.
Summary

items: Entities, value objects, aggregates, and repositories map cleanly onto Rust structs, enums, traits, and ownership boundaries.
Newtypes and constructors are practical tools for encoding invariants and defending domain language from primitive obsession.
Rich domain models in Rust do not rely on inheritance. They rely on `impl` blocks, composition, enums, and clear visibility.
Application services orchestrate use cases. Domain services are narrower and should exist only when a rule does not belong to one aggregate or value object.
Async repository seams usually want owned returns, and event sourcing is a domain choice with real operational tradeoffs, not a free architectural upgrade.

ch17.text: Idiomatic Rust refactoring reduces operational risk by clarifying ownership, error flow, data shape, and execution boundaries. This chapter turns review findings into small, verifiable code changes.
Builds on Chapters 04, 07, 08, 14, 15, and 16

Ownership from Chapter 04, clone economics from Chapter 07, safe abstraction boundaries from Chapter 08, traits from Chapter 14, enum-versus-trait modeling from Chapter 15, and aggregate boundaries from Chapter 16 all feed directly into good Rust refactoring work.
Opening scenario

A mature service has accumulated pointer-heavy objects, panic-based parsing, sentinel failures, public mutable records, and broad runtime dispatch. None of this is wrong in isolation; it is the residue of porting an existing C++, C#, or Go design and then bolting on features under deadline. The business requirement is not a rewrite. It is a staged refactor that makes ownership, fallibility, state shape, and test seams explicit before anyone touches syntax cosmetics or async structure.

The ordering matters more than any single change. When you correct ownership and error flow first, a surprising amount of the lifetime noise and clone pressure simply evaporates, because those problems were symptoms of the wrong boundary rather than independent defects. The three passes below run in that order on purpose: each one removes the pressure that was making the next one hard.
Read the pipeline left to right. Each pass takes the output of the previous one and is only worth attempting once the earlier boundary is clean.

ch17.chart:
flowchart TD
  Legacy[Ported legacy module] --> P1[Pass 1: ownership and errors]
  P1 --> P2[Pass 2: data model]
  P2 --> P3[Pass 3: async and ergonomics]
  P3 --> Out[Testable idiomatic module]
ch17.caption: Refactor in passes. Ownership and error flow first, data model second, async and ergonomics last; each pass clears the way for the next.

ch17.text: Mental model
What changes by background

Most of the friction in an idiomatic refactor is not about Rust syntax. It is about the instinct you brought from your previous language and where that instinct now points you wrong. The cards below name the specific mental-model shift for each background, not a library mapping. Find the one that fits you and keep it in mind while you read the core concepts.
Core concepts

Each concept below is a recurring move you make during the three passes. They are grouped roughly by the language habit they correct, but they share one theme: every one of them turns an implicit decision the old code made by convention into an explicit decision the type system can check. Where a concept has a shape worth seeing, a short pointer and a diagram come before the code so you read the structure first and the syntax second.
What to look at:
Clone audit checklist
Async refactor checklist
Testability patterns
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

An idiomatic Rust refactor is not a contest to remove every `clone`, every trait object, or every async call. It is a contest to make the remaining ones obviously correct, operationally justified, and easy to review.
Examples
Example 1: replace panic-based loading with an owned Result boundary
The refactor keeps borrowed input local, moves normalized output into an owned struct, and turns routine failure into a small error enum.

What to look at: follow the data left to right. Borrowed config text comes in, parsing either fails with a named error or produces an owned endpoint, and that owned value is what leaves the function so the caller never depends on the input buffer.

ch17.chart:
flowchart TD
  Cfg[borrowed config text] --> Parse{parse and validate}
  Parse -->|missing or invalid| Err[ConfigError, no panic]
  Parse -->|valid| Build[build owned Endpoint]
  Build --> Ret[return owned value]
  Ret --> Caller[caller, independent of input]
ch17.caption: Routine failure becomes a Result error and the normalized result is owned, so the signature alone tells the caller what they get and how it can fail.

ch17.text: Missing or invalid ports become ordinary Result errors, not panics or sentinel values.
The returned endpoint owns its normalized bind address, so the caller is not coupled to input buffer lifetime.
The signature now says exactly what the caller gets and exactly how failure is represented.
Example 2: replace hierarchy pressure with enum state and a narrow test seam
A closed mode becomes an enum, a notifier becomes a small trait seam, and the processor becomes easy to test with a fake implementation.

What to look at: the old hierarchy splits into three parts. The closed delivery mode is an enum the processor matches on, the notifier is a small trait the processor is generic over, and a fake notifier can stand in for the real one in tests without touching anything else.

ch17.chart:
flowchart TD
  Order[order id] --> Proc[Processor generic over N: Notifier]
  Mode{DeliveryMode enum} -->|Immediate or Retry| Proc
  Proc -->|charge| Charged[charged record]
  Proc -->|notify via trait seam| N{Notifier}
  N --> Real[EmailNotifier in prod]
  N --> Fake[FakeNotifier in tests]
ch17.caption: Closed state is an enum, behavior is a trait the processor is generic over, and the trait seam is where a test fake swaps in. Dispatch stays static because the concrete notifier is known at compile time.

ch17.text: The closed delivery mode is an enum, not a polymorphic class family with runtime type checks.
The notifier boundary is small enough to swap with a fake in tests without dragging in broad framework state.
The generic processor keeps dispatch static until a real runtime plugin boundary actually appears.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch17_refactoring_toward_idiomatic_rust/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to refactor a non-idiomatic module in three passes, replace panic-based routines with Result-based APIs, reduce lifetime noise by changing ownership, and design async and test seams deliberately.
Summary

ch18.text: Generics let one Rust API serve many types without giving up concrete contracts. This chapter covers trait bounds, where clauses, associated types, const generics, and the monomorphization costs that matter when you ship a production library: what the compiler checks, when it checks it, and what it stamps into the binary.
Builds on Chapter 17

Chapter 17 was about refactoring concrete code toward idiomatic Rust. Generics are the next step: once a pattern recurs across more than one concrete type, you lift it into a single parameterized API. This chapter is deliberately about doing that lifting late and on purpose, not as a reflex.
Opening scenario

A team is building a job-processing library. They start with one concrete batch of Job values, then a second caller needs the same batching logic over a different item type, then a third needs a fixed-size encoding buffer whose length is known at compile time. The temptation is to copy the code three times or to reach immediately for a fully generic abstraction. The business requirement is a single API that compiles to the same machine code as the hand-written versions, rejects misuse at the call site with a clear message, and does not quietly bloat the binary.
A practical decision order

items: Write the concrete version first and ship it if there is only one caller.
When a second real type appears, lift to a generic and name the trait bound the body actually uses.
Pick associated types over extra parameters when the trait has one natural related type.
Use const generics only when the size is genuinely fixed at compile time.
Drop to dyn Trait when runtime polymorphism or binary size, not raw speed, is the constraint.

ch18.text: Mental model

The shape worth memorizing is two checks at two different times. A C++ template defers all type checking until a caller instantiates it, so a missing operation surfaces deep inside the body. A Rust generic is checked twice: once at the definition against its declared bounds, and once again, trivially, when a caller supplies a type and the compiler confirms that type satisfies the bound. The body never gets re-typechecked per caller, which is why the diagnostics point at the call site instead of the template internals.

ch18.chart:
flowchart TD
  Def[Generic definition] -->|checked vs bounds| OK[Body type-checks once]
  Call[Caller supplies T] -->|does T satisfy bound| Yes[compile and monomorphize]
  Call -->|bound missing| Err[error at call site]
  OK --> Yes
ch18.caption: The body is checked once against its bounds at the definition; each caller is only checked for whether its type satisfies the bound.

ch18.text: Core concepts
Trait bounds, where clauses, associated types, const generics

These four features form a ladder. A bare type parameter such as Vec<T> says nothing about T. Adding a bound ( T: Keyed) lets the body call methods. A where clause keeps the bound legible as it grows. An associated type fixes a trait’s one natural related type so callers do not repeat it, and a const parameter like const N: usize lets the type carry a compile-time size such as [T; N].
Generics versus templates: where the difference lives

It is worth being precise about what is the same and what is different, because the runtime story is identical and only the front end changes. Both languages generate one specialized copy of the code per concrete type. The contrast is entirely in when type errors are reported and whether a contract has to be declared. The table below is the whole comparison in one view.

items: No declared contract; the body just tries operations.
Type-checked at instantiation, per caller.
Errors surface inside the template body.
Monomorphized to specialized machine code.
Trait bounds declare the contract explicitly.
Type-checked once at the definition against the bound.
Errors surface at the call site as a missing trait.
Monomorphized to specialized machine code.

ch18.text: Monomorphization and its costs

Monomorphization is the compiler stamping out a separate, fully specialized copy of a generic for each concrete type that uses it. That is what makes generics fast: the copy for u32 knows it is operating on four-byte integers and inlines accordingly, with no boxing and no vtable. The price is paid in the binary, not at runtime: one generic over many types becomes many functions in the output.

ch18.chart:
flowchart TD
  G["batch generic over T"] --> M[monomorphization]
  M --> A[batch for Job]
  M --> B[batch for Order]
  M --> C[batch for u32]
  A --> Bin[binary: 3 specialized copies]
  B --> Bin
  C --> Bin
ch18.caption: One generic becomes one specialized copy per concrete type. Runtime cost stays low; binary size and compile time scale with the number of instantiations.

ch18.text: Generics are free at runtime, not free at build time. A widely instantiated generic in a core crate can dominate compile time and binary size even when every call is as fast as hand-written code.
How this lands by background

Most engineers meet Rust generics with a model from another language, and the useful question is which part of that model transfers. The runtime behavior is rarely the surprise; the surprise is where and when the type contract is enforced, and whether you are allowed to leave it implicit.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

A generic is not automatically better than a concrete type. It is a contract you maintain and a set of instantiations you pay for. Generalize when a second real case proves the abstraction, not before.
Examples
Example 1: Generic batch with trait bounds
One Batch<T> holds any item type, but the helper that reads a key requires the items to implement a trait.

What to look at: notice which operations are gated by which bound. Batch<T> itself has no bound, so new and len work for every type. Only first_key adds where T: Keyed, which is what lets its body call item.key(). Trace the bound in the diagram, then read the same split in the code.

ch18.chart:
flowchart TD
  T[any T] --> Batch["Batch of T: new, len"]
  T -->|"only if T: Keyed"| FK["first_key: calls item.key()"]
  Job["Job impl Keyed"] -->|satisfies bound| FK
ch18.caption: The container is unbounded; only first_key requires T: Keyed, so only it may call key(). Job satisfies the bound, so the call compiles.

ch18.text: Batch<T> stores any type; storage needs no trait.
first_key requires Keyed because it calls a trait method.
Pass a type without Keyed and the error names the missing bound at the call.
Example 2: Associated types and const generics
An Encoder fixes its output type as an associated type, and a fixed window carries its length as a const parameter.

What to look at: two different parameterization choices in one file. The Encoder trait owns its result type via type Output, so HexPair pins it to [u8; 2] once and callers never spell it out. Separately, FixedWindow<T, N> is generic over a compile-time length N, so last() can index items[N - 1] with the size known at compile time. The diagram separates the by-type axis from the by-value axis.

ch18.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph ByType[Associated type]
    Enc["Encoder trait: type Output"] --> Hex["HexPair: Output = u8 array of 2"]
  end
ch18.caption: By type: an associated type lets the Encoder trait own its result type, so HexPair pins Output to a fixed array once and callers never spell it out.

ch18.text: The other axis parameterizes by a compile-time value rather than a type:

ch18.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph ByValue[Const generic]
    FW["FixedWindow of T and const N"] --> Sum["sum over N items"]
    FW --> Last["last = items at N minus 1"]
  end
ch18.caption: By value: a const generic makes the length N part of the type, so a FixedWindow sums over N items and indexes the last as items[N - 1] with the size known at compile time.

ch18.text: type Output fixes one result type per implementor, so callers do not repeat it.
const N: usize makes the length part of the type, so [T; N] stays on the stack.
A length mismatch becomes a compile error, not a runtime bounds check.

Try changing the inputs to feel the two cost models. Edit the byte passed to encode or the numbers in items and the output follows directly; change the number of items and the const length N moves with it because the length is part of the type.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to translate template-style helpers into bounded Rust generics, replace an extra type parameter with an associated type, and implement a const-generic fixed-size batch with len and sum.
Next chapter

Generics let one type or function serve many types in memory. Chapter 19 takes the same data across process and version boundaries: serialization and data contracts, where the question shifts from "what can this type do" to "how does this value survive being written, stored, and read back by possibly older code." The bounds-and-contracts discipline from this chapter carries directly into designing stable wire formats.
Summary

ch19.text: Serialization defines the contract between Rust services, files, queues, and external clients. This chapter covers versioned payloads, schema ownership, compatibility, and explicit transport boundaries.
Builds on Chapters 08, 14, 16, and 18

Chapter 08 established FFI and unsafe boundary discipline. Chapter 14 covered traits, which matter because Serde is trait-driven. Chapter 16 gave us domain events and aggregates worth serializing. Chapter 18 covered generics and associated types, which help explain why transport wrappers and wire DTOs stay composable.
Opening scenario

Serialization is where a Rust program stops being a self-contained world of owned values and starts being one participant in a larger system. Inside the process you have rich types, lifetimes, and a compiler that proves things hold together. The instant a value is written to a socket, a file, or a queue, all of that disappears, and what remains is bytes plus an implicit agreement about how to read them. That agreement is the data contract, and most serialization pain in production is really a contract that drifted without anyone deciding it should.

The running example for this chapter is an order system that emits the same domain events to four very different consumers. A public HTTP API needs human-readable, debuggable JSON. An internal event stream wants something compact and fast. A browser module across a WASM boundary needs a shape JavaScript can consume cheaply. A native integration across an FFI boundary needs an explicit byte contract rather than accidental Rust memory layout. One domain model, four boundaries, four trade-offs.

Look at where each contract lives in the diagram below: the domain model stays in the center, and each edge translates it into a format chosen for that consumer. The point is that no single edge dictates the shape of the core.

ch19.chart:
flowchart TD
  D[Order domain model] --> P[Public API DTO]
  D --> E[Internal event DTO]
  P -->|JSON| Api[External clients]
  E -->|compact binary| Stream[Event consumers]
ch19.caption: The first two boundaries: a human-readable JSON API and a compact internal event stream, both derived from the same core.

ch19.text: The same domain model also feeds two foreign-runtime boundaries:

ch19.chart:
flowchart TD
  D[Order domain model] --> W[WASM view]
  D --> F[FFI byte buffer]
  W -->|JsValue or JSON| Browser[Browser module]
  F -->|repr C or bytes| Native[Native integration]
ch19.caption: The WASM and FFI boundaries, again derived from the same core. Four edges, four contracts, and none of them dictates the shape of the center.

ch19.text: Repository note

The in-browser editor simulates output so you can focus on contract shape. In a real Cargo project, these examples assume Serde plus the chosen format crate such as serde_json, a YAML/TOML adapter, or a binary format adapter.
Mental model
How this maps from other languages

Every senior engineer arrives with serialization instincts that are mostly correct and quietly misleading in one specific spot. The list below names the mental-model shift, not a crate-to-library translation table. The recurring theme is the same one that runs through the rest of Rust: ownership and lifetime do not stop mattering at the boundary, and the wire shape is a contract you design rather than a side effect of your in-memory layout.
Core concepts
Serde: two traits and a format layer

Serde is built on two traits, Serialize and Deserialize, plus a clean split between your data model and the concrete format. Your type knows how to describe itself as a sequence of fields and values; a format crate such as serde_json or a binary adapter knows how to turn that description into bytes and back. This is why one derive can target JSON, YAML, MessagePack, or CBOR without rewriting the type: the type talks to an abstract data model, and the format sits underneath it.
The trace from a Rust value to bytes runs through this abstract model. Notice that the format is a swappable layer at the bottom, not something baked into your struct.

ch19.chart:
flowchart TD
  V[Your Rust value] -->|Serialize| M[Serde data model]
  M --> J[serde_json bytes]
  M --> C[CBOR bytes]
  M --> Mp[MessagePack bytes]
  J -->|Deserialize| V2[Your Rust value]
  C -->|Deserialize| V2
  Mp -->|Deserialize| V2
ch19.caption: One Serialize/Deserialize implementation talks to an abstract data model; the concrete format is a layer you swap underneath it.

ch19.text: Derive macros generate the trait implementations, but the design still lives in the attributes: field names, enum tagging strategy, defaults, borrowing, and which model is even allowed to cross the boundary. A generic envelope is a common starting shape because it lets a stable wrapper carry many payload types without re-deriving the wrapper for each one.

A strong default is to separate internal domain types from wire-facing DTOs when evolution pressure differs. Your aggregate may want one shape. Your public event or API contract may want another. Serde makes the conversion pleasant, which means you do not have to force one type to do both jobs badly. The cost of a second type and a From impl is usually far lower than the cost of a domain refactor that silently changes a public payload.
JSON, YAML, TOML, MessagePack, and CBOR

These five formats all map cleanly onto Serde's data model, so the choice between them is rarely about what Rust can express. It is about who reads the bytes and under what pressure. JSON, YAML, and TOML are text: easy to diff, log, and hand-edit, which matters enormously during an incident. MessagePack and CBOR are binary cousins of the same document model: smaller and faster to parse, at the cost of needing a tool to inspect. The decision usually collapses to two axes, human readability and payload size, with compatibility and tooling as tie-breakers.
Before the cards, look at the decision as a fork rather than a ranking. There is no single best format; there is a best format for a given boundary.

ch19.caption: First fork: if a human must read the bytes, the answer is a text format keyed on config versus data.

ch19.text: When the boundary does not need to be human-readable, the binary branch forks again:

ch19.chart:
flowchart TD
  Bin[Binary boundary] --> Q3{Same document model, smaller?}
  Q3 -->|Yes| Cbor[MessagePack or CBOR]
  Q3 -->|Need cross-language schema| Schema[Schema-first binary]
ch19.caption: Second fork: a binary boundary chooses between a compact document format and a schema-first contract. The format question is keyed on who reads the bytes and how much size matters, not a single winner.

ch19.text: The useful decision is not “which format is best?” It is “which format fits this boundary’s human-readability, payload size, compatibility, and debugging needs?” A public API and an internal control-plane message do not have to make the same trade, and there is no rule that one service must speak only one format.
Binary serialization formats

Once a boundary no longer needs to be human-readable, a different set of formats opens up, and they sort roughly by how much they commit to in exchange for speed and size. Rust-centric compact encodings are the fastest to adopt and the least portable. Schema-first formats cost you an interface-definition step but buy you a contract that other languages can compile against. Archived, zero-copy representations go furthest: they let you read a value straight out of a mapped buffer without parsing, in return for the strictest layout and evolution discipline. The cards move left to right along that same axis of convenience versus cross-language and durability guarantees.
Schema evolution

Contracts change, and the only question is whether old and new code can coexist during the change. The safe moves are the ones an old reader can survive without being redeployed first. Adding an optional field with a default is invisible to existing readers. Renaming a field is safe only if you keep the old name as an alias until every producer has moved. Changing the meaning of an existing field is the dangerous one, because it compiles, deploys, and corrupts data silently. The diagram below traces what a tolerant reader does when it meets each kind of change.

ch19.chart:
flowchart TD
  R[Reader parses a message] --> A{New optional field present?}
  A -->|Missing| Def[Use serde default]
  A -->|Present| Keep[Read it]
  R --> B{Field was renamed?}
  B -->|Old name| Alias[serde alias maps it]
  B -->|New name| Keep
  Def --> Ok[Parse succeeds]
  Keep --> Ok
  Alias --> Ok
ch19.caption: Added and renamed fields are survivable: a missing optional field falls back to a default, and a renamed field is mapped by an alias.

ch19.text: The same tolerant reader also handles fields it does not recognize at all:

ch19.chart:
flowchart TD
  R[Reader parses a message] --> C{Unknown extra field?}
  C -->|Yes| Ignore[Ignore unless deny_unknown_fields]
  Ignore --> Ok[Parse succeeds]
ch19.caption: An unknown extra field is ignored unless deny_unknown_fields is set. The change that breaks a tolerant reader is repurposing an existing field, which has no safe edge in either half.

ch19.text: A compatibility break is not only a code change. It is a deployment coordination problem. Make the version boundary visible in data, tests, and logs before a mixed producer-consumer rollout forces emergency repair.
Version-tolerant models

Version tolerance is usually about reader discipline. Readers should survive additive fields, tolerate missing optional fields with defaults, and keep deprecated aliases around long enough to drain old producers safely.

A practical pattern is this: internal domain type on one side, wire DTO on the other, plus explicit conversion. That makes compatibility work visible and prevents one old wire compromise from contaminating the core model forever.
Custom serializers and deserializers

Custom serializers are for boundary-specific representation: money as decimal text, compact IDs, legacy booleans, or normalized timestamps. The goal is to keep the internal model honest while still meeting an external contract.

Custom logic belongs at the edge. Do not store a decimal money string in the domain only because one API contract needed it. Keep the internal unit cheap and precise, then translate at serialization time.

Be careful with naive split-on-dot money parsing: it is a classic correctness trap. The fractional part must be validated as exactly two digits, or scaled by its length, before being added to the whole part. A reader that accepts "12.5" as 1205 cents has silently lost money.
Zero-copy deserialization

Some formats let a deserialized value borrow directly from the input buffer instead of copying each string out. A field typed as &str or Cow<’de, str> can point into the bytes you parsed, which avoids allocation and copying on a hot path. The catch is pure Rust: the borrowed view cannot outlive the buffer it points into. That is fine for parse-time validation, and wrong the moment the value needs to live on a queue, in a cache, or across an await point. The decision is therefore about lifetime, and the diagram makes the fork explicit.

ch19.chart:
flowchart TD
  Buf[Input buffer] -->|borrow| View[Parsed view with lifetime]
  View --> Q1{Crosses thread, queue, or await?}
  Q1 -->|No, stays local| Use[Validate and use in place]
  Q1 -->|Yes| Own[Convert to owned value]
  Own --> Send[Safe to send, store, or queue]
  Use --> Drop[Drop before buffer is freed]
ch19.caption: Borrow while the buffer is alive and the work stays local; convert to owned the moment the value must outlive the buffer or cross a boundary.

ch19.text: The operational rule is simple. Borrow while parsing if that reduces copying locally. Own the data once the message crosses a wider subsystem boundary.
Serialization for distributed systems

Across a network, the contract is no longer a convenience; it is the interface. Producers and consumers deploy on different schedules, so at any instant an old producer may be sending messages to a new consumer or the reverse. The patterns below all serve one goal: make the contract and its version explicit in the data, in the tests, and in the logs, so that a version skew is something you detect rather than something that detects you in production.
Serialization for WASM and FFI boundaries

Not every boundary is a network, but every boundary still has a contract. At the WASM edge you are handing data to JavaScript, and the choice is whether to translate into a structured JS value or pass a text or binary payload that JavaScript parses. At the FFI edge you are handing data to C, and the cardinal rule is to never let Rust’s in-memory layout become the contract by accident: a struct’s field order and padding are implementation details until you pin them with repr(C) or replace them with an explicit byte buffer and length. The honest move at either edge is to decide what the foreign side actually wants and give it exactly that.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The most expensive serialization bug is often not a parser crash. It is a silent contract drift between producer and consumer that still compiles, still deploys, and only breaks when mixed versions meet.
Examples
Example 1: a versioned domain event envelope
The envelope carries explicit versioning, and the event payload stays tagged so readers can tell what happened without guessing from field shape.

What to look at: the envelope wraps the payload and carries the version, while the inner enum is internally tagged with #[serde(tag = "kind")] so the kind travels inside the JSON object rather than being inferred from which fields happen to be present. Trace the round trip below before reading the code: serialize to JSON, parse back, then match on the tag.

ch19.chart:
flowchart TD
  Env[EventEnvelope schema 2] --> Ser[serde_json to_string]
  Ser --> Json[JSON with kind inside payload]
  Json --> De[serde_json from_str]
  De --> Env2[EventEnvelope]
  Env2 --> Match{match payload kind}
  Match -->|created| Out[read total_cents]
  Match -->|cancelled| Zero[total 0]
ch19.caption: The version rides on the envelope and the kind rides inside the tagged payload, so a reader recovers both from the bytes without guessing.

ch19.text: schema_version and event ID make the contract visible to code and logs.
The payload declares its kind explicitly instead of forcing consumers to infer it from a field pattern.
Optional envelope fields can be added with defaults without destabilizing older readers immediately.
Example 2: custom money format plus borrowed fields
The wire format wants decimal text. The internal model wants cents. The deserialized view borrows request text until the boundary decides whether ownership is needed.

What to look at: two boundary concerns sit side by side on one struct. The amount_cents field routes through a custom serializer pair so the wire sees decimal text while the domain keeps an exact integer, and the string fields are typed to borrow from the input buffer. Follow how the raw JSON splits into a borrowed view plus a converted integer below.

ch19.chart:
flowchart TD
  Raw["raw JSON bytes"] --> Parse[serde_json from_str]
  Parse -->|borrow| Id["request_id: &str"]
  Parse -->|borrow| Route["route: Cow str"]
  Parse -->|deserialize_with| Conv[decimal_as_cents]
  Conv --> Amt["amount_cents: u64 = 1250"]
  Id --> View[BorrowedAudit tied to raw]
  Route --> View
  Amt --> View
ch19.caption: The custom deserializer converts '12.50' into 1250 cents, while the string fields stay borrowed from the raw buffer the BorrowedAudit is tied to.

ch19.text: The boundary gets decimal text without forcing the domain to store money as strings.
The request ID and route can borrow from the input buffer while parsing stays local.
The next subsystem can still choose to own the fields before queueing or storing the event.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch19_serialization_and_data_contracts/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to round-trip a versioned domain event, add a custom Serde serializer, design a zero-copy parse boundary, and choose different contracts for distributed systems, WASM, and FFI edges.
Summary

items: Serde removes boilerplate, but the real work is still contract design.
Whatever language you came from, the shift is the same: the wire shape is a contract you design, and ownership and lifetime still matter at the boundary.
JSON, YAML, TOML, MessagePack, CBOR, and binary formats make different tradeoffs across readability, size, and interoperability.
Schema evolution is easiest when you prefer additive changes, defaults, aliases, and explicit envelopes.
Custom serializers protect the internal model from transport-specific compromises.
Zero-copy deserialization is useful at local parse boundaries, but owned handoff is usually better at wider system boundaries.
WASM and FFI edges need explicit contracts just as much as distributed systems do, even when the transport is not a network protocol.

ch20.text: Metaprogramming in Rust is a build-time tool for removing repetitive syntax while preserving clear APIs. This chapter treats macros and generated code as maintainable compile-time infrastructure: when each kind earns its place, how expansion fits into the compiler pipeline, and where a plain function, generic, or offline generator is the calmer answer.
Builds on Chapters 03, 14, 18, and 19

Chapter 03 matters because proc macros and larger code generation strategies live at crate and build-system boundaries. Chapter 14 matters because many derive macros emit trait impls. Chapter 18 matters because macros and generics solve different problems. Chapter 19 matters because derive and attribute macros often sit directly on serialization and contract surfaces.
Opening scenario

Picture a service platform that has grown a familiar set of repetitions: route declarations that all follow the same method-path-auth shape, DTO metadata duplicated next to every struct, validation boilerplate copied across handlers, and adapter glue generated by hand from an external schema. Each of these looks like a candidate for metaprogramming, but they are not the same kind of problem, and the same tool does not fit all four. The goal of this chapter is to remove the structural repetition without hiding runtime behavior behind decorative syntax.

The four mechanisms map onto four distinct shapes of duplication. Plain functions, generics, and traits handle anything where the variation is in values, types, or behavior. Declarative macros handle small, local syntax patterns. Procedural macros handle item-level generation that has to read the structure of a type or an attribute. Build-time codegen handles surfaces whose source of truth lives outside Rust entirely. The skill is matching the shape, not reaching for the most powerful tool by reflex.
A practical decision order

Read the decision as a ladder you climb only when the rung below genuinely cannot hold the weight. Each step up buys expressive power and pays for it in compile time, diagnostics, and the size of the API surface you commit to keeping stable.

ch20.caption: The decision ladder: most repetition is not syntactic at all. Only after ruling out functions, generics, and offline generation do the two macro forms come into play.

items: Start with a normal function, generic, trait, or enum and confirm why it is insufficient.
If the duplication is syntax-shaped inside Rust, try macro_rules! first.
If the API must attach to items, inspect attributes, or emit impls from type definitions, consider a procedural macro.
If the source of truth is external or the generated surface is large, prefer a build script or offline generator.

ch20.text: Mental model
Where expansion sits in the pipeline

The single fact that explains most macro behavior is ordering. Expansion runs near the front of compilation, and every safety check you rely on runs on the output. A macro can decide what code exists; it cannot decide what that code is allowed to do.

ch20.chart:
flowchart TD
  Src[Source tokens] --> Exp[Macro expansion]
  Exp --> Names[Name resolution]
  Names --> Borrow[Borrow checking]
  Borrow --> Traits[Trait solving]
  Traits --> Mono[Monomorphization and codegen]
ch20.caption: Macros transform tokens at the first stage. Borrow checking and trait solving run afterward on the expanded code, exactly as if you had written it by hand.

ch20.text: Core concepts
Declarative macros with macro_rules!

One correction to keep in mind: macro_rules! is not a type system escape hatch. It is a token-pattern expansion tool. Borrow checking, trait solving, and monomorphization still happen after expansion.
Procedural macros

Procedural macros are Rust functions that run at compile time, take a token stream in, and return a token stream out. They come in three forms, distinguished by what they are attached to and what they receive. The shape below is worth fixing in your head before reading the cards: a derive sees a copy of the type and adds alongside it, an attribute receives the item and replaces it, and a function-like macro receives whatever tokens sit inside its delimiters.

ch20.chart:
flowchart TD subgraph Derive["proc_macro_derive"] D1[Type definition] --> D2[Generated impls
added next to it] end subgraph Attr["proc_macro_attribute"] A1[Annotated item] --> A2[Rewritten or wrapped
item replaces it] end
ch20.caption: The two item-attached forms: a derive leaves the type intact and adds impls beside it, while an attribute consumes the item it sits on and replaces it with a rewritten version.

ch20.text: The third form is not attached to an item at all. It receives whatever tokens sit inside its call delimiters:

ch20.chart:
flowchart TD subgraph Func["proc_macro function-like"] F1[Tokens inside the call] --> F2[New items
or expressions] end
ch20.caption: The function-like form: it expands an arbitrary token blob into new items or expressions, with no surrounding item to inspect.

ch20.text: Procedural macros are powerful because they can inspect and rewrite item-level syntax. They are also heavy because they add a crate boundary, compile-time work, and a bigger diagnostic surface. Reach for them only when that power is actually needed.
Token streams

A procedural macro never sees your program as values or as a resolved type graph. It sees a TokenStream: a flat sequence of identifiers, literals, punctuation, and grouped sub-streams, each carrying a span that points back at the original source. Most real proc macros parse that stream into a syntax tree with the syn crate, build new code with quote, and convert back to a token stream for the compiler. The diagram shows that round trip.

ch20.chart:
flowchart TD
  In[Input TokenStream] --> Parse[Parse with syn]
  Parse --> AST[Syntax tree plus spans]
  AST --> Build[Build new code with quote]
  Build --> Out[Output TokenStream]
  Out --> CC[Compiler type-checks output]
ch20.caption: The typical proc-macro round trip: tokens in, parse to a syntax tree, generate new tokens, hand them back to the compiler for the usual checks.

ch20.text: One practical consequence follows immediately. Because the macro only ever holds syntax, it cannot consult inferred types or resolved trait impls to decide what to generate: that information simply does not exist yet at expansion time. If a design depends on knowing a field's concrete type or whether some trait is implemented, the macro is fighting the pipeline, and a different approach will be calmer.
Code generation strategies
Macro hygiene
Compile-time DSLs

A route table macro, a compact compile-time query wrapper, or a repetitive test-case generator can be excellent. A DSL that hides ownership, control flow, or expensive runtime work behind decorative syntax is usually not.
When not to use macros
If you are coming from another language

Every mainstream language has some form of metaprogramming, and that prior experience is the most common source of wrong instincts here. The cards below name the one mental-model shift each background tends to need. The through-line is that Rust does this work at compile time, on syntax, and feeds the result back through the same type checker that judges hand-written code.

The shared correction across all four: do not pick a macro because the borrow checker, the trait system, or type design felt inconvenient. A macro can change the syntax you write, but it cannot exempt the resulting code from any of those rules. When the friction is about ownership or types, the fix lives in ownership or types, not in a layer that runs before they are even checked.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

Macros compress source code, but they can expand maintenance cost. If the generated surface, diagnostics, and review burden are worse than the original repetition, the metaprogramming gave you nothing.
Examples
Example 1: macro_rules! repetition plus hygiene
One macro introduces a local binding, another expands a repeated list. The caller keeps its own total untouched.

What to look at: both the caller and the sum_values! macro define a binding called total, yet the final outer total = 40 proves they never collide. Hygiene gives the macro's internal name a different identity from the caller's, so expansion cannot accidentally overwrite a variable that happens to share a name.

ch20.chart:
flowchart TD
  Caller["Caller: let total = 40"] --> Call["sum_values!(1, 2, 3)"]
  Call --> Expand["Expansion: let total = 0; total += ..."]
  Expand --> Hyg{Same identifier text}
  Hyg -->|hygiene keeps them distinct| Sep["Macro total separate from caller total"]
  Sep --> Out["sum = 6, caller total still 40"]
ch20.caption: The macro's internal total and the caller's total share spelling but not identity. Hygiene keeps the expansion from clobbering the caller's binding.

ch20.text: $($value:expr),* removes the repeated accumulator code at the call site.
The macro's internal bindings do not steal the caller's total name.
This is the right scale for macro_rules!: small syntax compression, ordinary emitted Rust.
Example 2: a small compile-time DSL for route tables
The macro call site reads like a compact route declaration, but it still expands into ordinary Rust data with explicit fields.

What to look at: each line in the macro call is one route, and the recursive @auth arms turn the public and private markers into ordinary booleans. The whole DSL expands to nothing more exotic than a Vec<Route> of plain structs, which is exactly why it stays reviewable.

ch20.chart:
flowchart TD
  Call["routes! { GET /health public, ... }"] --> Per[For each entry]
  Per --> M[stringify! method]
  Per --> P[path literal]
  Per --> A["@auth arm to bool"]
  M --> R[Route value]
  P --> R
  A --> R
  R --> Vec["Vec of Route structs"]
ch20.caption: Each DSL entry expands into one Route struct, and the call as a whole becomes a plain vector of explicit values with no hidden IO or allocation policy.

ch20.text: The grammar is intentionally tiny: method, path, and one auth marker. Small DSLs survive reviews better.
The expansion is only a vector of Route values. No hidden IO, no hidden allocation policy surprise.
If this grammar grew much larger, a proc macro or an offline generator might become the better tool.

The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch20_metaprogramming/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor. The runnable editors focus on macro_rules! because real procedural macros require a separate proc-macro crate.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to choose between functions and macros on the merits, write a small macro_rules! helper for repetitive checks, sketch a derive macro API, and map real production needs to declarative macros, procedural macros, or build-time code generation.
Summary

items: macro_rules! is the lightest metaprogramming tool when token-pattern expansion is enough.
Procedural macros operate on token streams in a separate proc-macro crate and are best for derive, attribute, and token-level DSL use cases.
Macro hygiene helps, but public macros still create a public syntax contract that must be maintained carefully.
Compile-time DSLs should stay small and expand into understandable Rust data or items.
When the abstraction is about values, types, or behavior instead of syntax, a function, generic, trait, enum, or build script is usually the better tool.

ch21.text: Runtime introspection is limited in Rust, so production systems need explicit metadata and generated descriptors. This chapter covers trait-based inspection, registries, and schema surfaces.
Builds on Chapters 14, 19, and 20

Chapter 14 introduced traits and trait objects. Chapter 19 covered schema and wire contracts. Chapter 20 covered compile-time metaprogramming. Reflection and introspection in Rust sit across those boundaries.
Opening scenario

A service platform needs typed request extensions, plugin capability metadata, and admin-facing schema descriptors. The business requirement is narrow introspection: use TypeId and Any only for type-keyed registries, expose plugin metadata as ordinary trait methods, and generate schema artifacts where field structure must be documented.
A practical decision order

items: Start with ordinary structs, enums, and trait methods.
If one container truly must store heterogeneous values, consider `Any` plus `TypeId`.
If the source code already knows the shape, prefer macros or schema generation at compile time.
If operators or plugins need metadata, make that metadata an explicit API.

ch21.text: Mental model
Core concepts
The four tools, and what each one is for

It helps to see the whole landscape before the details, because “reflection” in Rust is not one feature but four narrow tools that solve four different problems. Two of them work at runtime and two of them work at compile time. The runtime pair, TypeId and Any, gives you type identity and checked recovery of a value you erased on purpose. The compile-time pair, derive macros and compiler-built labels such as type_name, lets the source code that already knows a type’s shape emit new code or descriptors before the program runs. Almost every real need maps onto one of these four; the trap is reaching for a fifth that does not exist.

ch21.chart:
flowchart TD
  N[I want to introspect a type] --> Q{When do I know the type?}
  Q -->|At runtime, erased| R[Runtime tools]
  Q -->|At build time, in source| C[Compile-time tools]
  R --> T1[TypeId: identity key]
  R --> T2[Any: checked downcast]
  C --> T3[derive macros: emit code]
  C --> T4[type_name / stringify: labels]
ch21.caption: The first question is when you know the type: erased at runtime, or visible in source at build time. Each answer leads to its own pair of tools.

ch21.text: Two of those four tools are routinely misused as stable identifiers. The second half marks which ones:

ch21.chart:
flowchart TD
  T1[TypeId: identity key] -.weak as.-> X[Not a schema or protocol key]
  T4[type_name / stringify: labels] -.weak as.-> X
ch21.caption: TypeId and the compiler-built labels are process-local or diagnostic only; neither is a stable schema or protocol key, so the dotted edges warn against persisting them.

ch21.text: Why Rust has limited runtime reflection

The absence of broad reflection is a design choice, not a missing feature. Rust specializes generic code by monomorphization and resolves most calls statically, which means the per-type metadata a reflective runtime would need to keep alive has usually been compiled away by the time the program runs. Carrying it anyway would add weight to every binary and pull assumptions that belong in source into runtime tables. The practical consequence is the three cards below: there is no field walk, layout and codegen stay explicit, and the needs people actually have turn out to be narrower than “reflect over anything.”
Any and TypeId: erase a type, then recover it safely

TypeId is a small, copyable token that uniquely identifies one concrete type, valid within a single process and a single build of your program. Any is the trait that lets you store a value behind an erased pointer such as Box<dyn Any> and later ask, at runtime, “is the thing in here actually a RetryBudget?” The two work together: you erase a value to put it in a heterogeneous container, you key or check it by TypeId, and you recover it as exactly one named type. The recovery is always checked, so a wrong guess returns None rather than reinterpreting bytes. One constraint shapes all of this: Any is for ’static types, because a runtime identity cannot encode a borrow that only lives for part of the program.

ch21.chart:
flowchart TD
  V[Concrete value: RetryBudget] -->|Box::new| E[Box dyn Any]
  E -->|store| M[(HashMap keyed by TypeId)]
  M -->|lookup by TypeId of T| E2[Box dyn Any]
  E2 -->|downcast_ref T| D{Type matches?}
  D -->|yes| Some[Some and ref to RetryBudget]
  D -->|no| None2[None]
ch21.caption: A value is erased into Box<dyn Any>, stored under its TypeId, and only ever comes back as the one concrete type you ask for; a mismatch is None, never a reinterpretation.

ch21.text: A key correction for reflection-heavy backgrounds: `TypeId` is runtime type identity, not a schema, not a field list, and not a stable public protocol key.
Downcasting: recovering one named type by borrow, by mut, or by value

Downcasting is the act of recovery, and it comes in three forms that mirror Rust’s ownership choices. The form you pick follows how the erased container holds the value and what the caller needs to do with it: read it, mutate it in place, or take ownership back. None of these is a cast in the C-language sense; each one checks the type first and only succeeds if it matches.
Downcasting is precise and explicit. You only recover a concrete type you already know how to name. That is why it is useful as an edge tool and weak as a general application architecture.
Trait-object-based reflection patterns
Compile-time introspection through macros

This is where most of what other languages call reflection actually happens in Rust, just earlier in the timeline. A derive macro reads the syntax of your struct or enum and writes more Rust before type checking, so a Serialize implementation that “knows” every field is generated rather than discovered. The result is the same capability a reflective serializer offers, with the cost paid at build time and the field walk visible to the compiler. The compiler-built labels in the third card are a separate, smaller tool: good for logs and panics, but never a contract.
Generating schema instead of inspecting values

When you need a machine-readable description of a type for documentation, client generation, or validation, generate it from the source rather than inspecting live values. A crate such as schemars uses the same derive machinery to turn a transport DTO into a JSON Schema at build time. That keeps the schema close to the type it describes and frees the domain model to evolve behind the wire DTO, instead of tying a public contract to whatever fields a value happens to expose at runtime.
Plugin systems that declare rather than infer

A plugin host is the classic place where engineers from reflective languages reach for runtime inspection: load a plugin, scan it for its name and capabilities, dispatch accordingly. The calmer Rust design inverts that. Each plugin returns a descriptor through an ordinary trait method, so the host reads metadata the same way it reads any other return value, and downcasting is held back as a rare escape hatch for the one specialized path that genuinely needs a concrete type. The diagram makes the split concrete: the wide path is trait dispatch, and the narrow dotted path is the occasional downcast.

ch21.chart:
flowchart TD
  H[Plugin host] -->|metadata| T[trait method: common path]
  H -->|run| T
  T --> A[Plugin A]
  T --> B[Plugin B]
  H -.as_any then downcast.-> S[One concrete plugin: rare path]
ch21.caption: The common path is a trait method every plugin implements; downcasting via as_any is the narrow dotted exception, not the main API.

ch21.text: Designing explicit metadata systems
What changes by background

Reflection is one of the topics where prior experience cuts both ways: the vocabulary transfers, but the reflexes mislead. The shift to keep in mind is that Rust moves structural introspection from a runtime capability you call to a compile-time capability you generate, and keeps only a narrow runtime identity check for the cases that truly need it. Read the card for your own background before the production patterns.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
If the code only works after many downcasts, the system is probably missing an explicit contract. Rust reflection tools are strongest when they stay narrow and explicit.
Examples
Example 1: a small `TypeId` + `Any` registry
The container is erased, but recovery is still type-checked and explicit.

What to look at: every method on TypeMap uses the generic parameter T twice over, once to compute TypeId::of::<T>() as the map key and once to drive the downcast_ref::<T>() on the way out. The store itself is untyped (HashMap<TypeId, Box<dyn Any>>), yet the public API only ever returns the concrete type the caller named. Trace one insert and one get through the diagram, then read the same two paths in the code.

ch21.chart:
flowchart TD
  Ins[insert RetryBudget] -->|TypeId of T as key| Put[(values map)]
  Ins -->|Box::new value| Put
  Get[get RetryBudget] -->|TypeId of T| Look{key present?}
  Look -->|no| N[None]
  Look -->|yes| Dc[downcast_ref T]
  Dc -->|matches| Ref[Some and ref to RetryBudget]
ch21.caption: insert keys the box by TypeId::of::<T>(); get recomputes the same TypeId, then downcast_ref::<T>() turns the erased box back into a typed reference.

ch21.expected:
has context = true
retries = 3
trace = req-7

ch21.text: `TypeId` keys the erased store by concrete type, not by string name.
downcast_ref::<T>() recovers one known type and returns Option.
Request extensions and typed registries are simpler than trying to reflect arbitrary structs.
Example 2: explicit plugin metadata plus optional downcast
The common path uses trait methods. Downcasting exists only for the rare specialized path.

What to look at: two of the three results come straight off the trait. Listing the names and reading metadata().kind never touches Any at all, because that data lives on the trait every plugin implements. Only the third result, the pretty flag, is specific to one concrete plugin, so it is the single place that calls as_any() and downcast_ref::<JsonFormatter>(). The diagram shows that asymmetry: the wide trait path and the one narrow downcast.

ch21.chart:
flowchart TD V["Vec of
Box dyn Plugin"] --> M[metadata:
name and kind] M --> Names[plugins =
json,redact] M --> Kind[first kind =
formatter] V --> F[find_map as_any
downcast
JsonFormatter] F -->|matched once| P[json
pretty = true]
ch21.caption: Names and kinds come from the trait method on every plugin; only the pretty flag requires a downcast to the one concrete JsonFormatter.

ch21.expected:
plugins = json,redact
json pretty = true
first kind = formatter

ch21.text: Names and kinds are ordinary trait data, not values inferred at runtime.
`as_any()` is there for one narrow specialized query, not for every call.
Plugin systems are usually easiest to operate when capabilities and config formats are explicit.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch21_reflection_and_type_introspection/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to build a small `TypeId` registry, downcast safely from erased values, and design explicit metadata for a plugin boundary instead of leaning on broad runtime reflection.
Summary

items: Rust has limited runtime reflection on purpose. It offers narrow tools, not broad object inspection.
`Any` and `TypeId` are useful for erased storage and checked recovery inside one process.
Downcasting is an edge tool. Common behavior should stay on traits, enums, and explicit descriptors.
Compile-time macros and schema generation cover many reflection-like needs more cleanly than runtime inspection.
Plugin systems, admin surfaces, and public protocols are usually best served by explicit metadata systems.

ch22.text: Multithreaded Rust systems need clear ownership transfer, shared-state policy, and shutdown behavior. This chapter covers threads, scoped work, channels, and synchronization as production boundaries.
Builds on Chapters 04, 07, 09, and 14

Chapter 04 established ownership and borrowing. Chapter 07 separated moves, copies, and clones. Chapter 09 introduced Arc, Mutex, and related pointer choices. Chapter 14 explained trait-based boundaries. This chapter applies those ideas to OS threads directly.
The problem this chapter solves

Picture a request-processing service with three kinds of work happening at once. It does CPU-heavy preprocessing on incoming payloads, it keeps a shared metrics index up to date, and it hands off slower background jobs to a pool of worker threads. In another language you might reach for one shared object guarded by a lock and call it a day. In Rust the more durable design names each boundary by its ownership story: jobs are moved into the workers that run them, immutable configuration is shared read-only through an Arc, genuinely shared mutation goes behind a lock and nothing else does, and a one-shot parallel pass over local data uses a scoped split so the threads can borrow instead of clone.

That is the spine of the chapter. Each of those four moves, move, share, synchronize, and borrow-in-scope, is a distinct primitive with a distinct cost, and the skill is matching the primitive to the workload rather than defaulting to whichever one compiled first.
One distinction to hold onto: this is about OS threads

Everything here concerns OS threads, the kind the operating system schedules and that cost real memory and scheduler attention. It is deliberately not about async tasks, futures, or executors, even though those also do concurrent work. The two models look similar from a distance and solve different problems, so keep them in separate boxes: threads are scheduled by the OS, async tasks are scheduled by an executor inside your process, and distributed workers are other processes or machines entirely. We cover the async model in its own chapter.
Mental model
Core concepts
Naming the execution models before the APIs

Most confusion in this area is vocabulary, not code. "Concurrency" gets stretched across several unrelated mechanisms with different schedulers, different costs, and different ownership rules. Before any API, fix the terms. The diagram shows who schedules what: the OS schedules threads, an executor schedules tasks inside one process, and distributed work runs in other processes entirely.

ch22.chart:
flowchart TD
  W[Concurrent work] --> OS[OS thread]
  W --> AT[Async task]
  W --> DP[Data parallel job]
  W --> DW[Distributed worker]
ch22.caption: One label, four execution models. Each branch is a different kind of concurrent work with a different cost.

ch22.text: Each of those four kinds is scheduled by something different. The same four branches map to four schedulers:

ch22.chart:
flowchart TD
  OS[OS thread] -->|scheduled by| Kernel[OS scheduler]
  AT[Async task] -->|polled by| Exec[Executor in-process]
  DP[Data parallel job] -->|balanced by| Pool[Work-stealing pool]
  DW[Distributed worker] -->|carried by| Net[Network and serialization]
  AT -.drives.-> Fut[Future state machine]
ch22.caption: Four schedulers for the four models. This chapter is the OS-thread branch; the others have their own contracts and costs.

ch22.text: Rust’s thread safety model
The important part is not the number. It is that the closure owns what it uses, and the caller decides when failure from the child thread becomes visible by joining.
Send and Sync: the two traits that gate every thread boundary

These two auto traits are the entire mechanism behind "data races do not compile." They are marker traits with no methods; the compiler derives them automatically for a type when all of its fields qualify. When you call thread::spawn, its signature quietly requires the closure (and everything it captures) to be Send. A type that is not Send simply will not fit through that boundary, and you get a compile error pointing at the capture rather than a race at 3 a.m. The diagram shows the two questions the compiler is really asking.

ch22.caption: Two questions the compiler asks: moving a value across a thread needs Send; sharing a reference needs Sync.

ch22.text: Those two questions are exactly what separates the two reference-counted pointers at a thread boundary:

ch22.chart:
flowchart TD
  RC[Rc] -->|not Send, not Sync| Reject[rejected at compile time]
  ARC[Arc] -->|Send and Sync if T is| Accept[crosses the boundary]
ch22.caption: Rc fails both checks because its refcount is non-atomic; Arc passes when its contents do, so only Arc crosses the boundary.

ch22.text: Manual unsafe impl Send or unsafe impl Sync is only correct if you can prove the type’s hidden aliasing, mutation, and destruction behavior is thread-safe. Most application code should never need to write those impls.
Spawning threads
Use std::thread::spawn when you need a new OS thread. The closure usually needs move because the child may outlive the current stack frame.
Production code often uses std::thread::Builder when thread names, stack size, or clearer diagnostics matter. Thread names are cheap observability.
Moving data into threads

A move closure transfers ownership of captured non-Copy values into the child thread. That is the calm default for jobs, owned buffers, and request-local domain data that must survive independently in the worker.
Clone only when two threads truly need independent ownership. Share through Arc when the data is genuinely shared. Borrow only inside a scope that guarantees the borrow cannot outlive the parent.
Shared state concurrency
A good default question is this: if only one thread should really own the mutable state, why not send owned commands to that thread instead of putting the state behind a global lock?
Message-passing concurrency
Unbounded and bounded channels tell different operational stories. Use the one that matches memory, latency, and producer-pressure expectations.
Scoped threads
Work stealing

A useful production rule: if the work is CPU-bound collection processing, a Rayon-style work-stealing pool is often calmer than hand-rolling many thread::spawn calls. If the work is IO-bound waiting, an async executor is usually the more honest model. If the work crosses the network, you are in distributed systems.
Coming from another language
If you already write concurrent code somewhere else, the syntax is the easy part. What trips people up is the mental-model shift, so read whichever card matches your background before the examples.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The right concurrency primitive is the one that makes ownership calm under load. A channel, a scoped thread, and a lock can all be correct. The mistake is using one of them because it resembles another language rather than because the workload actually wants it.
Examples
Example 1: spawn workers, move owned jobs, collect by channel
This is an OS-thread design with owned job batches and message passing for results. No worker mutates a shared central map directly.

What to look at: ownership flows in one direction. Each job Vec is moved into its worker, so the worker is the sole owner while it runs; results travel back as small owned tuples over the channel, and only the main thread builds the final map. No worker ever touches that map, so there is nothing to lock.

ch22.chart:
flowchart TD
  M[main] -->|move ingest jobs| W1[ingest worker]
  M -->|move index jobs| W2[index worker]
  W1 -->|send worker total| Ch[(mpsc channel)]
  W2 -->|send worker total| Ch
  M -->|join both| J[handles joined]
  Ch -->|drain rx| Agg[main aggregates totals]
ch22.caption: Jobs move out to the workers; totals come back over one channel; aggregation happens in a single owner. Move out, message back.

ch22.expected:
ingest total = 5
index total = 5
grand total = 10

ch22.text: Each worker is a real OS thread with a join handle.
The job vectors cross the boundary by ownership through a move closure.
Workers return results by channel, so the aggregation boundary stays explicit and deterministic.
Example 2: shared state with Arc<Mutex<...>>
Shared state is sometimes the honest model. The important engineering work is then lock scope, contention, and who really needs to mutate what.

What to look at: the two wrappers do two separate jobs. Arc is what lets every thread reach the same map (each thread gets its own clone of the handle, all pointing at one allocation), and Mutex is what serializes the writes so two increments cannot collide. Read the diagram as: everyone shares the pointer, but only the lock holder may mutate.

ch22.chart:
flowchart TD
  Arc[(Arc Mutex HashMap)] --> T1[thread api]
  Arc --> T2[thread api]
  Arc --> T3[thread billing]
  Arc --> T4[thread api]
  T1 -->|lock, increment, unlock| Crit{Mutex held by one}
  T2 -->|wait then lock| Crit
  T3 -->|wait then lock| Crit
  T4 -->|wait then lock| Crit
  Crit --> Main[main reads final counts]
ch22.caption: Shared ownership via Arc, exclusive mutation via Mutex. The lock is the bottleneck, so keeping the critical section tiny is the whole optimization.

ch22.text: Arc makes the counter map reachable from several threads.
Mutex narrows mutation to one thread at a time.
The model is honest, but lock contention is now a real runtime cost to observe.
Example 3: scoped threads over borrowed slices
This is still multithreading, but the parent keeps ownership and children borrow from it safely inside the scope.

What to look at: nothing is cloned and nothing is wrapped in Arc. The parent owns the array the whole time; the children borrow non-overlapping slices of it. This compiles only because thread::scope guarantees every child joins before the scope returns, so the borrows provably cannot outlive the data. That join-before-exit guarantee is the entire reason scoped threads can do what a plain spawn cannot.

ch22.chart:
flowchart TD
  Arr[values owned by parent] --> Split[split_at index 3]
  Split -->|borrow left slice| L[scope child: sum left]
  Split -->|borrow right slice| R[scope child: sum right]
  L -->|join| P[parent combines]
  R -->|join| P
  P --> Exit[scope exits, borrows end]
ch22.caption: The parent keeps ownership; children borrow disjoint slices and are joined before the scope can return. No Arc, no clone, no 'static requirement.

ch22.text: The slices are borrowed from the parent array instead of cloned into separate owners.
The scope guarantees both child threads join before the borrowed data can disappear.
This pattern is excellent for local CPU-bound slice processing with no detached worker lifetime.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch22_multithreading_in_rust/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to classify types by Send and Sync, repair non-’static thread captures, compare channel-based and shared-state designs, and choose among scoped threads, work stealing, async tasks, and distributed workers from the shape of a workload.
Summary

items: Rust multithreading is ordinary ownership plus two auto traits, Send and Sync, that turn most data races into compile errors.
OS threads, async tasks, futures, executors, data parallelism, and distributed workers are different execution models with different schedulers and different costs.
thread::spawn usually wants owned captured data; thread::scope is the tool when borrowing local stack data is the honest model.
Shared state with Arc and a lock can be correct, but a channel is often calmer when only one thread should own the mutation.
Work stealing is a scheduler strategy used by data-parallel libraries, not a synonym for spawning threads by hand.
Good production thread design is observable, join-aware, and explicit about queue growth, lock contention, and panic handling.

ch23.text: Synchronization primitives protect shared state and coordinate progress under contention. This chapter covers mutexes, read-write locks, atomics, barriers, and channels as explicit workload choices.
Builds on Chapters 04, 09, and 22

Chapter 04 gave us ownership and borrowing. Chapter 09 explained Arc, Mutex, and related pointer choices. Chapter 22 established OS-thread ownership boundaries and message passing. This chapter zooms into the synchronization contracts themselves.
Opening scenario

Picture a small retry service running several worker threads. It holds three pieces of state with three very different access patterns: a table of in-flight requests that workers mutate constantly, a configuration snapshot that is read on every request and rewritten only when an operator pushes a change, and a queue of jobs that really wants a single consumer draining it. Each piece is a different concurrency problem, and the mistake that causes the most pain is reaching for the same primitive for all three.

The discipline this chapter teaches is to derive the primitive from the access pattern rather than from habit. A short, contended mutation wants a mutex. A read-mostly snapshot wants a read-write lock. A single-word flag or counter wants an atomic. A thread that must wait for state to change wants a condvar tied to that state. And a job stream with one owner wants a channel, because the real model is ownership transfer, not sharing. Naming the access pattern first turns primitive selection from a guessing game into a lookup.
A useful decision order
Read the diagram top to bottom: the first fork is the most important one, because deciding whether state is shared at all often eliminates locks entirely in favor of message passing.

ch23.caption: The decision order: rule out handoff first, then pick by access shape, and only add a condvar when a thread genuinely needs to wait on a predicate.

items: Decide whether the state is actually shared or whether ownership transfer is the cleaner model.
If the state is shared, decide whether it is write-heavy, read-mostly, or just one-word atomic state.
If threads wait, name the predicate they wait on before choosing condvars, barriers, or channels.
Only consider lock-free patterns after a simple design has been measured and found wanting.

ch23.text: Mental model
What changes by background

Every reader brings a synchronization model from another language. Most of the friction in Rust comes not from the primitives, which look familiar, but from where Rust moves the safety boundary. The shift to internalize is the same in each case: things that were team discipline or runtime conveniences elsewhere become facts the compiler checks here.
Core concepts
Mutex and RwLock

The structural idea that distinguishes Rust here is that the lock owns the data. A Mutex wraps the value of type T, and the only way to reach the value is to call lock, which hands back a guard. While you hold the guard you have exclusive access; when the guard is dropped, the lock is released. There is no path to the data that skips the lock, which is why a forgotten lock is not a category of bug that exists in safe Rust.

Look at the relationship below before the listings: the guard is a borrow with a lifetime, and releasing the lock is simply that borrow ending. The diagram shows the single path data takes through a mutex versus the two paths a read-write lock allows.

ch23.chart:
flowchart TD
  M[Mutex of T] -->|lock returns guard| G[MutexGuard derefs to T]
  G -->|guard dropped| M
ch23.caption: A mutex offers a single exclusive path to the value. The guard's lifetime is the critical section; dropping it releases the lock.

ch23.text: An RwLock splits that single path into two guard kinds:

ch23.chart:
flowchart TD
  R[RwLock of T] -->|read: shared| RG[many read guards at once]
  R -->|write: exclusive| WG[one write guard, blocks readers]
ch23.caption: An RwLock offers many shared read guards or one exclusive write guard, so reads can overlap while a write still excludes everyone.

ch23.text: A common misconception is worth correcting: an RwLock is not “a faster mutex.” It is a different fairness and contention trade. Multiple readers can hold the lock at once, but a writer must wait for all of them to leave and then excludes everyone, so under frequent writes or tiny read sections the bookkeeping can cost more than a plain mutex would. Reach for it only when you can show the workload is genuinely read-mostly.
Condvar

A condition variable solves a specific problem: a thread needs to wait until some shared state changes, and busy-spinning on the mutex would waste a core. The condvar lets the waiter atomically release the mutex and sleep, then re-acquire the mutex when it is woken. The crucial detail is that a wakeup is only a hint to re-check; it is not a promise that the predicate is now true, because of spurious wakeups and because another thread may have consumed the state first. That is why the wait always sits inside a while loop that tests the predicate.
The condvar is not the source of truth. The mutex-protected predicate is. The wait loop exists to keep that distinction explicit.
Atomics and memory ordering

An atomic operation is indivisible: no other thread can observe it half-done. That alone covers counters and flags. The harder concept is memory ordering, which controls whether the other writes a thread made before an atomic store become visible to a thread that observes that store. Modern CPUs and compilers reorder ordinary memory accesses freely, so without an ordering constraint a reader can see the flag flip to true while the data it was supposed to publish is still stale. The ordering you choose is a contract about that visibility, not about the atomic value itself.

A practical rule is simple. If one atomic flag publishes other writes, the writer usually uses Release on the flag store and the reader uses Acquire on the flag load. If you cannot explain the publication story in one paragraph, a mutex or channel may be the better tool.
Barriers and channels

Channels deserve to stay in this chapter because they are often the simplest synchronization primitive for a one-owner mutable subsystem. The standard library gives mpsc::channel and sync_channel as solid baselines, and the ecosystem offers richer channel semantics when the workload needs them.
Lock-free patterns

In real systems, lock-free structures usually imply unsafe code somewhere in the implementation, plus a memory reclamation story. That is why “avoid all locks” is not a mature design principle by itself.
Deadlock prevention

Almost every classic deadlock is a cycle: thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1, and neither will ever yield. The diagram contrasts that cycle with the fix, which is to impose one global order on locks so every thread always acquires them in the same sequence. With a total order there is no cycle to form.
