Most of deadlock prevention is this kind of design discipline rather than any special primitive.

ch23.chart:
flowchart TD
  A[Thread A holds L1] -->|wants L2| B[Thread B holds L2]
  B -->|wants L1| A
ch23.caption: The deadlock: a wait cycle. A holds L1 and wants L2 while B holds L2 and wants L1, so neither can proceed.

ch23.text: The fix is a single global lock ordering that both threads obey:

ch23.chart:
flowchart TD
  T1[Thread A: lock L1 then L2] --> Order[Global order: L1 before L2]
  T2[Thread B: lock L1 then L2] --> Order
ch23.caption: With one global order, every thread takes L1 before L2, so no cycle can form and the deadlock disappears.

ch23.text: Choosing the right primitive
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
The hardest synchronization bug is often not a missing lock. It is choosing shared mutable state when the workload really wanted one owner and message passing.
Examples
Example 1: Mutex plus Condvar for a tiny shared queue
The condvar only wakes the worker. The queue state under the mutex remains the real predicate.
What to look at: the worker holds the lock, then loops on while jobs.is_empty() && !closed, calling wait inside the loop. Follow that loop in the diagram before reading the code.

ch23.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Locked: lock the mutex
  Locked --> CheckPredicate: jobs empty and not closed?
  CheckPredicate --> Wait: yes
  Wait --> CheckPredicate: woken, re-check
  CheckPredicate --> Drain: no, job available
  CheckPredicate --> Exit: no, closed and empty
  Drain --> CheckPredicate: pop one, loop
  Exit --> [*]: return processed count
ch23.caption: The worker re-checks the mutex-protected predicate every wakeup. The condvar only says re-check now; the queue state is the source of truth.

ch23.text: The queue state has one synchronized owner at a time.
The worker sleeps until the predicate might have changed, then re-checks in a loop.
This is correct shared-state synchronization, but a channel would be simpler if one thread should own the queue.
Example 2: RwLock plus Barrier for read-mostly configuration
The write happens once before the phase boundary. Readers then observe the same snapshot together.

What to look at: the write to the config happens before the main thread reaches start.wait(), so when the barrier releases all three threads, both readers see the same updated snapshot. The timeline below shows that gate.

ch23.chart:
sequenceDiagram
  participant M as Main thread
  participant R1 as Reader 1
  participant R2 as Reader 2
  participant B as Barrier (3)
  R1->>B: wait()
  R2->>B: wait()
  M->>M: write lock, set version=2, mode=burst
  M->>B: wait() (third arrival)
  B-->>R1: release all
  B-->>R2: release all
  R1->>R1: read lock, see version 2
  R2->>R2: read lock, see version 2
ch23.caption: Readers park at the barrier; the writer updates the snapshot and then arrives third. The barrier releasing is the phase gate that makes the write visible to both readers.

ch23.text: The configuration is shared and read-mostly, so parallel reads make sense.
The barrier is a phase gate, not a data container.
If writes become common, this design should be re-measured against a simpler mutex or one-owner model.
Example 3: Atomic publication with Acquire and Release
The data word stays relaxed. The publication flag carries the ordering relationship.
What to look at: the value is stored with Relaxed, but the flag is stored with Release and loaded with Acquire. That one pairing is the synchronization edge. Trace it in the diagram first.

ch23.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Writer
    W1[store value = 42, Relaxed] --> W2[store ready = true, Release]
  end
  subgraph Reader
    R1[load ready, Acquire] -->|false, spin| R1
    R1 -->|true| R2[load value, Relaxed]
  end
  W2 -.happens-before.-> R1
  W1 -.now visible.-> R2
ch23.caption: The Release store paired with the Acquire load forms a happens-before edge. Crossing it makes the earlier Relaxed write to value visible, so the reader is guaranteed to see 42.

ch23.text: The flag is the synchronization edge. The reader only trusts the payload after the Acquire load succeeds.
Release on the writer and Acquire on the reader express the visibility contract directly.
This pattern is for small publication state, not for a whole shared object graph.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch23_synchronization_primitives/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to replace a mutex with an RwLock where it fits, reason about Acquire and Release ordering in a toy publication example, and repair a deadlock-prone lock design before it becomes a production incident.
Summary

items: Choose a synchronization primitive from the ownership and state model, not from fashion.
Mutex, RwLock, Condvar, atomics, barriers, and channels each answer a different concurrency question.
Acquire and Release are about visibility between threads, not about preserving source-code order by wishful thinking.
Deadlock prevention is mostly design discipline: lock ordering, short critical sections, and avoiding nested shared-state ownership where channels would be clearer.
Lock-free structures are specialist tools. Measure before you replace a simple lock, and prefer proven implementations when the complexity is justified.

ch24.text: Async Rust services depend on futures, executors, cancellation, and ownership across await points. This chapter defines the runtime contract behind coroutines and asynchronous state machines.
Builds on Chapters 09, 14, 22, and 23

Chapter 09 introduced pinning. Chapter 14 covered traits and object safety. Chapter 22 separated OS threads from other execution models. Chapter 23 covered synchronization primitives that still matter in async flows. This chapter puts those pieces together into Rust’s async model.
Repository note

The in-browser editor uses tiny std-only examples so the poll model stays visible without pulling in a full runtime. In production, you will usually pair these ideas with an ecosystem executor and reactor such as Tokio or another async runtime.
The problem async is solving

You are refactoring a service that performs request parsing, several outbound RPCs, cache lookups, and a final database write. Most of that wall-clock time is spent waiting on sockets, not burning CPU. The threads chapter already taught you not to dedicate one OS thread to every waiting connection: threads have stack and scheduler cost, and ten thousand mostly-idle threads is a poor use of the machine. Async is the alternative. It lets a single thread hold thousands of in-flight operations and only do work for the ones that are actually ready to make progress.

That efficiency is not free, and the price is paid in questions the runtime makes you answer explicitly. Which values stay borrowed only locally, and which must become owned before a task is spawned? What happens to the other outbound requests if one of them times out and the fan-out should stop? Who is responsible for cleanup when work is cancelled halfway through? In a thread-per-request model many of these answers are implicit in the stack; in async they become part of your types. Rust’s async story holds up in production precisely because it refuses to hide them.
A practical decision order

items: Decide which boundaries are truly IO-bound and therefore worth making async.
Decide which data must become owned before a spawned or retried future can outlive the current scope.
Decide how cancellation propagates when the parent request no longer cares.
Only then choose runtime-specific spawn, join, timeout, or task-group APIs.

ch24.text: Three ideas to anchor the rest of the chapter
If you keep only three things in mind, keep these. Everything later in the chapter is a consequence of them.
Coming from another language

Async exists in C++, C#, Go, and Python too, so you already have an instinct for it. Each of those instincts is right about something and wrong about something else when applied to Rust. The corrections below are the mental-model shifts that matter most before you write any code.

The thread that runs through all four: in Rust, calling an async function produces a value and starts nothing. Execution, thread placement, and cancellation are decisions made by the executor and visible in your types, not conveniences supplied by an ambient runtime.
Core concepts
Coroutines are the intuition, futures are the mechanism

“Coroutine” is a fine word for the shape of the code: a function that can pause in the middle and pick up later. But coroutine is not what Rust actually exposes. What you get is a plain value that implements the Future trait, and the only way it ever runs is for an executor to call poll on it. Keeping that distinction sharp explains almost every surprise newcomers hit.
Rust’s async model

An async fn is sugar for a function that returns an opaque future. Inside that future, each .await is a place where the current future may hand control back to the executor instead of blocking the thread. Read the listing below as three phases: the call builds a future, the executor drives it, and the first .await is the seam where waiting turns into a return of Pending rather than a blocked thread.

ch24.chart:
flowchart TD
  Call["load_user(id)"] -->|builds, runs nothing| Fut[Future value]
  Fut -->|executor polls| Body[Run until first .await]
  Body -->|fetch_row not ready| Pending[Return Pending]
  Pending -->|IO ready, waker fires| Resume[Resume after .await]
  Resume --> Done[Return Ready User]
ch24.caption: Calling the async fn only builds the future. The executor polls it, the body runs up to fetch_row().await, yields Pending, and resumes from there once the row is ready.

ch24.text: The operational point is simple: no thread is blocked by the syntax itself. At .await the current future yields Pending, the executor is free to run other tasks, and it polls this one again only after a waker signals that fetch_row can make progress.
What the compiler builds from your async function

The single most useful model of async Rust is this: the compiler rewrites your function into one enum-shaped state machine. Each .await becomes a variant, the variant holds exactly the locals that must survive that suspension, and poll is a match that advances from one variant to the next. The diagram shows the shape for load_user above.

ch24.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Start
  Start --> AwaitingRow: poll, begin fetch_row
  AwaitingRow --> AwaitingRow: poll returns Pending
  AwaitingRow --> Done: row ready, parse_user
  Done --> [*]: return Ready
  note right of AwaitingRow: stores id and the fetch_row future
ch24.caption: Each .await is a state. The AwaitingRow variant carries the locals that must outlive suspension, and poll moves Start to AwaitingRow to Done.

ch24.text: A useful senior-level translation is this: an async function is ordinary Rust control flow lowered into one enum-like state machine plus the locals it must keep alive between polls. Once you see it that way, the lifetime and Send rules later in this chapter stop being surprises and start being consequences.
Why poll takes a pinned reference

Here is the one subtle part. The state machine the compiler generates can hold a reference into itself, for example a borrow of one local that lives across an .await. Such a self-referential value would be corrupted if it were moved in memory, because the internal pointer would still point at the old address. Pin is the type-system promise that, once polling has begun, the future will not move. That is why poll takes Pin<&mut Self> and not a plain mutable reference.
Many everyday futures are effectively movable and implement Unpin. The runtime boundary still has to respect the general pinned case, which is why the poll signature stays as strong as it does.
Who actually runs the future: executors and reactors

A future is inert, so something has to drive it. In production that something is a runtime, and a runtime is really two cooperating parts. The executor is the scheduler that decides which ready task to poll next; the reactor (or IO driver) is the part that watches the operating system for readiness and fires the waker that makes a sleeping task ready again. The two cards name the pieces; the sequence below shows how one waiting operation travels between them.

ch24.chart:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App as Your code
  participant Ex as Executor
  participant Fut as Future
  participant Re as Reactor / OS
  App->>Ex: spawn(future)
  Ex->>Fut: poll(cx)
  Fut->>Re: register interest, store waker
  Fut-->>Ex: Poll::Pending
  Note over Ex: run other tasks meanwhile
  Re-->>Ex: IO ready, call waker
  Ex->>Fut: poll(cx) again
  Fut-->>Ex: Poll::Ready(value)
ch24.caption: The executor polls, the future parks itself with the reactor and returns Pending, and a readiness event wakes the task so the executor polls it to completion.

ch24.text: Cancellation means dropping the future

In a thread, cancellation is awkward because you cannot safely stop a thread at an arbitrary instruction. In async Rust it is the opposite: a future only advances when polled, so to cancel it you simply stop polling it and drop it. A timeout, a select! that picks the other branch, or a parent task that finishes will all drop the loser. The catch is that the future stops at whatever .await it was parked on, and only its destructors run. Anything that needed a second .await to finish is left undone.

ch24.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Running
  Running --> Suspended: hits .await, Pending
  Suspended --> Running: polled again
  Running --> Completed: returns Ready
  Suspended --> Dropped: timeout or select, no more polls
  Dropped --> [*]: only Drop impls run
  Completed --> [*]
ch24.caption: A suspended future is cancelled by being dropped instead of polled again. Cleanup is whatever runs in Drop; logic past the await point never executes.

ch24.text: The important correction is this: “cancel” usually means “drop the future.” If the future must clean up partially acquired state, that cleanup must be explicit in the future’s own design.
Keeping child tasks tied to a parent scope

Back to the opening service: one request fans out to several outbound calls and then joins their results. Structured concurrency is the discipline of making the parent own that whole fan-out, so that the children cannot outlive it. The parent waits for all of them, surfaces the first failure, and drops the rest, which (as the cancellation section just showed) is how you cancel them. The alternative, detaching tasks and forgetting them, is easy to type and hard to operate.

ch24.chart:
flowchart TD
  P[Parent request task] --> A[child: pricing RPC]
  P --> B[child: inventory RPC]
  P --> C[child: cache lookup]
  A --> J{Join all}
  B --> J
  C --> J
  J -->|all ok| R[Combine results]
  J -->|one fails| X[Drop siblings, propagate error]
ch24.caption: The parent owns every child. Join collects all results, or the first failure drops the remaining siblings and the error flows back up one scope.

ch24.text: In runtime-specific code, this often translates to join-set style task groups, request-scoped task scopes, or parent-owned cancellation tokens. The runtime API may differ. The ownership rule should not.
Async methods in traits, and where they get sharp

You will want async methods on traits the moment you have a repository or service seam with more than one implementation. Recent stable Rust supports async fn in traits directly, which covers most generic, statically dispatched code. The edge appears at runtime polymorphism: a dyn Trait with an async method has to erase the returned future type, which is where boxing, object safety, and Send bounds come back into the design.
Where lifetimes bite in async code

Almost every async error message that mentions lifetimes or Send is the state-machine model from earlier coming back to collect. A borrow held across an .await becomes a field of the future and therefore lives as long as the future does; a future handed to spawn may be moved across threads and must be Send + ’static. The recurring fix is the same one from Chapter 1: own the data before it crosses the boundary.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
Async Rust is not hard because the syntax is exotic. It is hard because suspension makes ownership, task lifetime, and cancellation more visible. That is exactly why it holds up well in production.
Examples
Example 1: `async fn`, `.await`, and a tiny `block_on`
The future is lazy. The tiny executor polls it. Each awaited subfuture yields once before becoming ready.
Watch the loop, not the syntax: each printed poll = pending is one trip around block_on, and the future only returns its label after it has been polled enough times to advance through its states.

ch24.chart:
flowchart TD
  Build["build_label()"] -->|lazy future| Loop[block_on loop]
  Loop -->|poll| Pend1[Pending: print pending]
  Pend1 -->|poll| Pend2[Pending: print pending]
  Pend2 -->|poll| Ready["Ready: label = billing:/ready"]
ch24.caption: build_label returns a lazy future; the block_on loop polls it repeatedly, printing pending until the state machine reaches Ready.

ch24.expected:
poll = pending
poll = pending
label = billing:/ready

ch24.text: Calling build_label only constructs a future value.
Each awaited subfuture yields one Pending before the state machine advances.
The tiny block_on loop is the component turning description into progress.
Example 2: a manual `Future` that looks like a state machine
This is the low-level shape the compiler normally generates for you: explicit states, explicit pending, explicit ready.

Follow the Stage field and the retry counter: the future stays in Waiting and returns Pending while retries remain, then transitions to Ready. This is exactly the machine the compiler wrote for you in Example 1, only spelled out by hand.

ch24.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Waiting
  Waiting --> Waiting: poll, retries left, return Pending
  Waiting --> Ready: retries exhausted
  Ready --> [*]: return Ready connected
ch24.caption: The hand-written poll matches on Stage. Waiting decrements retries and returns Pending; once they hit zero it moves to Ready and returns the value.

ch24.expected:
pending stage = Waiting
pending retries = 1
pending stage = Waiting
pending retries = 0
ready = connected

ch24.text: The enum-like Stage values are the shape the compiler usually hides.
Even a tiny manual future must accept Pin<&mut Self> in its poll method.
Compiler-generated async futures are easier to write, but they obey the same poll protocol.

The repository also includes standalone Rust files under examples/ch24_coroutines_futures_and_async_rust/ including extra files for a Send-safe spawn boundary and drop-based cancellation cleanup beyond the in-browser editors.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to trace an async function as a state machine, repair a Send-bound spawn problem, model cancellation cleanup explicitly, and choose structured concurrency patterns from workload shape.
Summary

ch25.text: Tokio provides the runtime layer for network services, timers, tasks, and blocking work isolation. This chapter covers backpressure, task ownership, shutdown, and runtime configuration.
Builds on Chapters 22, 23, and 24

Chapter 22 established OS-thread boundaries and message passing. Chapter 23 covered synchronization and visibility. Chapter 24 explained futures, async fn, and Pin. Tokio turns those concepts into an operational runtime for production services.
Opening scenario

An ingress service accepts TCP traffic, sends owned jobs through internal queues, reads filesystem snapshots, handles UDP health messages, and must shut down without losing in-flight work. The business requirement is to use Tokio where work is waiting, isolate blocking or CPU-heavy stages, bound internal queues, and make graceful shutdown part of the runtime contract.
Repository note

The in-browser editor simulates output so you can focus on runtime shape. In a real Cargo project, the Tokio dependency normally enables the runtime, macros, time, net, fs, sync, and signal features used by this chapter.
Mental model
Core concepts
What the runtime is made of

The runtime macro on main hides four moving parts. The thing to notice in the diagram below is that the scheduler never blocks waiting for IO or time: the IO driver and the timer driver turn external events into wakeups and feed ready tasks back to the scheduler, while genuinely blocking work is shunted onto a separate pool so it cannot freeze the workers.

ch25.chart:
flowchart TD
  SOCK[Socket readiness] --> IOD[IO driver]
  TMR[Timer deadline] --> TD[Timer driver]
  IOD -->|wake task| RQ[Ready task queue]
  TD -->|wake task| RQ
  RQ --> SCHED[Scheduler polls future]
  SCHED -->|await point| RQ
  SCHED -.->|spawn_blocking| BP[Blocking pool]
  BP -.->|owned result| SCHED
ch25.caption: IO and timer events become wakeups, the scheduler polls ready futures on its workers, and blocking closures run off to the side so they never stall the workers.

ch25.text: The usual default for a service is the multithread runtime, because it can schedule Send tasks across a pool of worker threads and steal work to keep them busy. A current-thread runtime is still the right choice when the application is small, embedded, or deliberately built around non-Send local tasks.
Tasks and scheduling

A task is one future scheduled by the runtime. It is cheap enough to use widely, but not free enough to spray without a policy. A task that never reaches an await point monopolizes its worker thread, and a service that spawns without bounds builds its own backlog and memory pressure even when every individual task is small. The first design question for any unit of work is therefore not how to spawn it, but where it belongs.

The decision tree is short. Work that mostly waits on IO stays inline or goes to tokio::spawn; work that mostly computes goes to spawn_blocking. Putting CPU work on the IO workers is the single most common way to make a Tokio service mysteriously slow.

ch25.chart:
flowchart TD
  W[Unit of work] --> Q{Mostly waiting or mostly computing}
  Q -->|waiting on IO| C{Needs to run concurrently}
  Q -->|CPU heavy or blocking API| SB[spawn_blocking on blocking pool]
  C -->|no, await it here| INLINE[Run inline on this task]
  C -->|yes| SP[tokio::spawn on the IO workers]
  SP --> SEND[Future must be Send and 'static]
ch25.caption: Decide by the nature of the work: inline for local IO, tokio::spawn for concurrent IO that must satisfy Send, spawn_blocking for anything CPU-bound or blocking.

ch25.text: A common production mistake is to reach for tokio::spawn when the real problem was concurrency control. Spawning faster than downstream work can finish is not throughput. It is queue growth with nicer syntax.
Tokio channels

A bounded mpsc is one of the simplest backpressure tools in Tokio. If a producer should slow down when the consumer falls behind, make the capacity explicit so a full queue makes send await, instead of discovering the policy later from a memory graph.
Graceful shutdown
The shape to keep in mind is a small state machine: the accept loop races a stop signal against the next connection, and once the signal wins, the service moves to draining before it exits.

ch25.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Accepting
  Accepting --> Accepting: connection, spawn handler
  Accepting --> Draining: ctrl_c or shutdown signal
  Draining --> Draining: wait for in-flight tasks
  Draining --> Exit: drained or timeout
  Exit --> [*]
ch25.caption: Stop admitting first, drain in-flight work, then exit. The select! below is the Accepting state choosing between a new connection and the stop signal.

ch25.text: Backpressure
How this lands by background

Almost no one meets Tokio with an empty mental model; they arrive with async habits from another ecosystem. The useful thing to know is which of those habits transfer and which one will quietly mislead you. The shift is rarely about API names. It is about where the runtime stops being ambient and starts being something you configure, and where the compiler now insists on facts your previous language let you assume.
Production Tokio patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

Tokio is excellent at waiting and multiplexing. It is not a free pass to ignore CPU budgets, queue budgets, cancellation, or ownership. The runtime gets calmer when those policies are explicit in the design.
Examples
Example 1: bounded channel, interval pacing, and spawn_blocking
The queue is bounded, so producer speed has a budget. The async side waits on the channel and the timer, and the CPU step moves to the blocking pool explicitly.

Read the pipeline before the code: items flow producer to bounded channel to consumer, the consumer paces itself on a timer, and the only CPU-heavy step is pushed across the blocking boundary so it never holds an async worker. Watch how a channel capacity of one is what couples producer and consumer speed.

ch25.chart:
flowchart TD
  P[Producer task] -->|send, awaits when full| CH[Bounded mpsc cap 1]
  CH --> C[Consumer task]
  TICK[interval tick] -.->|pace| C
  C -->|owned batch| SB[spawn_blocking subtotal]
  SB -->|owned result| C
  C --> OUT[total]
ch25.caption: A capacity-1 channel makes the producer wait for the consumer, the interval paces the loop, and the CPU subtotal runs on the blocking pool.

ch25.text: A capacity of one forces producer and consumer speed to meet, instead of buffering without limit.
Async waiting stays on the workers; the CPU subtotal step moves behind spawn_blocking.
The interval is a runtime wakeup, not a background thread and not a busy loop.
Example 2: TCP accept loop with graceful shutdown
The listener owns admission, per-connection work is spawned deliberately, and a watch signal stops the accept loop cleanly before process exit.

The key moment is the race inside the accept loop: each turn waits on both the next connection and the stop signal at once, and whichever resolves first decides what happens. Follow the messages below to see how a normal accept and a shutdown signal flow through the same loop.

ch25.chart:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Sig as Shutdown signal
  participant L as Accept loop
  participant Lis as TcpListener
  participant H as Connection task
  L->>Lis: select! accept or signal
  Lis-->>L: new connection
  L->>H: spawn handler
  H-->>L: pong written
  Sig-->>L: changed() resolves
  L->>L: break accept loop
  Note over L,H: stop admitting, let spawned tasks finish
ch25.caption: Every loop turn races accept against the stop signal; a connection spawns a handler, while the signal breaks the loop so no new work is admitted.

ch25.text: Bind plus accept is the core server loop. Admission is an explicit task, not implicit magic.

A watch channel carries the stop signal into the loop, and select! makes that branch visible in code. changed() also resolves with an error when every sender is dropped, so the branch treats that as a stop; the borrow() re-check exists because a watch can carry values other than the stop sentinel.
Connection tasks are separate from listener ownership, which keeps admission, draining, and metrics easier to reason about.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch25_tokio/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises
The companion exercise page asks you to build a small Tokio TCP service, add graceful shutdown with explicit cancellation signals, and separate blocking CPU work with spawn_blocking.
Summary

items: Tokio is a runtime made of a scheduler plus IO and timer drivers, not only a macro on the main function.
tokio::spawn runs async work concurrently; spawn_blocking is the honest boundary for blocking or CPU-heavy work.
Timers, TCP, UDP, filesystem APIs, and channels all become calmer once task ownership and shutdown behavior are explicit.
Bounded queues, semaphores, and admission control are backpressure tools, not optional polish.
Graceful shutdown is part of the design surface in production Tokio services, not a final cleanup task.

ch26.text: Parallel execution requires matching the library to the workload: async IO, CPU-bound data parallelism, scoped threads, or coordination primitives. This chapter compares those choices through ownership and scheduling.
Builds on Chapters 22 through 25

Chapter 22 covered OS threads and ownership across them. Chapter 23 covered synchronization and visibility. Chapter 24 explained futures and async state machines. Chapter 25 explained Tokio itself. This chapter puts those models side by side with Rayon, Crossbeam, and the futures crate.
Opening scenario

A service has a socket-heavy front door, CPU-heavy enrichment, bounded control-plane queues, and retry handling under overload. The business requirement is to match each execution lane to its workload: Tokio for waiting, Rayon for CPU-parallel batches, Crossbeam for thread coordination, and futures combinators for local async orchestration.
A practical decision order

items: Ask whether the work is mostly waiting or mostly burning CPU.
Ask whether the unit should be a spawned task, a local future, a pool job, or a channel message.
Ask where backpressure and cancellation should be visible.
Then choose Tokio, Rayon, Crossbeam, futures utilities, or a combination.

ch26.text: The same decision drawn as a flow: one question about the nature of the work splits almost every case, and a second question about whether you want a runtime-owned task or a locally driven future splits the rest.

ch26.chart:
flowchart TD Start[New unit of work] --> Q1{Mostly waiting
or mostly CPU?} Q1 -->|waiting on IO| Q2{Own a task
or drive locally?} Q1 -->|burning CPU| Rayon[Rayon
parallel pool] Q2 -->|own a task| Tokio[tokio spawn
or JoinSet] Q2 -->|drive in place| Futures[FuturesUnordered
or join_all] Q1 -->|threads only| Crossbeam[Crossbeam channels
and scope]
ch26.caption: The workload nature decides the executor family; the ownership question then picks the exact tool within the async branch.

ch26.text: Mental model
Core concepts
The tool families at a glance
Async task orchestration
A useful distinction is this: use JoinSet when runtime-spawned tasks are the unit you own. Use FuturesUnordered when you already have futures and only need to drive them together.

The two differ in where the work actually runs. A JoinSet hands each future to the runtime as an independent task, so the runtime’s worker threads make progress on them even while you are not awaiting the set. A FuturesUnordered keeps the futures inside your own task and only advances them while you poll the collection, so it never crosses a task boundary and never requires the futures to be Send.

ch26.chart:
flowchart TD
  J[JoinSet] -->|spawn| T1[runtime task 1]
  J -->|spawn| T2[runtime task 2]
  T1 --> RW[runtime worker threads]
  T2 --> RW
ch26.caption: JoinSet path: each future becomes a separate runtime task that the worker threads advance on their own.

ch26.text: The local path keeps every future inside one task instead, so nothing crosses a task boundary:

ch26.chart:
flowchart TD
  F[FuturesUnordered] -->|polled in place| FA[future a]
  F -->|polled in place| FB[future b]
  FA --> ME[your single task]
  FB --> ME
ch26.caption: FuturesUnordered path: futures advance inside your own task only while you poll the collection, so they never need to be Send.

ch26.text: CPU-bound vs IO-bound workloads
The usual production bug is not using the wrong syntax. It is running CPU-heavy work on the async worker pool or using an async runtime where a straight CPU pool would have been clearer and faster.
Thread pools

A production service rarely has just one pool. The shape that keeps latency predictable is to route each kind of work to the pool built for it: async tasks on the Tokio worker pool, blocking bridges on the Tokio blocking pool, dense compute on a Rayon pool. The diagram below shows the routing, and the one edge to avoid is a CPU loop landing directly on a Tokio worker, where it stalls every unrelated future on that thread.

ch26.chart:
flowchart TD Req[Incoming work] --> Async[Async task] Req --> Block[Blocking or
legacy call] Req --> CPU[CPU-heavy batch] Async --> TW[Tokio
worker pool] Block -->|spawn_blocking| TB[Tokio
blocking pool] CPU -->|par_iter or
send to pool| RP[Rayon
work-stealing pool] CPU -.->|wrong, stalls futures| TW
ch26.caption: Async work stays on Tokio workers, blocking calls move to the blocking pool, and CPU batches go to Rayon. The dotted edge is the bug to avoid.

ch26.text: Backpressure and bounded queues
Cancellation and retry patterns
Designing task APIs
What changes by background

Engineers arriving from other languages tend to carry one habit that misfires here: a single concurrency tool that quietly covered both waiting and computing. Rust splits that into separate executors on purpose, so the useful mental adjustment is less about syntax and more about which assumption from your previous runtime no longer holds.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
The most common mistake is solving all concurrency with the library you learned first. Tokio, Rayon, Crossbeam, and futures combinators are complementary, not interchangeable.
Examples
Example 1: Tokio tasks, JoinSet, bounded admission, and a visible shutdown signal
The queue is bounded, tasks are explicit runtime units, and retry accounting stays in one orchestration shell instead of being hidden inside many handlers.

What to look at: every job flows through one bounded channel before it ever becomes a task, the tasks live in a JoinSet that drains results as they finish, and the retry and shutdown bookkeeping stays in the orchestration shell rather than scattered across handlers. Trace that path in the diagram before reading the code.

ch26.chart:
flowchart TD
  Prod[Producer] -->|send, blocks if full| Ch[(bounded mpsc, cap 2)]
  Ch --> Adm[Admission loop]
  Adm -->|spawn task| JS[JoinSet]
  JS --> W1[task: process job]
  JS --> W2[task: process job]
  W1 -->|ok| Done[completed count]
  W2 -->|transient err| Re[retry within budget]
  Re --> JS
  Shut[shutdown flag] -.->|observed at drain| Adm
ch26.caption: Producers push into a bounded channel; the admission loop spawns each job into the JoinSet, accounts retries centrally, and watches one shutdown flag.

ch26.text: `tokio::spawn` creates owned runtime tasks. `JoinSet` drains them as they finish.
The `mpsc` capacity is visible at the boundary, so producer speed already has a budget.

The worker drains its queue, then observes an explicit shutdown flag at exit. Wiring the signal in once here makes adding real mid-flight cancellation, with select! and abort, a small step rather than a redesign.
Example 2: Rayon CPU pool plus Crossbeam bounded queue
One pool owns the CPU-parallel loop. One bounded queue controls intake. This is a clearer model than forcing a waiting-oriented runtime to do dense CPU scheduling.

What to look at: the bounded Crossbeam channel is the only intake, each batch that comes off it is handed to Rayon’s parallel iterator so the work fans across the pool and rejoins into one sum, and the two stages stay separate (admission is sequential, compute is parallel). The diagram shows that split before the code.

ch26.chart:
flowchart TD
  Src[Batches] -->|send, bounded| Q[(crossbeam bounded queue)]
  Q --> Drain[Sequential drain]
  Drain -->|per batch| PI[par_iter over batch]
  PI --> T1[pool thread]
  PI --> T2[pool thread]
  T1 --> Sum[reduce to scaled total]
  T2 --> Sum
ch26.caption: Admission is one sequential bounded queue; the per-batch compute fans out across the Rayon pool and reduces back to a single total.

ch26.text: `par_iter` and a small CPU pool make batch arithmetic parallel without manual thread choreography.
The bounded channel makes admission policy visible and keeps the thread-based pipeline simple.
This is CPU work, so a work-stealing data-parallel pool is the right boundary.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch26_task_libraries_and_parallel_execution/ including an extra FuturesUnordered fan-in example for the futures crate path.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to choose Tokio, Rayon, Crossbeam, or futures combinators from real workload shape, implement a bounded worker queue, and add retry and cancellation behavior to task orchestration.
Summary

items: Tokio is the right default for waiting-heavy service orchestration, not for every CPU-heavy inner loop.
Rayon is the right default for CPU-bound data parallelism, especially when work stealing helps uneven batches.
Crossbeam remains a strong tool for thread-based coordination, bounded queues, and scoped concurrency outside async runtimes.
The futures crate helps compose futures as data, while Tokio’s task tools help schedule runtime-owned async work.
Backpressure, cancellation, retry budgets, and queue capacity should be visible in task APIs and production metrics.

ch27.text: Systems IO performance comes down to a few measurable quantities: how many syscalls you make, how many times bytes are copied, who owns each file descriptor, and whether overload is bounded or hidden. This chapter applies those constraints to ordinary Rust IO and process-boundary code.
Builds on Chapters 10, 22, 23, 24, 25, and 26

Chapter 10 gave us contiguous buffers and slice-first APIs. Chapter 22 gave us thread ownership. Chapter 23 covered synchronization and visibility. Chapters 24 through 26 separated futures, Tokio, and CPU pools. This chapter ties those ideas to practical IO pipelines and systems edges.
Opening scenario

A log and event pipeline tails files, parses line-oriented records, proxies small TCP responses, and moves bursts through an internal queue. The business requirement is to reduce syscall churn, copies, and unbounded buffering by assigning clear ownership to bytes and handles, then choosing buffering, batching, vectored IO, or async orchestration from measured cost rather than from instinct.

The shape worth holding in your head is a pipeline of stages connected by a bounded queue. Bytes arrive at a reader, get parsed into records, get grouped into batches, cross the queue under backpressure, and leave through a buffered writer. Every box in that pipeline is a place where a copy can be saved or wasted, and the queue in the middle is the only thing that keeps a slow writer from forcing the reader to buffer the whole file in memory.

ch27.chart:
flowchart TD
  Src[(file or socket)] --> R[BufReader]
  R -->|read_line| P[parse record]
  P --> Ba[batch records]
  Ba -->|send, blocks if full| Q[[bounded queue]]
  Q -->|recv| W[BufWriter]
  W -->|flush| Sink[(file or socket)]
ch27.caption: The pipeline shape matters more than any single wrapper: a bounded queue between reader and writer is what makes backpressure visible instead of letting memory grow without limit.

ch27.text: A practical decision order

items: Count copies, syscalls, and queue hops before rewriting the whole subsystem.
Decide where one clear owner should hold the bytes or the handle.
Decide whether the hot path wants buffering, batching, or both.
Make overload behavior explicit with bounded queues or admission limits.

ch27.text: Mental model
Core concepts
Buffered IO, batching, and backpressure

These three levers are often discussed together and confused for one another, but they act on different parts of the pipeline. Buffering changes how often bytes cross into the kernel. Batching changes how many logical records a single flush or wakeup covers. Backpressure changes what happens when the downstream stage cannot keep up. You usually want all three, and you want to know which one you are reaching for.

That pipeline shape is often more important than the specific wrapper type. If the queue is unbounded or the writer flushes every record, the best parser in the system still loses to syscall churn and memory growth.
Zero-copy concepts, scatter/gather, and memory mapping

"Zero-copy" is a precise claim, not a mood. The useful version names exactly which copy you removed and admits which copies remain. Scatter/gather and memory mapping are two concrete techniques that remove specific copies, each with its own cost: vectored IO removes the stitching of small buffers, and mapping removes the read syscall in exchange for page faults and a sharper lifetime story.

The vectored-write idea is the easiest one to picture. Instead of allocating a new buffer to hold the header followed by the body, you hand the kernel a small array of slices and let it gather them in one syscall. The header and body keep their own owners; nothing is concatenated in user space.

ch27.chart:
flowchart TD
  H[header slice hdr] --> V[write_vectored]
  Bo[body slice payload] --> V
  V -->|one syscall| K[(kernel socket buffer)]
  K --> Net[network]
ch27.caption: Scatter/gather hands several borrowed slices to one syscall, so a framed response is sent without first building one contiguous owned buffer.

ch27.text: Rust’s standard library does not expose a cross-platform memory-mapping API directly. In practice, this is an ecosystem-level choice plus an OS contract. That is exactly why the workload and lifetime story should be clear before you adopt it.
Blocking IO, async IO, and handle ownership

The choice between blocking and async IO is a queueing and scheduling decision, not a matter of taste. A blocking read parks one thread until data arrives, which is simple and cheap when you have a small, fixed set of workers. An async read parks a task and frees the thread to serve thousands of other waiting tasks, which is the right trade only when waiting genuinely dominates and the concurrency is high.

ch27.chart:
flowchart TD
  Q{What dominates the work?}
  Q -->|waiting, high concurrency| A[Async runtime]
  Q -->|small fixed worker set| B[Blocking threads]
  Q -->|CPU bound| C[Dedicated CPU pool]
  A -->|never block a worker| C
  B -->|offload heavy compute| C
ch27.caption: Pick the IO model from where the time actually goes: waiting-heavy and highly concurrent leans async, a small worker set leans blocking, and CPU work needs its own budget either way.

ch27.text: Whichever IO model you pick, the handle underneath is a resource with a close protocol, and ownership is what keeps that protocol correct. Moving a handle into a worker is the calm default; duplicating it with try_clone is a real semantic choice; and dropping to a raw descriptor integer is where double-close and use-after-close bugs live. Socket tuning is a smaller, related set of decisions you make per workload.

ch27.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Owned: open returns File or TcpStream
  Owned --> Borrowed: lend a mutable ref for a read or write
  Borrowed --> Owned: borrow ends
  Owned --> Moved: move into worker thread or task
  Owned --> Duplicated: try_clone makes a second owner
  Moved --> Closed: drop runs close once
  Duplicated --> Closed: each owner closes its own
  Closed --> [*]
ch27.caption: A handle has one owner at a time. Borrowing is temporary, moving transfers responsibility, try_clone makes a real second owner, and drop runs the single close path.

ch27.text: Blocking versus async is not a style preference. It is a queueing and scheduling choice. Low-concurrency dedicated workers often want blocking simplicity. Large waiting-heavy front doors often want async orchestration. CPU work wants its own budget either way.
IO profiling

An IO subsystem that is slow for an unknown reason cannot be fixed with folklore. Before reaching for a fancy technique, measure where the time and the syscalls go. The checklist below is the minimum set of signals that tells you whether the bottleneck is copying, flushing, queueing, waiting, or parsing, so the optimization you choose addresses the cost that actually exists.
How this lands by background

Most engineers reach this chapter already knowing the IO vocabulary from another ecosystem. The buffering and vectored-IO ideas transfer almost unchanged; the part that trips people up is ownership. In Rust a file handle or a buffer is a value with a single owner and a deterministic close, so the mental shift is about where that ownership lives as bytes cross thread, task, and process boundaries, not about new API names.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
The fastest-looking IO optimization is often the wrong one. If you do not know whether the hot cost is copying, flushing, queueing, waiting, or parsing, you are still choosing by folklore.
Examples
Example 1: buffered reads, buffered writes, and bounded handoff
The producer reads line by line, the queue is bounded, and the consumer batches two records per buffered flush. This is a practical shape for line-oriented log or event pipelines.

What to look at: the producer thread and the consumer run on two clocks joined only by a sync_channel(1). Because the channel holds at most one in-flight item, a fast reader cannot race ahead of a slow writer; the send simply blocks until there is room. On the consumer side, records accumulate in a small pending vector and are flushed two at a time, with a final partial flush so nothing is left behind. Follow one line through the diagram, then read the same path in code.

ch27.chart:
flowchart TD
  In[(Cursor of 3 lines)] --> BR[BufReader.read_line]
  BR -->|String| TX[tx.send, blocks if full]
  TX --> CH[[sync_channel cap 1]]
  CH -->|rx.recv| Pend[pending vec]
  Pend -->|len reaches 2| Flush[writeln batch then count]
  Pend -->|loop ends| Tail[flush leftover]
  Flush --> BW[BufWriter into Vec]
  Tail --> BW
ch27.caption: Three lines flow reader to bounded channel to consumer; the consumer flushes in batches of two and then drains the final leftover, giving two batches for three records.

ch27.text: BufReader and BufWriter smooth many small reads and writes into fewer kernel interactions.
sync_channel(1) means the producer eventually waits when the consumer falls behind.
Two logical records per flush is a small but explicit batching policy.
Example 2: scatter/gather response with socket tuning and stream handoff
The listener moves the accepted stream into one owner, sets a latency-sensitive socket option, and writes a small header plus body with vectored IO.

What to look at: the accepted stream is moved into the server thread so exactly one owner drives the response, and the response is two borrowed slices, a header and a body, that are never concatenated. The write_all_vectored helper is the load-bearing detail: a single write_vectored can write only part of the buffers, so the loop calls IoSlice::advance_slices to skip the bytes already sent and keeps going until both slices are fully drained. The diagram is that retry loop.

ch27.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Accept
  Accept --> Tune: set nodelay true
  Tune --> Write: write_vectored over parts
  Write --> Advance: wrote some bytes, advance_slices
  Advance --> Done: all slices empty
  Advance --> Write: bytes remain
  Write --> Err: wrote zero bytes
  Done --> [*]: flush and report
  Err --> [*]: WriteZero error
ch27.caption: Partial writes are part of the contract: advance past the bytes already sent and loop until both slices are empty, treating a zero-byte write as a closed socket.

ch27.expected:
nodelay = true
vectored parts = 2
client = hdr:payload

ch27.text: This example already uses a small write_all_vectored helper so the logical response is fully sent even if one vectored syscall only writes part of the buffers. Keep that pattern near the socket boundary in real services instead of assuming small responses always finish in one call.
IoSlice avoids stitching a tiny response together just to make one small write call.
The accepted stream moves into one thread and one closure. That keeps ownership simple.
set_nodelay(true) is a workload decision. Small request-response protocols often care more about latency than about coalescing tiny writes.

The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch27_io_tricks_and_systems_programming_patterns/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to compare buffered and unbuffered reads, reason about file-descriptor ownership, design a backpressure-aware IO pipeline, and choose when vectored IO, memory mapping, or async orchestration are the right tool.
Next chapter

This chapter kept everything inside Rust, where ownership decided who held each buffer and handle. Chapter 28 pushes those same ownership and lifetime questions across a language boundary into C and C++, where the compiler can no longer check the contract for you and the handoff has to be encoded by hand.
Summary

items: Buffered IO reduces syscall churn, but it does not remove parse cost or ownership decisions.
Zero-copy is only meaningful when you say which copy disappeared and which copies still remain.
Memory mapping, vectored IO, and raw handle escape hatches are strongest when the workload and invariants are explicit.
Blocking and async IO solve different scheduling problems. CPU work still needs its own budget either way.
Backpressure and profiling belong in the design from the start: bounded queues, flush policy, syscall counts, and p99 latency all matter.

ch28.text: Linking Rust to a C or C++ library is not a syntax detail; it is a binary contract the compiler cannot check for you. Calling convention, memory layout, who frees what, how long a pointer stays valid, and what happens on failure all become things you state by hand. This chapter treats that boundary as a small, deliberate seam to design rather than a library to call.
Builds on Chapters 08, 09, and 17

Chapter 08 established unsafe Rust and explicit invariants. Chapter 09 covered raw-pointer-adjacent ownership tools such as Box, Arc, and pinning. Chapter 17 showed how to refactor toward honest boundaries. C++ integration is where all three become operational.
Opening scenario

A product is replacing one hot native subsystem with Rust while keeping an existing host process, plugin loader, and native test harness. The business requirement is a narrow ABI contract with explicit layout, pointer validity, memory ownership, status-code errors, and no cross-language unwinding.
A reliable decision order

items: Flatten the seam to a C ABI contract unless you have a strong reason for a richer direct C++ bridge.
State ownership in raw terms: pointer plus length, caller-allocated buffer, or opaque handle.
Translate errors to status codes or explicit error payloads.
Ban cross-language unwinding and test the wrapper as a first-class subsystem.

ch28.text: Mental model
Core concepts
The four FFI fundamentals

Almost every Rust interop layer is built from the same four primitives. They are small, but together they are what turns an internal Rust function into a symbol another language can call without guessing about representation. The diagram shows how a single call splits into a thin unsafe edge over a larger safe core; the cards below name each piece.

ch28.chart:
flowchart TD
  Foreign[C or C plus plus caller] -->|C calling convention| Edge[extern C symbol]
  Edge -->|raw ptr len status| Unsafe[Thin unsafe wrapper]
  Unsafe -->|owned Rust types| Safe[Safe Rust core]
  Safe -->|Result| Unsafe
  Unsafe -->|status code| Edge
ch28.caption: One narrow unsafe edge sits between the foreign caller and a large safe Rust core. Raw types live only on the edge; rich types live behind it.

ch28.text: What may and may not cross a C ABI boundary

The single most useful filter when designing an interop layer is to sort every type into one of two buckets: representations with a stable, agreed-upon shape that may cross the seam, and Rust-specific types whose layout is an implementation detail that must stay behind it. The rules below are that filter spelled out.

A useful correction for C++ teams is this: “C++ integration” often still means “a deliberate C ABI seam around C++ code.” That seam buys you a smaller contract surface and fewer compiler- and standard-library assumptions.
Calling C from Rust

When Rust is the caller, you describe the foreign function in an extern "C" declaration block, which tells the compiler the symbol exists elsewhere and must be called with the C calling convention. The call itself is unsafe, because Rust cannot verify that the foreign code honors the signature, so the practice is to wrap that one call in a small safe function whose body documents why the call is sound. In a real Cargo build the native library is linked through build-system configuration, typically a build.rs that points the linker at the artifact. In this chapter’s runnable demo the symbol is defined in Rust with the C ABI so the example stays self-contained while exercising the exact same declaration-and-wrap pattern.
Calling Rust from C and C++

When Rust is the callee, the goal is to expose a deliberately tiny surface that another language can rely on: extern "C" functions marked so their names are not mangled, C-friendly layout for any shared struct, raw buffers or opaque handles instead of Rust ownership types, and an explicit destroy function for anything Rust allocates and foreign code later frees. The crate is built as a C-facing static or dynamic library rather than as a Rust ABI artifact, and the public header that describes these symbols becomes the real contract. Keeping that header small is the whole discipline: every symbol on it is something you have promised to keep stable.
Modelling ownership across the seam

Ownership is the part of the contract that has no syntax in C, so you express it by choosing which of a few fixed shapes each parameter takes. The decision is always the same question asked precisely: who allocated this memory, who is allowed to read or write it, and who is responsible for freeing it. The diagram sorts the four common answers; the cards below give the signature pattern for each.

ch28.chart:
flowchart TD
  Q{Who owns the memory?} -->|Caller, read only| In[const ptr plus len]
  Q -->|Caller, Rust writes| Out[mut ptr plus capacity]
ch28.caption: Caller-owned memory: a const pointer plus length for read-only views, or a mutable pointer plus capacity for buffers Rust fills.

ch28.text: When Rust owns the memory instead of the caller, the same question routes to the other two shapes:

ch28.chart:
flowchart TD
  Q{Who owns the memory?} -->|Rust owns across calls| Handle[opaque handle plus new and free]
  Q -->|Rust allocates a string| Str[returned ptr plus one free fn]
ch28.caption: Rust-owned memory: an opaque handle with explicit new and free functions, or a returned pointer paired with exactly one free function.

ch28.text: A Rust reference encodes aliasing and lifetime promises the C or C++ side cannot honor, which is why a mature FFI surface flattens everything into these four shapes. The payoff is that ownership becomes readable from the function signature instead of relying on a comment everyone has to remember.
Returning errors across the seam

A Rust Result<T, E> has no C representation, so failure has to be re-expressed in terms the foreign side can read. The conventional answer is an integer status as the return value, with any successful payload delivered through caller-owned out parameters. The richness of your error type stays inside Rust; only its outcome crosses the line.
Keeping unwinding inside its own language

The most dangerous thing that can cross an FFI boundary is not a bad value but an in-flight unwind. A Rust panic or a C++ exception unwinding through frames the other language does not know how to clean up is undefined behavior, and it tends to crash far from the cause. The operable policy is to stop every unwind at the boundary: catch it, convert it to a status code, and let only ordinary return values cross. The diagram shows that gate; the rules below state it precisely.

ch28.chart:
flowchart TD
  Body[Exported fn body] --> Catch{catch_unwind}
  Catch -->|Ok value| Status[return status code]
  Catch -->|panic caught| Err[return error status]
  Status --> Foreign[Foreign caller]
  Err --> Foreign
  Body -.->|never| Leak[unwind into foreign frames]
  Leak -.-> UB[undefined behavior]
ch28.caption: An exported function catches its own panic and returns a status. The dashed path, an unwind leaking into foreign frames, is the one you must make impossible.

ch28.text: The conservative rule is also the most operable one: no cross-language unwinding. Translate failure to an integer status or explicit error object before control crosses the boundary.
Choosing a binding tool: bindgen, cxx, or autocxx

These tools do not change the contract you owe; they change how much of the boilerplate is written for you. The choice mostly follows two questions: do you control both sides of the boundary, and how large is the C++ surface you need to reach. The decision tree below routes those questions to a default; the cards explain what each tool is actually for.

ch28.chart:
flowchart TD
  Start{Headers exist, C-like surface?} -->|Yes, generate from C| Bindgen[bindgen]
  Start -->|No, control both sides| Both{How big is the C plus plus surface?}
  Both -->|Small, curated| Cxx[cxx bridge]
  Both -->|Large, want automation| Autocxx[autocxx]
  Bindgen --> Wrap[Wrap raw output in narrow safe API]
  Cxx --> Wrap
  Autocxx --> Wrap
ch28.caption: The tool depends on whether headers already exist and how much C++ you must reach. Whatever the tool, the generated surface still gets wrapped in a narrow safe API.

ch28.text: ABI stability
Testing and sanitizing FFI layers
How this lands by background

Most engineers reaching for FFI already carry a model from another ecosystem, and the useful question is which part of that model transfers and which part will quietly mislead you. The shift is almost never about which functions to call. It is about who is now responsible for ownership, lifetime, and failure once a boundary the compiler cannot see sits between your code and the other language.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The most expensive FFI bug is rarely a missing semicolon in the header. It is a boundary that looked simple, but never actually said who owns the memory, who catches the panic, or which compiler contract is supposed to stay stable over time.
Examples
Example 1: call a C ABI symbol from Rust through a safe wrapper

The demo keeps the symbol self-contained by defining it in Rust with the C ABI, then calling it through an extern "C" declaration as if it came from native code. Even a trivial exported function needs a panic policy at the boundary: the body uses wrapping_abs so an i32::MIN input cannot panic across the C ABI seam.

What to look at: there are three layers, and only the middle one is unsafe. The foreign symbol on the left is reached through an extern "C" declaration; the one-line unsafe wrapper safe_abs performs the actual call and documents why it is sound; and main only ever sees a normal safe function. Trace that one call left to right in the diagram, then read the same three layers in code.

ch28.chart:
flowchart TD
  Main[main calls safe_abs] --> Wrap[safe_abs safe wrapper]
  Wrap -->|unsafe block| Decl[extern C declaration]
  Decl --> Sym[ffi_demo_abs C ABI symbol]
  Sym -->|i32| Wrap
  Wrap -->|i32| Main
ch28.caption: safe_abs is the only place the unsafe call lives; main and the rest of the program see a plain safe function.

ch28.text: The raw call stays in one small wrapper instead of leaking through the rest of the codebase.
The seam is plain i32 -> i32, so no ownership transfer is required.
In production, the same wrapper pattern works when the symbol really comes from a C or C++ library.
Example 2: export a Rust function with a C ABI-safe wrapper
The exported entry point uses raw pointers, length, an out parameter, integer status codes, and explicit null checks. The richer Rust model can stay behind this seam.

What to look at: the function is a guard sequence before any real work happens. It validates the out pointer, then the input pointer, returning a distinct nonzero status for each failure; only once both are known non-null does it build a slice from ptr and len, compute the sum, write it through the out parameter, and return 0. The caller owns both buffers; Rust only borrows them for the call. Follow the branches in the diagram, then read them top to bottom in code.

ch28.chart:
flowchart TD
  Enter[sum_i32s entry] --> NullOut{out_total null?}
  NullOut -->|yes| R1[return 1]
  NullOut -->|no| NullPtr{ptr null?}
  NullPtr -->|yes| R2[return 2]
  NullPtr -->|no| Build[build slice from ptr and len]
  Build --> Sum[sum into i64]
  Sum --> Write[write through out_total]
  Write --> Ok[return 0]
ch28.caption: Validate the out pointer, then the input pointer, each with its own status code, before any memory is read or written. Success returns 0.

ch28.text: The foreign edge speaks in raw addresses and sizes, not Rust references.
The caller owns the input array and the output storage. Rust only borrows both for the duration of the call.
Status integers make the contract portable without leaking Rust’s Result shape.
The same pattern extends naturally to opaque handles, caller buffers, and explicit free functions.

The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch28_cpp_integration/. That directory includes a small opaque-handle example alongside the two editor labs so the ownership patterns can be reviewed outside the browser.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to flatten higher-level Rust types into a C ABI-safe surface, map ownership across the seam, build a wrapper around a Rust function, and choose between a C shim, generated bindings, and a curated Rust/C++ bridge for a legacy codebase.
Summary

items: FFI is a binary contract the compiler cannot check for you. ABI, layout, ownership, and unwind policy must all be stated explicitly.
A narrow C ABI seam is usually the most stable integration layer even when the far side is C++, because C is the one calling convention every toolchain agrees on.
Rust references, String, Vec<T>, Result, and panics normally stop at the Rust side of the wrapper and are rebuilt the moment control returns to safe Rust.
bindgen, cxx, and autocxx reduce boilerplate but do not remove the obligation to wrap their output in a narrow, stable interop layer.
Testing the interop layer means more than “it linked once.” Include null, length, ownership, sanitizer, and foreign-caller harness coverage.

ch29.text: WebAssembly integration needs explicit host calls, memory ownership, data batching, and ABI rules. The module and its JavaScript host keep separate heaps, so every value richer than a number is encoded and copied across a boundary you design. This chapter defines the boundary contracts for browser-facing modules and the native shims they call.
Builds on Chapters 19 and 28

Chapter 19 covered wire data contracts and versioned encodings; the WebAssembly boundary is one more wire, with the same evolution and encoding concerns. Chapter 28 covered the C ABI and Rust FFI; the C and C++ shim in this chapter is that same seam, now compiled into a browser-shaped module instead of a native binary.
Opening scenario

A web product is moving its hot client-side work, image processing, parsing, and a routing-score calculation, from JavaScript into a Rust WebAssembly module, and part of the routing logic already exists as a small C++ function the team wants to reuse rather than rewrite. The requirement is concrete: expose a clean JavaScript-callable surface, keep the per-call cost honest by choosing the right boundary representation, and wire the existing C++ code through a thin, auditable shim, all without leaking copy and lifetime concerns into the rest of the application.
A practical decision order

items: Decide what actually has to cross the boundary, and how often.
Pick the representation per value: a number, a copied slice, a serialized blob, or a resident handle.
Batch hot loops into one call that runs inside the module.
Confine any C or C++ seam to a thin unsafe shim with stated invariants.

ch29.text: Mental model

The shape worth memorizing is two separate heaps with one shared byte array between them. JavaScript holds its own objects; the module holds its own stack and heap inside a single linear memory. The only thing both sides can touch is that linear memory, so every string, array, or struct that crosses is written into it as bytes by one side and read out by the other. Trace one string across the diagram below: it leaves the JavaScript heap, lands as bytes in linear memory, and is reconstructed as a Rust value, with a copy at the crossing.

ch29.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Host[JavaScript host]
    JS[JS object heap]
  end
  subgraph Module[Wasm module]
    LM[(linear memory)]
    RH[Rust heap and stack]
  end
  JS -->|encode and copy| LM
  LM -->|decode| RH
  RH -->|encode and copy| LM
  LM -->|decode| JS
ch29.caption: Two heaps, one shared byte array. Every non-numeric value is copied into linear memory at the crossing and reconstructed on the far side.

ch29.text: Core concepts
From Rust to WebAssembly

A browser-facing crate is built as a cdylib so the linker produces a single .wasm artifact, then wasm-bindgen post-processes it to emit the JavaScript glue that knows how to lay out and read back each annotated value.
JavaScript interop and boundary data choices

The interop surface is where the design lives. wasm-bindgen will happily generate glue for a string, an array, or a serialized struct, but the four representations below have very different costs. Choosing among them deliberately, rather than reaching for the most convenient type, is what keeps a boundary fast and auditable.

The decision is essentially a cost ladder. A number rides the native interface for free. A string or byte array costs one copy per crossing. A struct costs an encode plus a copy plus a decode. A resident handle costs almost nothing per call but adds a lifetime you must manage. Reading these as a ladder makes the right representation obvious for any given call frequency and payload size.

ch29.chart:
flowchart TD
  V[Value to cross] --> Q1{Is it a number?}
  Q1 -->|yes| N[Pass directly, no copy]
  Q1 -->|no| Cont[Not a number, continues below]
ch29.caption: Step one of the ladder: a number rides the native interface for free. Anything else falls through to the next question.

ch29.text: For everything that is not a number, the remaining questions decide how it crosses:

ch29.caption: Steps two and three: a frequently crossed big payload stays resident behind a handle, flat bytes cost one copy, and a rich struct costs an encode plus a copy.

ch29.text: Calling C and C++ from a WebAssembly module

Reusing existing C or C++ code inside the module means crossing a second, lower boundary: the C ABI. This is the same FFI seam covered in Chapter 28, and it behaves the same way under WebAssembly. The shim exports plain functions, Rust calls them through an unsafe extern block, and the safety of the whole thing rests on invariants you state rather than the compiler checks.

The two boundaries stack but stay distinct. The outer edge, Rust to JavaScript, is managed by generated glue. The inner edge, Rust to the C shim, is raw pointers and lengths with manual invariants. Keep them conceptually separate so a fault at one seam is not misdiagnosed at the other.
WASI and host capabilities

A module has no ambient operating system. In the browser it can compute freely but can only reach the outside world through functions the host imports into it. WASI is the standardized way a non-browser host grants files, clocks, and randomness, but the underlying rule is the same in both worlds: capabilities are imports, not assumptions.
Performance limits and serialization at the boundary

WebAssembly computes at near-native speed inside the module, so the performance conversation is almost never about the arithmetic. It is about the boundary. A design that crosses the seam per element, or copies a large buffer on every call, will be slower than the JavaScript it replaced no matter how fast the inner loop is. The fixes are structural: batch bulk work into a single call, and keep large state resident so it crosses once instead of repeatedly.

Serialization is the other half of this. A rich struct that crosses as JSON pays an encode and a parse on top of the copy; the same struct crossing as a compact binary layout the host reads as a typed array can be dramatically cheaper. As in Chapter 19, the encoding is a contract: pick one that both sides can read, evolve it additively, and measure it rather than guessing.
Debugging WebAssembly

A fault inside a module is harder to read than a native crash because, by default, you see a trap and an offset into linear memory rather than a Rust line. The good news is that a small amount of setup recovers most of the familiar debugging experience: a panic hook surfaces messages to the console, source maps map traps back to source, and logging at the seam exposes the pointer and length values where the hard bugs actually live.
How this lands by background

Most engineers reach WebAssembly with a marshalling model from somewhere else, and the useful question is which part of that model still holds. The shift is rarely about API names. It is about accepting that the host and the module keep separate heaps, that every non-numeric value is copied across the seam, and that you now name the representation and ownership of each value instead of trusting a bridge to do it invisibly.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
WebAssembly does not make the boundary disappear; it makes it explicit. The cost you used to pay invisibly in a marshaller is now a copy you can see, measure, and design around.
Examples
Example 1: wasm-bindgen string and byte boundary
Two exported functions show the two common non-numeric crossings: a string in and out, and a byte slice in with a number out.

What to look at: the #[wasm_bindgen] attribute is what makes each function callable from JavaScript, and the parameter types decide how the data crosses. build_label takes two borrowed &str values, each copied into linear memory, and returns an owned String copied back out; sum_bytes receives a &[u8] slice and returns a plain number, so only the bytes in are copied and nothing comes back but an integer. Follow each value across the diagram, then read the same crossings in code.

ch29.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph JS[JavaScript]
    A[strings and bytes]
  end
  subgraph W[Wasm module]
    B[build_label borrows str]
    C[sum_bytes borrows slice]
  end
  A -->|copy in| B
  A -->|copy in| C
  B -->|copy String out| R1[label]
  C -->|number out| R2[sum]
ch29.caption: Strings and the byte slice are copied into the module; the label String is copied back out, while the sum returns as a plain number with no copy.

ch29.text: A &str or &[u8] is copied into linear memory for the call and not owned by the module afterwards.
The returned String is copied back into the host, which then owns its own separate value.
The summed u32 rides the native interface with no allocation and no copy.
Example 2: Wasm plus C ABI boundary
A safe Rust function hands a string's bytes to a C-ABI shim as a pointer and a length, mirroring how a reused C or C++ routine is called inside the module.

What to look at: the safe wrapper route_score is the only place that touches raw pointers, and it does so inside a narrow unsafe block with a written SAFETY comment naming each invariant. It passes route.as_ptr() and route.len() to the shim, which reconstructs a slice for the duration of the call and computes a score from its length. The contract is pointer plus length plus a promise the bytes stay valid and are only read while the call runs. Trace that single crossing in the diagram, then read it in code.

ch29.chart:
flowchart TD
  S[route as str] -->|as_ptr, len| W[route_score wrapper]
  W -->|ptr, len in unsafe| Shim[cpp_route_score C ABI]
  Shim -->|from_raw_parts, read only| Slice[reconstructed slice]
  Slice -->|len times 10| Score[u32 score]
  Score --> W
ch29.caption: One crossing: the wrapper passes pointer and length into the C-ABI shim, which rebuilds a read-only slice for the call and returns a number. Validity of the bytes is a stated invariant, not a compiler check.

ch29.text: The C ABI has no slice type, so the borrowed bytes cross as a raw pointer and an explicit length.
The SAFETY comment names what must hold: valid pointer, correct length, read-only for the call's duration.
Only the wrapper and the shim are unsafe; the rest of the program stays in safe Rust.

Both examples run here as ordinary Rust so the boundary logic is testable without a browser or a WebAssembly runtime. In a real build, the first compiles to a cdylib processed by wasm-bindgen, and the second links the C or C++ shim into the same module, but the crossing contracts, copy in, copy out, and pointer plus length, are exactly what you see above.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to export Rust to JavaScript with wasm-bindgen, choose serialization and memory boundaries for a given workload, reason about the copying cost of crossing the seam, and decide when to batch or keep state resident instead of copying per call.
Next chapter

This chapter handed values across a boundary inside one machine. Chapter 30 widens that boundary to a message broker between services, where the wire contract, copy semantics, and explicit ownership habits from this chapter reappear as durable messages, acknowledgments, and idempotent consumers.
Summary

ch30.text: A message broker lets services hand work to each other without being online at the same time. That convenience comes with a bill: routing, redelivery, idempotent consumers, dead-letter policy, and backpressure all become your responsibility. This chapter treats AMQP not as a library to call but as an operational contract to design.
Builds on Chapters 19, 22, 23, 25, and 26

Chapter 19 covered wire DTOs and versioned envelopes. Chapters 22 and 23 covered ownership across threads, message passing, and synchronization. Chapters 25 and 26 covered Tokio, bounded queues, retries, and task orchestration. AMQP systems sit across all of that.
Opening scenario

An order pipeline is being split into checkout, billing, search indexing, and notification services. The business requirement is reliable asynchronous handoff: route messages by contract, preserve idempotency, ack only after durable effects, isolate poison messages, and expose queue depth and retry pressure.
A practical decision order

items: Pick the broker boundary only when producer and consumer should truly decouple in time or failure.
Design topology second: exchange, routing key, queue boundaries, dead-letter flow.
Ack only after the durable effect or durable checkpoint.
Cap consumer admission both in the broker and in the local worker pool.

ch30.text: Mental model
Core concepts
Message broker fundamentals

The shape worth memorizing is a one-way pipeline with the broker sitting in the middle. A producer never names a queue; it publishes to an exchange with a routing key. The exchange consults its bindings, copies the message into every matching queue, and each queue feeds its own consumers at their own pace. Everything between the publish call and the ack is the broker's responsibility, which is exactly why it can buffer a burst or survive a consumer restart.

ch30.chart:
flowchart TD
  P[Producer] -->|publish key| X{Exchange}
  X -->|binding match| Q1[(orders queue)]
  X -->|binding match| Q2[(search queue)]
  Q1 --> C1[Billing consumer]
  Q2 --> C2[Search consumer]
  C1 -->|ack| Q1
  C2 -->|ack| Q2
ch30.caption: The producer talks only to the exchange; bindings fan one message out to the queues that subscribed, and each consumer acks its own queue.

ch30.text: AMQP concepts: exchanges, queues, bindings, and routing keys

The critical operational point is this: the producer chooses a routing key, but the exchange owns routing policy. That lets teams change routing topology without turning every publisher into a queue-aware special case.
RabbitMQ with Rust

In a real Cargo service, the transport adapter typically holds the AMQP client connection and channel setup, then hands owned envelopes or commands into ordinary Rust handlers. Keep the transport edge narrow so the retry, idempotency, and serialization logic remains testable without a live broker.
Producers and consumers

The single most important sequence in this chapter is the order in which a consumer commits its side effect and sends its ack. The broker holds the message as unacknowledged until the consumer says it is done. If the consumer commits the durable effect first and then acks, a crash in between costs you only a redelivery, which an idempotent handler absorbs. If it acks first, the broker forgets the message and a crash loses the work for good.

ch30.chart:
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Broker
  participant C as Consumer
  participant D as Database
  B->>C: deliver message
  C->>C: deserialize and validate
  C->>D: commit side effect
  D-->>C: committed
  C->>B: ack
  Note over B,C: crash before ack to redelivery, safe if idempotent
ch30.caption: Commit the durable effect, then ack. A crash before the ack only causes a safe redelivery; acking first would lose the work.

ch30.text: Acknowledgments and retries

An ack is a promise that the work is safely done and the broker may forget the message. A retry is a decision that the work is not done yet and deserves another attempt. Both are choices the consumer makes explicitly, and getting them right is most of what separates a robust consumer from one that quietly drops or endlessly reprocesses work.
Dead-letter queues

Not every failure should be retried. A malformed payload or an unsupported command will fail the same way on every attempt, and requeuing it forever just blocks the queue behind a message that can never succeed. A dead-letter queue is the escape hatch: the broker moves a message there after it has exhausted its retries or been explicitly rejected, so the main queue keeps flowing and a human can inspect the casualties later.
Idempotency

Because delivery is at-least-once, the only way to make duplicates harmless is to make the handler idempotent: applying the same message twice must leave the system in the same state as applying it once. Sometimes that is free, when the operation is naturally a set-it-to-this upsert. More often you need a durable record of which message IDs have already been applied, committed in the same step as the effect, so a second delivery sees the record and does nothing.
A duplicate delivery is not a surprising edge case. In broker-based systems, it is the design center.
Backpressure

A queue is a shock absorber, but a shock absorber with no limit just hides the fact that you are overloaded. Backpressure is how the system says no gracefully instead of falling over. It has two layers that are easy to confuse: the broker side, which caps how many unacked messages a consumer may hold at once, and the local side, which caps how much in-process work those messages can spawn. Set one without the other and you have only moved the overload from the broker into your own heap.
Serialization for messages

A message often outlives the code that produced it: it can sit in a queue across a deploy, be replayed weeks later, or be consumed by a service on an older version.
