That is why broker payloads earn their keep when they travel inside an explicit envelope rather than as a bare struct dump. The envelope carries a schema version so consumers can branch on format, a message ID so they can deduplicate, and optional trace metadata for debugging, while the tagged payload keeps the wire shape stable. Evolve it additively with optional fields rather than redefining what existing fields mean, and old and new consumers can keep reading the same stream.
Observability in broker-based systems

A broker is a place work can pile up invisibly, so you cannot run one on faith. The signals below are the minimum set that tells you whether the system is healthy or merely quiet because nothing is being processed. A growing queue with rising message age, a climbing retry rate, or a dead-letter queue that keeps filling are early warnings; treat them as first-class production metrics rather than transport trivia you only look at during an incident.
How this lands by background

Most engineers do not arrive at message brokers as a blank slate; they arrive with a mental model from another ecosystem. The useful thing to know is which part of that model transfers and which part will quietly mislead you. The shift is almost never about API names. It is about where reliability and consistency work has to happen now that a durable, distributed boundary sits between your services.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs
A broker can decouple services, but it will not decouple you from consistency. It merely changes where the consistency work must be done.
Examples
Example 1: direct exchange routing
The example keeps the routing model tiny: producers publish one routing key, the exchange owns binding policy, and queues receive only what their bindings match.

What to look at: the exchange holds a map from routing key to the set of bound queues, and publish is just a lookup that copies the message into each match. The key orders.created is bound to two queues, so one publish produces two deliveries; an unbound key produces zero and is counted as unrouted instead of silently vanishing. Trace one message through the diagram below, then read the same path in code.

ch30.chart:
flowchart TD
  Pub[publish orders.created] --> Ex{direct exchange}
  Pub2[publish orders.cancelled] --> Ex
  Ex -->|orders.created| Bill[(billing)]
  Ex -->|orders.created| Search[(search)]
  Ex -->|orders.cancelled| Bill
ch30.caption: Bound keys: created fans out to billing and search, cancelled goes to billing only.

ch30.text: An unbound key takes the other exit instead of silently vanishing:

ch30.caption: The refunded key matches no binding, so the exchange charges it to the unrouted counter.

ch30.text: The exchange owns routing policy and binding state.
Producers publish one semantic key such as orders.created.
Queue selection stays declarative instead of being hard-coded into every publisher.
Example 2: idempotent consumer with retries and a DLQ
The handler only acks successful unique work. Duplicates are counted and ignored, transient failure retries are capped, and terminal failures move to a DLQ.

What to look at: every delivery flows through one small decision machine. First the handler checks whether the message ID is already in the seen set; if so it is a duplicate and is acked without doing the work again. Otherwise it runs the handler, and the outcome routes it: success records the ID and acks, a transient failure under the attempt cap goes back for a counted retry, and a failure that exhausts the cap is sent to the dead-letter queue rather than requeued forever. The diagram is that state machine; the four output counters are just tallies of which path each message took.

ch30.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Check
  Check --> Duplicate: id already recorded
  Check --> Handle: new id
  Handle --> Done: success
  Handle --> Retry: transient, attempts left
  Handle --> DeadLetter: attempts exhausted
  Retry --> Handle: redeliver
  Done --> [*]: record id and ack
  Duplicate --> [*]: ack, no work
  DeadLetter --> [*]: park for inspection
ch30.caption: One delivery, four exits: duplicate, done, retry, or dead-letter. The counters in the output map directly to these edges.

ch30.text: A completed message ID is recorded so replay becomes harmless.
Retry remains explicit, counted, and bounded by attempt number.
After the last allowed attempt, the delivery stops cycling and moves to a terminal bucket.
Processed, duplicate, retry, and DLQ counts become ordinary metrics, not incident archaeology.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch30_amqp_and_message_brokers/ including a small versioned message-envelope example alongside the two runnable worked examples.
Exercises
The companion exercise page asks you to choose ack timing, model an idempotent consumer, add retry and DLQ handling, and design a versioned message contract that can survive mixed deployments.
Next chapter

A broker hands single messages between services. Chapter 31 scales that idea up to distributed task execution: dispatching units of work across many workers, tracking their state, and recovering when a worker dies mid-task. The acknowledgment, retry, and idempotency habits from this chapter become the foundation for that work.
Summary

ch31.text: Once work leaves your process for another machine, the borrow checker can no longer help. What protects you instead is durable handoff, leases, retries, idempotency, and traceable recovery. This chapter shows how those requirements show up as concrete shapes in Rust worker and queue boundaries.
Builds on Chapters 22, 25, 26, and 30

Chapter 22 covered thread ownership and channels inside one process. Chapter 25 covered Tokio task orchestration and graceful shutdown. Chapter 26 separated waiting-heavy runtimes from CPU pools and bounded queues. Chapter 30 covered AMQP brokers and at-least-once delivery. This chapter generalizes those ideas to distributed task systems as a whole.
Opening scenario

A media platform ingests an upload, transcodes several quality variants, generates thumbnails, scans the content for policy violations, and finally publishes one completion record that the rest of the product reads. None of those steps run in the request that triggered them. They run on a fleet of workers that can be deployed, scaled, and killed at any moment. The business requirement is durable distributed work: leases so a dead worker's task is recovered, retry budgets so a flaky dependency does not turn into an infinite loop, idempotent completion so a redelivered task does not double-publish, graph-aware aggregation so the final record waits for every variant, and tracing so an operator can reconstruct what happened after the fact.

The trap for an engineer arriving from a single-process background is to reach for the queue brand first. The queue is the easy part. The hard part is the contract you wrap around it: what an in-flight task means, what a duplicate means, and what recovery looks like when a machine disappears mid-job. The decision order below puts that contract before the throughput tuning.
A practical decision order

items: Define the owned task envelope before choosing a queue backend.
Choose delivery semantics assumptions next, usually at-least-once.
Pick lease, retry, and failure-isolation policy before tuning throughput.
Make tracing and profiling part of the scheduler contract, not an afterthought.

ch31.text: The shape of the whole scenario is a fan-out followed by a fan-in. One submission turns into several independent worker tasks, each pulling from the same durable queue, and a single coordinator waits for all of them before it writes the completion record. Hold this picture in mind for the rest of the chapter: the queue is the shared boundary, the workers are interchangeable and disposable, and the coordinator is the one place that knows the job is truly done.

ch31.chart:
flowchart TD
  Submit[Upload submitted] --> Q[(durable task queue)]
  Q --> W1[transcode worker]
  Q --> W2[thumbnail worker]
  Q --> W3[content scan worker]
  W1 --> Agg[completion coordinator]
  W2 --> Agg
  W3 --> Agg
  Agg --> Done[publish completion record]
ch31.caption: One upload fans out to disposable workers through a shared queue, then fans back in to a single coordinator that publishes the final record.

ch31.text: Mental model
Core concepts
Task queues and work distribution models

A task queue exists to separate the moment a request is made from the moment the work is done. The submitter writes a durable record and returns immediately; a worker picks the record up later, when it has capacity. That decoupling is what buys you elasticity and failure isolation, but it also means three things you used to ignore become part of your service budget: how deep the queue is, how old the oldest task is, and how a task that fails halfway gets replayed. The cards below contrast the common ways work is handed from queue to worker; the diagram after them is the lifecycle every one of those models has to implement.

Every task moves through the same small state machine no matter which distribution model you pick. The two branches worth staring at are the loop back to Queued on retry and the one-way exit to DeadLetter. A system without that terminal exit will requeue a permanently broken task forever, which is the most common way a queue quietly turns into an infinite loop.

ch31.chart:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Queued: submit
  Queued --> Leased: worker claims
  Leased --> Running: handler starts
  Running --> Acked: success
  Running --> Queued: lease expires (crash)
  Running --> Retry: transient failure
  Retry --> Queued: requeue with backoff
  Running --> DeadLetter: permanent failure
  Acked --> [*]
  DeadLetter --> [*]
ch31.caption: The task lifecycle. Retry loops back to Queued; a lease expiry also returns the task to the pool; only DeadLetter and Acked are terminal.

ch31.text: Exactly-once vs at-least-once processing

Delivery semantics describe what the system promises about how many times your handler runs for one logical task. There are three honest answers, and only one of them is the production default. At-least-once is what durable queues actually give you, because the safe move after a crash is to redeliver. At-most-once trades that safety for the risk of silently dropping work. True exactly-once across the whole path is not a setting you enable; it is something you assemble from at-least-once delivery plus deduplication you own.
When another engineer says “exactly once,” ask whether they mean transport delivery, handler execution, or durable side effects. Those are different claims.
Leasing and visibility timeouts

A lease is how the queue answers the question every distributed system eventually faces: what happens to a task whose worker stopped responding. When a worker claims a task, the queue hands it a lease with an expiry and hides the task from everyone else for that window, which is the visibility timeout. As long as the worker is healthy it finishes the work and acknowledges the task before the lease runs out. If it crashes, the lease simply expires and the task becomes claimable again by a peer. Nothing detects the crash directly; the absence of an acknowledgement is the signal.

Lease design is really failure-recovery design. A distributed worker should be assumed killable at any point. The queue recovers by lease expiry. The application recovers by idempotent completion. Those are two separate guarantees, and you need both: lease expiry alone gets the task run again, but only idempotent completion keeps the second run from doing damage.
Distributed retries and failure isolation

Retry is the most over-applied tool in this whole space, because the transport usually makes blind requeue a one-line call. The discipline is to classify failures before you retry them. A timeout to a throttled dependency is worth another attempt after a backoff; a malformed payload or a rule violation will fail identically every time, so retrying it just burns capacity and delays the moment someone notices. The diagram below shows the second half of the discipline, isolation: keeping a noisy task class on its own queue and worker pool so its retry storm cannot starve the lanes that are still healthy.

ch31.chart:
flowchart TD
  In[incoming task] --> C{classify failure}
  C -->|transient| R[retry with backoff]
  R -->|budget left| In
  R -->|budget spent| DLQ[(dead-letter queue)]
  C -->|permanent| DLQ
ch31.caption: First half: retry is a budgeted loop. A transient failure retries with backoff while budget remains; a spent budget or a permanent failure goes to the dead-letter queue.

ch31.text: The second half is the isolation discipline. Classification decides whether a task retries; isolation decides where its retries run, so one noisy class cannot starve healthy lanes:

ch31.chart:
flowchart TD
  In[incoming task] -.runs on.-> PoolA[domain A pool]
  Other[noisy task class] -.isolated to.-> PoolB[domain B pool]
ch31.caption: Second half: routing tasks of different classes onto separate worker pools keeps one retry storm contained to its own pool instead of starving the rest.

ch31.text: Result aggregation and scheduling large task graphs

Most real work is not one task; it is a small graph of tasks with dependencies. A scheduler for that graph does not run nodes in source order. It maintains a ready frontier, the set of nodes whose dependencies are all complete, and it only schedules from that frontier. When a node finishes, its outputs are folded into a running aggregate and any successors that just became unblocked join the frontier. The genuinely hard part is rarely the topological order; it is the bookkeeping around it, dependency tracking, fairness between graphs, resource quotas, and the fact that fan-in concentrates load on one reducer.

Read the diagram as a sequence of frontiers, not a static picture. The graph starts with fetch alone in the frontier. Once it completes, parse unblocks. Parsing then unblocks enrich and store together, which is where parallelism appears, and notify is the join point that must wait for both before it can run. That final join is exactly the fan-in pacing boundary the cards warn about.

ch31.chart:
flowchart TD
  fetch[fetch] --> parse[parse]
  parse --> enrich[enrich]
  parse --> store[store]
  enrich --> notify[notify]
  store --> notify
ch31.caption: A four-frontier task graph. fetch then parse run alone; enrich and store run in parallel; notify is the join point that waits for both.

ch31.text: Distributed tracing

In one process a stack trace tells you the causal chain. Across a queue there is no shared stack, so the causal chain has to be carried inside the message itself. That is why a production task envelope holds more than the business payload: it carries the identity and lineage that let an operator stitch a span in one worker to its parent in another. The struct below is the minimum useful envelope. Note that attempt and dedupe_key are not tracing fields by accident; the same metadata that makes a task traceable also makes it safe to replay.
Distributed tasks profiling

The reflex carried over from single-process work is to profile the handler, find the hot function, and optimize it. In a distributed task system that reflex usually points at the wrong thing. A task can be cheap to run and expensive to wait for, so the first number worth separating is queue wait time versus handler run time. After that, the costs that hide are the ones that only exist because work crosses a process boundary: serialization, redelivery, and the reducer that everything fans into.

A distributed task system often fails because it is profiled like an in-process function call. Queue wait, replay, serialization, and aggregation are the real cost centers more often than the task body alone.
How this lands for each background

Most engineers arrive at distributed tasks with a mental model from another language's concurrency story, and the model is usually close enough to be dangerous. The shift is the same in every case: the primitives you trusted assumed one process with one lifetime, and a task system assumes many processes that fail independently. Each card below names the specific instinct to drop and the one to put in its place.
Production patterns

These are the habits that separate a task system that survives its first incident from one that creates it. None of them are exotic; the value is in doing them before you need to, because each one is much cheaper to build in than to retrofit under load.
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

Nearly every one of these starts as a reasonable assumption carried over from single-process work. They are listed not because they are obscure but because they are easy to ship and slow to notice, surfacing only when the system is already under the load that exposes them.
The hardest distributed-task bug is often not a worker crash. It is a silently wrong recovery model: replay without idempotency, retry without a budget, or tracing without queue-age visibility.
Examples

Both examples are deliberately small enough to run in the editor, and each one models a flow we have already drawn. Read the short note and the diagram above each listing before the code, so the variables in the program map onto a shape you already recognize. Press Run first to anchor the baseline output, then change something and re-run.
Example 1: lease queue with visibility timeout and idempotent completion
One worker claims a task, misses its lease, and another worker reclaims it. The application-side completion path still makes the duplicate harmless.

What to look at: this is the lease lifecycle from the core-concepts diagram, played out between two workers. Worker A claims the task and then goes quiet, so its lease expires and the queue hands the same task to worker B. The line that matters most is the completion check: when worker B finishes, it records the completion against the task ID, and a second completion for the same ID is simply ignored. That single guard is what turns an at-least-once delivery into an exactly-once side effect. Trace the sequence below, then find each step in the code.

ch31.chart:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Q as Queue
  participant A as Worker A
  participant B as Worker B
  participant S as Completion store
  A->>Q: claim task-1 (lease starts)
  Note over A: stalls, lease expires
  Q->>B: redeliver task-1
  B->>S: record completion(task-1)
  S-->>B: first time, accepted
  A->>S: record completion(task-1)
  S-->>A: already done, ignored
ch31.caption: Worker A's lease expires and task-1 is redelivered to B. Both workers try to complete, but the completion store dedupes by task ID, so the effect happens once.

ch31.expected:
claimed = task-1
redelivered = task-1
completed = 1
duplicates ignored = true

ch31.text: The queue records one temporary ownership claim plus a deadline.
The task disappears locally until the lease expires.
A redelivery is expected behavior after lease expiry, not a surprise incident.
Completion recording makes the second finish attempt harmless.
Example 2: task-graph scheduling, result aggregation, and trace propagation
A tiny DAG scheduler runs tasks whose dependencies are complete, accumulates outputs, and keeps one trace lineage for the whole graph.

What to look at: the scheduler never iterates the nodes in declaration order. On each pass it builds the ready set, the nodes whose dependencies have all completed, runs them, folds their outputs into one aggregate, and repeats until nothing is left. Watch how the same trace ID rides along through every node so the whole run shares one lineage. The five nodes complete across the frontiers shown below; notify is the join that runs last because it depends on the parallel pair before it.

ch31.chart:
flowchart TD
  fetch[fetch] --> parse[parse]
  parse --> enrich[enrich]
  parse --> store[store]
  enrich --> notify[notify]
  store --> notify
  notify --> agg([aggregate = 31])
ch31.caption: Example 2's graph. The scheduler advances frontier by frontier; outputs fold into one aggregate, and a single trace ID spans every node.

ch31.expected:
completed = 5
aggregate = 31
final = notify
trace = trace-7

ch31.text: Only dependency-satisfied nodes enter the runnable set.
Partial outputs roll into one final aggregate under one owner.
One trace ID ties the graph together across several task boundaries.
Large graphs need fairness, quotas, and persistence beyond this tiny demo.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch31_distributed_task_execution/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to design a lease-based worker, reason about at-least-once execution with idempotency, centralize retry and DLQ policy, and trace one distributed task graph end to end.
Summary

items: Distributed task execution begins with an owned task envelope and a recovery model, not with a queue brand.
At-least-once processing is the durable default assumption; exactly-once side effects require application-level design.
Leases and visibility timeouts are crash-recovery tools whose duration is a tradeoff, not a magic number.
Retries, DLQs, and failure isolation belong in one explicit control plane instead of being copied into each handler.
Result aggregation, task-graph scheduling, distributed tracing, and profiling all need their own visible budgets and metrics.

ch32.text: A cluster job is not one program running faster. It is dozens or thousands of separate processes, on separate machines, agreeing on when to exchange data. This chapter is about writing the Rust half of that agreement: partitioning work into flat buffers, choosing collective operations that match the exchange you actually need, and keeping the cost of communication visible instead of buried.
Builds on Chapters 12, 22, 26, and 31

Chapter 12 established dense layout and matrix views. Chapter 22 separated processes, threads, and thread-safety inside one address space. Chapter 26 compared waiting-heavy orchestration with CPU pools. Chapter 31 showed that once work crosses process boundaries, recovery and replay matter. MPI sits across all four.
Opening scenario

A scientific simulation that already runs on a cluster is being ported to Rust. The team wants to keep everything that works about the existing setup: the MPI launch model, the scheduler that places one rank per socket, and the per-rank threading that fills each socket with local CPU work. What they want from Rust is the part that has been fragile in the old code base, namely confidence about which buffer is owned by which rank and which thread, so that a layout mistake fails at compile time rather than as a silent wrong answer at scale.

That goal turns into four concrete commitments, and the rest of the chapter is really an expansion of them. Partition the data into flat, contiguous buffers so a rank’s share is a slice, not a graph. Use collective operations when the whole group participates in one structured exchange, and reserve point-to-point messages for the irregular cases. Keep general-purpose serialization off the hot numeric paths, where a flat typed buffer is both faster and easier to reason about. And measure communication separately from computation, because at cluster scale the time a job spends waiting in collectives is usually the number that decides whether it scales.
A practical decision order

items: Choose the data layout before choosing the abstraction vocabulary.
Choose the partition function before tuning the collective pattern.
Choose process count and per-rank thread count together, not independently.
Profile communication, packing, and imbalance before blaming the arithmetic kernel.

ch32.text: Mental model

The single most useful idea to hold onto is that an MPI program has two completely different boundaries stacked on top of each other, and they obey different rules. The outer boundary is between ranks. A rank is a full operating-system process with its own address space, so nothing inside it is reachable from another rank except through data you explicitly send. The inner boundary is between threads inside one rank. There the familiar Rust concurrency model applies unchanged: shared references, Send, Sync, channels, and locks all mean what they mean everywhere else. The diagram below is the shape worth memorizing before reading any further.

ch32.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Cluster
    subgraph Node0["Node 0"]
      R0["Rank 0 process"]
      R1["Rank 1 process"]
    end
    subgraph Node1["Node 1"]
      R2["Rank 2 process"]
      R3["Rank 3 process"]
    end
  end
  R0 -. MPI messages .- R1
  R1 -. MPI messages .- R2
  R2 -. MPI messages .- R3
  R0 --> T0["threads + owned slice"]
  R3 --> T3["threads + owned slice"]
ch32.caption: Two boundaries: explicit messages between ranks (processes), ordinary Rust ownership between threads inside a rank.

ch32.text: Core concepts
The three nouns every MPI program starts from

MPI has a large API surface, but almost everything is built from three ideas. A communicator is the group of processes that are allowed to talk to each other. A rank is one process’s integer index inside that group. The size is how many ranks the group has. Every partition decision in this chapter is just arithmetic on a rank and a size: rank 1 of 3 takes this slice, rank 2 of 3 takes the next one. The cards below name the building blocks, and the snippet after them is the opening of essentially every MPI program written with the Rust mpi crate.
What to read for: initialize() hands back a universe whose lifetime is the MPI session, and rank and size are the two numbers the rest of your code branches on.
Why ranks and threads are not the same tool

This is the distinction that most often trips up engineers arriving from a shared-memory background. Both ranks and threads give you parallelism, so it is tempting to treat them interchangeably, but they solve different problems and fail in different ways. Ranks give you more memory and more machines at the price of having to move every shared byte explicitly. Threads give you cheap sharing at the price of having to reason about exclusive mutation. A real cluster job almost always uses both, and the skill is keeping clear about which one you are reaching for in any given line.
Message passing at HPC scale

At small scale, many communication patterns look cheap enough to ignore. At cluster scale, collective count, message size, synchronization frequency, and packing cost often dominate. A barrier inside a hot loop is not a style choice. It is a global pacing decision across every rank.

This is one reason Rust fits HPC work well. Once the buffers and ownership are explicit, the remaining questions are the same ones HPC engineers already ask: what is contiguous, what is copied, and which ranks are waiting for which other ranks?
Choosing a Rust MPI crate

Rust does not ship its own MPI implementation, and it should not. MPI is a standard with several mature implementations (Open MPI, MPICH, and vendor variants) that are tuned for specific interconnects and already installed on the cluster. A Rust crate is a binding to whichever one is present, not a replacement for it. That framing matters because it tells you where your real dependency lives: not in Cargo.toml, but in the system library and launcher your job will actually link and run against.
Keep crate choice subordinate to system choice. The real dependencies are the installed MPI runtime, the launcher, the scheduler, and the fabric assumptions on the cluster.
Why flat buffers win in MPI

Data layout is the decision that quietly determines how hard everything else will be. MPI sends operate on contiguous regions described by a starting pointer and a count, and so do the caches and the FFI boundary into the system MPI library. A flat row-major buffer satisfies all three at once: a rank’s rows are a single slice, the send is one range, and the CPU walks memory in order. The moment you reach for a nested structure such as a vector of vectors, you trade that single predictable buffer for many scattered allocations, and every collective and every FFI call now has to reassemble what should have stayed contiguous. The rules below are how to stay on the easy path.
The arithmetic that makes this work is one line: a cell’s position in the flat buffer is row * cols + col, so a rank’s row range maps to a cell range by multiplying both ends by cols.
When to serialize and when not to

Rust’s serialization story is excellent, and that is exactly why it is worth saying clearly where it does not belong. A dense numeric exchange (an allreduce over a million doubles, repeated every iteration) should move as raw f64 bytes, because the data already has a fixed shape and any envelope is pure overhead on the hottest path in the program. A control message that says "reconfigure to this topology" runs once and benefits from a real schema. The guideline below is just that split made explicit: match the ceremony of the payload to how often it crosses the wire.
A useful rule is simple: the hotter the collective, the less general the payload should be. Dense numeric exchange wants flat typed buffers. Rich envelopes belong on colder control paths.
Collective operations and the shapes they make

A collective is a single operation that every rank in a communicator calls together. The payoff over hand-rolled sends and receives is twofold: far less boilerplate, and a synchronization contract the MPI implementation can optimize as a whole (often using tree or ring algorithms you would not want to write by hand). The trick to choosing among them is to picture the direction the data flows. Broadcast pushes one buffer out to everyone; scatter splits one buffer into pieces; gather collects pieces back; reduce folds them into one value at the root; allreduce folds them and hands the result back to everyone. The diagram makes those four shapes concrete.

ch32.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Broadcast
    B0["root"] --> B1["rank 1"]
    B0 --> B2["rank 2"]
    B0 --> B3["rank 3"]
  end
  subgraph Scatter
    S0["root buffer"] --> S1["chunk 1"]
    S0 --> S2["chunk 2"]
    S0 --> S3["chunk 3"]
  end
ch32.caption: Fan-out collectives: broadcast pushes one buffer to everyone, scatter splits one buffer into per-rank pieces.

ch32.text: The other two shapes run in the opposite direction, collecting data back toward the root:

ch32.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Gather
    G1["local 1"] --> G0["root buffer"]
    G2["local 2"] --> G0
    G3["local 3"] --> G0
  end
  subgraph Allreduce
    A1["partial"] --> AS["sum"]
    A2["partial"] --> AS
    A3["partial"] --> AS
    AS --> AB["every rank"]
  end
ch32.caption: Fan-in collectives: gather collects pieces back to the root, allreduce folds them then redistributes the result to every rank.

ch32.text: Combining MPI ranks with per-rank threads

The dominant production layout is not "one rank per core." It is one rank per socket or per NUMA domain, with each rank running a thread pool (Rayon, or plain threads) across the cores it owns. The reasoning is economic: crossing the network is expensive, so you want as few ranks as the memory budget allows, and you fill each rank’s cores with cheap shared-memory parallelism. This gives you two ownership layers to keep straight. Between ranks, ownership moves by message. Inside a rank, ownership is the ordinary Rust story of owned chunks and scoped borrowed slices handed to the pool. The one configuration mistake that wrecks this is oversubscription: if every rank spawns a full machine’s worth of threads, the node thrashes on context switches instead of computing.
Where the time actually goes

The instinct from single-process work is to profile the arithmetic kernel, and in HPC that instinct is frequently wrong. A collective is a barrier: it does not complete until the slowest rank arrives. So when a profiler shows ranks blocked in an allreduce, that time is usually not the cost of the reduction itself, it is the cost of one rank having more work to do than the others. The first question to ask of a slow cluster job is therefore not "which line is hot" but "are all the ranks finishing their local work at the same time." Measure compute, packing, and time-blocked-in-collectives as three separate numbers, and look at load imbalance before you touch the math.
What the cluster environment demands

A surprising share of failed cluster jobs have nothing to do with the algorithm and everything to do with the environment the job runs in. The binary must link against the same MPI family it launches against, the launcher and scheduler have to agree on how many ranks go where, and logging has to survive the fact that there are now many processes producing output at once. None of this is exotic, but it is easy to leave implicit until the first run at scale fails in a way that single-machine testing never reproduced. The cards below name the assumptions worth writing down before launch day.
How to think about this coming from another language

MPI predates Rust by decades and exists in C, C++, Fortran, and Python, so most readers arrive with some prior model of either MPI or of parallelism in their home language. The useful question is not "what is the Rust API for X" but "what mental habit do I need to drop." Each card below is one such shift, not a library cheat sheet.
Production patterns
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The hardest MPI performance bug is often not one slow instruction. It is one wrong boundary: too many collectives, the wrong layout, one rank doing more work, or one node running too many local threads.
Examples
Example 1: block partitioning for dense row-major work

This is the partition math every MPI rank runs before it touches any data. In a real program rank and size come from the communicator; here they are constants so the example runs standalone. The function is identical either way.

What to look at: block_range turns the pair (rank, size) into a half-open row range, handing one extra row to each of the first few ranks so the eight rows split as 3, 3, 2 instead of leaving a remainder stranded. Then local_sum converts that row range into a cell range by multiplying by cols and sums only that slice. Follow the data through the three boxes below before reading the code.

ch32.chart:
flowchart TD
  IN["rows=8, ranks=3, rank=1"] --> BR["block_range"]
  BR --> P["range 3..6 (3 rows)"]
  P --> CELLS["cells 9..18 = range x cols"]
  CELLS --> SUM["local_sum over slice"]
  SUM --> OUT["subtotal = 126.0"]
ch32.caption: Rank and size in, a contiguous row range out, then a slice sum on only this rank's rows.

ch32.text: Extra rows are distributed to the first ranks so the load stays balanced when the row count is not divisible evenly.
One flat buffer plus one row-major offset keeps both cache behavior and MPI send ranges simple.
The repository example file shows the same idea with real `mpi` crate calls and an allreduce.
Example 2: counts, displacements, and collective-friendly layout

A scatter or gather needs two parallel tables: how many elements go to each rank, and at what offset each rank’s slice begins. Most scatter and gather bugs are simply one of these tables computed in the wrong unit. The discipline is to keep counts in the unit the algorithm thinks in (rows) and convert to the unit the collective wants (cells) at exactly one place.

What to look at: row_counts answers the load question in rows (10 rows over 3 ranks becomes 4, 3, 3). Then displacements_in_cells walks those counts once, multiplying by cols to produce the per-rank starting offset a real scatter would consume. The final allreduce is a separate fan-in that hands every rank the same total. The diagram traces those two tables and the reduction.

ch32.chart:
flowchart TD
  RC["row_counts: 4, 3, 3"] --> D["displacements_in_cells (x cols)"]
  D --> DI["offsets: 0, 16, 28"]
  DI --> SC["scatter slices to ranks"]
  SC --> LC["each rank computes a partial"]
  LC --> AR["allreduce sum"]
  AR --> ALL["same total on every rank"]
ch32.caption: Counts in rows, displacements in cells, then a scatter feeds local work that an allreduce folds back together.

ch32.text: Row counts answer the load question first.
Collective APIs often want offsets in typed elements, not in rows.
Every rank can receive the same final scalar when the next phase needs it locally.
Keep the hot numeric path flat and typed; send richer metadata elsewhere.

The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch32_mpi_and_high_performance_computing/ including real `mpi` crate examples for row partitioning, collective planning, and hybrid MPI plus Rayon execution.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to partition matrix rows across ranks, choose flat layouts for collectives, profile a communication-heavy workload conceptually, and decide where hybrid MPI plus threads is worth the extra complexity.
Summary

items: MPI is process-based message passing, so cross-rank ownership is always a buffer or protocol boundary.
Processes and threads solve different problems. Hybrid MPI plus threads is common, but the two levels should stay conceptually separate.
Rust MPI work is usually easiest when dense payloads stay flat, contiguous, and explicit about layout.
Serialization for hot numeric collectives should stay minimal; richer envelopes belong on colder orchestration paths.
Collective choice, queueing inside ranks, thread budgets, and cluster build assumptions are all part of the production design.
Profile communication, packing, and imbalance before blaming the arithmetic kernel or the language.

ch33.text: Performance work starts with allocation, data movement, cache behavior, and measurement. This chapter turns Rust optimization into a repeatable review process tied to workload evidence.
Builds on Chapters 10, 18, 22, 27, and 32

Chapter 10 covered arrays, slices, and vectors as layout choices. Chapter 18 covered generics and monomorphization. Chapter 22 covered multithreading costs and ownership across workers. Chapter 27 covered IO and batching. Chapter 32 covered flat buffers and communication-heavy HPC thinking. This chapter turns those threads into a practical Rust performance model.
Opening scenario

A request-processing service regressed after a refactor that was meant to improve readability. p99 latency climbed, heap traffic rose, and queue wait that had been invisible became a line on the dashboard. Nobody changed an algorithm; the team changed where data was owned and copied, and the cost showed up downstream. The job now is not to guess. It is to rebuild the cost model deliberately, measuring allocation, data movement, layout, dispatch, synchronization, and live production latency before touching any lower-level code.

That last clause is the whole chapter. The fastest way to waste a week is to start by rewriting the inner loop. The reliable path is to ask the questions in order, let each one rule out a class of explanation, and only descend to instruction-level work once the evidence points there. The diagram below is the order; the sections after it explain each box.

ch33.chart:
flowchart TD
  A[State workload and metric] --> B[Count allocations, copies, layout, sync]
  B --> C[Benchmark alternatives in release mode]
  C --> D[Profile the slow variant]
  D --> E[Confirm with traces and production metrics]
  E -->|matters in prod| F[Change lower-level code]
  E -->|does not matter| G[Stop: the hot path was elsewhere]
ch33.caption: The performance review runs top to bottom. Each step can end the investigation before you reach the code.

ch33.text: The review order, in words

items: State the workload and the metric first, so every later number has a question it answers.
Count allocations, copies, cache-unfriendly layout, and synchronization boundaries by reading the code.
Benchmark the alternatives in release mode, never in debug.
Profile the slow one to learn where the time actually goes, then confirm the live system with traces and production metrics.

ch33.text: Mental model

Before any technique, fix the frame. Rust does not make programs fast; it removes whole categories of accidental cost and then hands you a clear view of the cost that remains. The phrase “zero-cost abstraction” is often misread as “zero work.” It means the opposite of free: it means an abstraction does not add overhead beyond the hand-written equivalent, so the real work is still entirely present and still entirely yours to manage. The three ideas below are the lens for the rest of the chapter.
Core concepts
The four costs worth tracking

Almost every Rust performance problem reduces to one of four costs. Keeping the list short is the point: when latency regresses, you walk these four in order and ask which one the change touched. Most regressions announce themselves here long before you need a profiler.
Allocation awareness

Allocation is the cost most engineers underestimate because no single call looks expensive. The damage is cumulative: a per-request String here, a clone() there, a Vec that grows by reallocating instead of being sized once, and suddenly the allocator is on your hot path and your tail latency depends on it. The practical moves are unglamorous and they pay reliably.

A useful correction for senior engineers is this: ownership clarity and performance clarity often improve together. The cleanest API shape frequently allocates less because the borrow or owned boundary is now explicit instead of accidental.
Cache locality and branch prediction

Two data shapes can hold identical values and run at very different speeds. The difference is what the hardware sees while it walks them. A single flat allocation lets the prefetcher pull the next cache line before you ask for it; a structure made of many small allocations forces the CPU to chase a pointer, stall on the load, then chase the next one. The diagram below is the same data in both shapes — this is the picture to keep in mind whenever you reach for a nested collection.

ch33.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Flat["flat Vec: one allocation"]
    direction LR
    F0[a] --> F1[b] --> F2[c] --> F3[d]
  end
  Flat -.prefetcher friendly.-> Fast((fast scan))
ch33.caption: Flat layout: one allocation, values adjacent, the prefetcher pulls the next line ahead of you.

ch33.text: The same values stored as a graph of small allocations look very different to the hardware:

ch33.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Nested["Vec of boxes: many allocations"]
    direction LR
    H[handles] --> P0[ptr] --> B0[a]
    H --> P1[ptr] --> B1[b]
    H --> P2[ptr] --> B2[c]
  end
  Nested -.pointer chasing.-> Slow((cache misses))
ch33.caption: Boxed layout: each element is a separate allocation, so the CPU stalls chasing one pointer after another.

ch33.text: Static dispatch and inlining

Generics and trait objects are the two ways Rust calls behavior you do not know concretely at the call site, and they sit at opposite ends of the cost spectrum. A generic function is monomorphized: the compiler stamps out a separate copy per concrete type, so each copy sees an exact call target it can inline and optimize through. A dyn Trait value carries a pointer to a vtable, and the call goes through that pointer, which the optimizer usually cannot see past. The diagram shows where the indirection lives.

ch33.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Static["Generic: monomorphized"]
    GC[call site] --> GT[concrete fn body]
    GT --> GI[inline and specialize]
  end
ch33.caption: Static dispatch: the call site sees the concrete body, so the optimizer can inline and specialize through it.

ch33.text: Dynamic dispatch puts a vtable on the same path, and the indirection is where the optimizer loses sight of the target:

ch33.chart:
flowchart TD
  subgraph Dynamic["dyn Trait: vtable"]
    DC[call site] --> DV[vtable pointer]
    DV --> DF[indirect call]
    DF --> DB[opaque to optimizer]
  end
ch33.caption: Dynamic dispatch: the call routes through a vtable pointer the optimizer usually cannot follow past.

ch33.text: Iterator performance, bounds checks, and unnecessary clones

There is a persistent folklore that iterator chains are slow and hand-written index loops are fast. The truth is closer to the reverse, and the reason is bounds checks. When you index a slice manually with a data-dependent index, the compiler must insert a check that the index is in range, because it cannot prove otherwise. When you iterate — over a slice, over chunks, over windows — the range is encoded in the iterator itself, so the check is provably unnecessary and the compiler removes it. The honest answer is always to read the generated code, but the default instinct should be: express the loop in terms of slices and let the compiler discharge the proof for you.
Picking the right measuring tool

The four tools below are not a hierarchy where one replaces the others; they answer four different questions, and a confident answer from the wrong tool is how teams optimize code that was never on the critical path. Match the tool to the question first. The diagram is that mapping; the cards explain each one.

ch33.chart:
flowchart TD
  Q1[Which variant is faster?] --> Bench[Benchmark]
  Q2[Where does the time go?] --> Prof[Profile]
ch33.caption: Comparing alternatives is a benchmark question; finding where the time goes is a profiling question.

ch33.text: The other two questions are about timeline and real load, and they map to two more tools:

ch33.chart:
flowchart TD
  Q3[What happened, and when?] --> Trace[Trace]
  Q4[Does it matter in prod?] --> Obs[Observability]
ch33.caption: Reconstructing a timeline is a tracing question; whether it matters under real load is an observability question.

ch33.text: Do not claim a speedup without workload context. A cleaner benchmark is not a substitute for profiling, and a flatter profile is not a substitute for production latency or throughput data.
Release builds and compiler flags

Measure performance in release mode. Debug builds are for fast iteration and diagnostics, not for trustworthy throughput or latency numbers. The first repair for “Rust is slow” is often simply --release.
Release profile settings are workload tradeoffs. More optimization or LTO may help hot binaries, but it also affects compile time, binary size, and sometimes panic behavior.
How performance thinking shifts by background

Senior engineers do not arrive at Rust as blank slates. The useful question is not which crate replaces which library; it is which of your instincts still hold and which one quietly leads you wrong. Each card names the mental-model shift for one background.
Production patterns

These are the habits that keep a service fast without a heroics phase. None of them is a micro-optimization; each one shapes the data and the API so the expensive cost is paid once, at a boundary you chose, instead of silently on every request.
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

Each of these is a true story that started with a reasonable-sounding sentence. The common thread is declaring victory from one number while a different number quietly got worse, or reaching for a lower-level change before the evidence pointed there.
The most common performance mistake in senior Rust code is not “using iterators.” It is skipping the step where the team states what is actually expensive and how that expense will be measured.
Examples

Both examples are small on purpose. Each one is a single design decision from the sections above, made concrete and runnable. Read the flow diagram first, then the code, then press Run and confirm the output before changing anything — the point is to see the cost decision in the signature, not just to watch it print.
Example 1: allocation-aware filtering without route clones
The function preallocates once, borrows route labels from the input slice, and keeps the hot path allocation-light.

What to look at: the return type is Vec<&str>, not Vec<String>. The function never copies a route; it borrows each label out of the input and hands back views that live exactly as long as the input slice. The one allocation in the whole function is the result vector, and Vec::with_capacity sizes it once up front so the push loop never reallocates. The flow is: size the buffer, then for each request keep or skip on a single threshold test.

ch33.chart:
flowchart TD
  In[requests slice] --> Cap[with_capacity once]
  Cap --> Loop{bytes over threshold}
  Loop -->|yes| Push[push borrowed route]
  Loop -->|no| Skip[skip]
  Push --> Out[vec of borrowed routes]
  Skip --> Out
ch33.caption: One allocation for the result, borrowed labels throughout, one branch per request.

ch33.text: `Vec::with_capacity` makes the result budget visible instead of relying on repeated growth.
The output stores `&str` views because the result only needs to live as long as the input slice.
The loop does one clear threshold test and pushes only on the hot predicate.
Example 2: row-major scanning for predictable locality
The grid stays flat and contiguous. Row sums are derived with chunked iteration instead of nested owners or scattered indexing.

What to look at: the grid is one Vec<u32>, not a Vec<Vec<u32>>. The rows are not separate allocations; they are slices carved out of the same flat buffer by chunks(self.cols). That single choice is what keeps the scan contiguous and lets the compiler drop bounds checks, because the chunk width proves the row boundary instead of a hand-written index. The flow is: take the flat buffer, split it into row-width chunks, sum each chunk.

ch33.chart:
flowchart TD
  Flat[flat Vec, rows*cols] --> Chunk[chunks of cols]
  Chunk --> R0[row 0 slice]
  Chunk --> R1[row 1 slice]
  R0 --> S0[sum row 0]
  R1 --> S1[sum row 1]
  S0 --> Out[Vec of row sums]
  S1 --> Out
ch33.caption: One contiguous buffer, sliced into rows by width. No nested allocation, no manual index proof.

ch33.text: One flat buffer plus `chunks(self.cols)` keeps row traversal predictable for the CPU.
The iterator is working with exact slices, which is often easier to optimize than ad hoc indexing.
Chunking expresses the row boundary structurally instead of relying on a manual index proof.
The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch33_performance_oriented_rust/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
Exercises

The companion exercise page asks you to build a benchmark plan for allocation-heavy code, refactor storage for better locality, compare iterator and loop implementations responsibly, and separate benchmarking from profiling, tracing, and production observability.
