The key idea in the next listing is that submit_to_dma takes the slot by value. Once you call it, you no longer have the slot, so the compiler will reject any attempt to read or write that buffer while the transfer is in flight. The peripheral conceptually owns the memory until it signals completion and the handle is returned. The diagram shows that round trip of authority first, so the by-value parameter reads as deliberate rather than incidental.

ch56.chart:
stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> CpuOwns: slot allocated CpuOwns --> DmaOwns: submit_to_dma(slot)
(slot moved by value) DmaOwns --> DmaOwns: transfer in flight
CPU cannot touch buffer DmaOwns --> CpuOwns: completion irq
handle returned CpuOwns --> [*]: slot freed
ch56.caption: The slot handle is the authority token. While DMA owns it, the borrow checker forbids any CPU access to the buffer.

ch56.text: Here the entire unsafe footprint is two one-line functions. Wrapping the raw pointer in a Register type means the rest of the driver works with a safe API, and any audit of MMIO correctness reduces to reviewing these two reads and writes plus the validity of the address that produced the pointer.
Embedded Rust layering: PAC, HAL, BSP, RTIC or Embassy-style execution, interrupts, and critical sections

Interrupt safety usually combines ownership discipline with either atomics or a critical-section model. Do not assume a `Mutex` from std exists, and do not assume an interrupt boundary behaves like a thread boundary.
FFI and ABI boundaries for `no_std` code: C, C++, kernels, hypervisors, and wasm hosts
Keep panic and allocation policy explicit at the ABI seam. A freestanding or host-constrained caller cannot safely consume an implicit unwind or an unexpected heap contract.
Testing, simulation, debugging, fuzzing, and profiling `no_std` crates from a host-side std environment
Safety boundaries: unsafe, atomics, MMIO, interrupt concurrency, panic handlers, and audit checklists

items: State the invariant before the unsafe block: valid register address, valid buffer slot, or valid FFI pointer contract.
Use atomics only when the target supports them and the interrupt or multi-core memory model is actually understood.
Never treat memory-mapped registers like normal Rust references with ordinary aliasing and optimization rules.
Keep panic behavior explicit: abort, custom panic handler, or host-defined trap semantics.
Audit custom allocators, linker scripts, startup objects, and boundary layout attributes as part of the release surface.

ch56.text: Production tradeoffs: portability, specialization, observability, binary size, linker scripts, and release engineering
Comparison callout
Production patterns
Keep the smallest cross-target logic in `core`, then add `alloc` or `std` at explicit adapter boundaries instead of letting the runtime surface spread inward accidentally.
Prefer fixed-capacity or fallible-memory paths where bounds are real, and make buffer ownership transfer explicit for peripherals, DMA, or host ABI handoff.
Separate host-side tests from target-specific tests so the portable logic stays fast to validate even when device or guest runtime harnesses are slower.
Treat linker scripts, panic mode, startup, allocator choice, and target runners as part of the release contract, not only as build-system trivia.
Pitfalls and tradeoffs

The common senior mistake is not unsafe syntax. It is an unspoken runtime assumption: assuming an allocator, assuming logs exist, assuming unwind exists, or assuming one dependency will behave the same across all targets.
Examples
Example 1: a portable crate surface split across core, alloc, and std
The smallest API stays slice-based. Owned helpers are alloc-gated. Host diagnostics stay std-gated. This is the shape to prefer before a library accidentally commits to a wider runtime than it needs.

ch56.expected:
portable modes = core|alloc|std
checksum = 6
alloc-gated api = encode_frame

ch56.text: `checksum` depends only on slices and integers, so it stays portable across firmware, wasm, kernels, and servers.
`encode_frame` is an owned convenience API, not the baseline contract every target must support.
Host formatting or IO belongs at the edge so constrained targets do not inherit it accidentally.
Example 2: fixed-capacity buffer ownership with a DMA-style slot handle
This example uses no heap at all. Allocation is fallible, slots are explicit, and release is visible. That is often calmer than pretending a constrained runtime can always grow another queue.
Capacity is part of the type, not a loose operational hope.
Option<SlotId> makes exhaustion explicit and easy to test under load or device stress.
The slot handle is the authority token. That is the same pattern many DMA, queue, and driver APIs want.

The repository also includes standalone Rust source under examples/ch56_no_std_rust_constrained_runtime_derivatives/ so the chapter examples can be reviewed as ordinary files outside the in-browser editor.
